rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Jagdish Prasad Agrawal v. Union of India** addressed the legality of **blocking Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. The petitioner, a partnership firm, had challenged the blocking of its **IGST ITC**, including a **negative balance**, and sought a declaration that the blocking was illegal and void, plus restoration/re-credit of any ITC that had been unlawfully adjusted against the demand. By the time of hearing, the respondents conceded that the **Electronic Credit Ledger had already become operational again**, because the blocking had **ceased by operation of law after one year**, so the live dispute was whether the original blocking was valid.

The Court focused on the procedural safeguards under **Rule 86A**, and the respondents were **unable to show that those mandatory requirements had been followed before the ITC was blocked**. They admitted the omission was a **bona fide mistake** and also acknowledged that, although the authority may have had reasons to act, **no proper reasoned order** had been passed and **no opportunity of hearing** had been given to the petitioner before the credit was blocked. In substance, the ruling underscores that ITC blocking under Rule 86A cannot be done informally or mechanically: the department must comply with the rule’s mandatory preconditions and record proper reasons before restricting a taxpayer’s Electronic Credit Ledger.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **ITC blocking under Rule 86A is not self-executing or discretionary without process**; the department must be able to justify the action through **documented, reasoned decision-making**, and the measure is **time-limited, expiring after one year**. The case confirms that where blocking is imposed without following Rule 86A safeguards, the action is vulnerable to challenge, and taxpayers may seek restoration of credit and related relief. The respondents’ statement that any future blocking would be done properly indicates that the Court viewed compliance with Rule 86A’s procedure as essential, not optional.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The company was a 100% export-oriented service provider supplying Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements and exporting those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed a refund under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, but the department rejected ₹78,79,939 of the claim on the theory that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services did not have a nexus with the exported output services.

The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that taking CENVAT credit, using it, and seeking refund are separate issues, and held that where the department had not first challenged the credit’s availment under Rule 14, it could not later deny the Rule 5 refund by re-litigating eligibility of the underlying credit. It also accepted the broader argument that the disputed services could qualify as “input service” under Rule 2(l), and that a strict direct nexus with the exported output service was not required in the manner applied by the lower authority. As a result, the refund denial was set aside and the appeal was allowed, confirming that export-oriented service providers cannot be denied Rule 5 refunds merely by questioning, at the refund stage, credits that were never separately disallowed or recovered under Rule 14.

Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad, in **Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise**, set aside Service Tax demands, interest, and penalties raised by the department in an **Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014** for **2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012**. The case involved two principal allegations: first, that charges deducted by **foreign/intermediary banks** while export proceeds were remitted from overseas buyers constituted taxable **“Banking and Other Financial Services”** received by the exporter under the **reverse charge mechanism**; and second, that payments made for overseas regulatory approval-related support allegedly amounted to **“Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.”**

On the banking issue, the Tribunal held that **mere reduction in export realization because foreign banks deducted charges does not, by itself, make the exporter the recipient of banking services**. The department had argued that because the appellant ultimately received a net amount after deductions, it must have received and paid for banking services; the Tribunal rejected this as insufficient. It emphasized that there was **no evidence of any contract, engagement, or obligation by Aurobindo Pharma to pay the foreign banks for services rendered to it**, and therefore no service provider–service recipient relationship could be established.

The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier favorable precedent, **Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020**, to support its conclusion that such bank deductions in export transactions are not automatically taxable on the exporter. As a result, the demand raised on that basis was not sustainable.

On the second issue, the Tribunal held that **services related to obtaining foreign regulatory approvals for pharma products do not fall under “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” merely because they involve technical or expert assistance**. The ruling indicates that compliance, documentation, and approval-support services for overseas pharmaceutical regulatory processes were wrongly classified by the department under that taxable category for the relevant period. The consequence for compliance teams is that, for the period covered by the case, **export-related bank deduction charges and pharma regulatory approval support services were not treated as taxable service receipts on the facts found by the Tribunal**, and the associated **tax, interest, and penalties were set aside**.

The defence completely denied involvement. It admitted that Rajendra Bane was on leave and at his native place on the relevant day, but contended that the seizure had actually followed information transmitted by him to the Superintendent on duty at Pune International Airport. The defence claimed that the information involved privileged communication with an informer and therefore its source could not be disclosed. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected this explanation. He considered the statement
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai decision in **Ranjita Rajendra Bane v. Commissioner of Customs** sets aside personal penalties imposed on the deceased customs officer’s legal representative because the department failed to prove any actionable role by the officer in the smuggling operation. The case arose from the recovery of smuggled gold from the **gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport** after passengers arrived from **Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52 on 16.08.2018**; the department alleged that **Rajendra Bane, then a Customs Hawaldar**, had facilitated the offense even though he was on **sanctioned leave** and at his native place near Ratnagiri. The original adjudication had imposed penalties of **₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962**, relying mainly on **Section 108 statements**, statements of co-accused/accomplices, **telephone call records**, and the recovery of gold from the airport and a passenger.  

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the Tribunal found the evidence too weak to sustain a penalty: the officer’s alleged involvement was not established by any direct material, and the defense version—that he had actually informed the Superintendent on duty at the airport about the suspected activity and that the source was protected as confidential informer communication—was not properly disproved. The Commissioner (Appeals) had rejected this explanation, but the Tribunal held that suspicion and derivative statements were insufficient to fasten personal liability under **Section 112(a)** without proof of active participation, aiding, or knowledge. The practical compliance takeaway is that penalties against customs personnel or other individuals alleged to have assisted smuggling must be supported by concrete, corroborated evidence of involvement; mere association, call records, or untested statements from co-accused will not necessarily be enough to survive appellate scrutiny. No new filing deadline, regulatory change, or prospective procedural requirement is announced in this case; it is a fact-specific appellate ruling on the evidentiary threshold for imposing customs penalties.

rows.summary:
The Patna High Court dealt with a GST dispute involving M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered taxpayer that performs Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness programmes, mainly on assignments from government departments. For financial year 2022-23, the department issued a notice under Section 73 of the CGST Act based on gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100 received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya, and the adjudicating authority later confirmed tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452 by order dated 20.08.2025. The petitioner appealed under Section 107(1), but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on 28.02.2026 solely because it was filed 21 days late.

The petitioner argued that a later Collectorate, Gaya memo dated 28.11.2025 (Memo No. 322) clarified that GST was not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak, and that Nukkad Natak teams consisting of 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from the GST regime. In substance, the petitioner was asking the High Court to consider whether the exemption/clarification defeated the tax demand, rather than letting the case end on a procedural delay in appeal. The High Court did not decide the GST exemption merits itself; instead, it remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority for reconsideration, so the appeal issue was sent back for fresh handling in light of the later memo and the taxpayer’s arguments. For compliance purposes, the case highlights that GST exposure was asserted on government-linked Nukkad Natak receipts, that the disputed demand covered tax, interest, and penalty of Rs. 1,63,452, and that the procedural issue was a 21-day appeal delay, but the ultimate exemption question remains to be determined by the appellate forum.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12609 Case Name N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GSTAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); N. R. Builders Vs Commissioner of commercial taxes (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, allowed the appeal of M/s. N. R. Builders by way of remand in a dispute concerning alleged excess Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502/- for Financial Year 2018–19. The disputed amount comprised CGST of ₹1,16,751/- and SGST of ₹1,16,751/-. Interest of ₹2,03,730/- and penalty of ₹23,350/- had also been imposed, resulting in a total demand of ₹4,60,582/-. The Appellant, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, contended that the apparent mismatch between FORM GSTR-3B and FORM GSTR-2A did not represent excess ITC. According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). The Appellant also challenged the proceedings on the ground that no personal hearing was granted and that no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 had preceded the proceedings. A pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A was issued on 22.01.2024, followed by a Show Cause Notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73. The Show Cause Notice itself recorded the date, time and venue of personal hearing as “NA”. The Proper Officer subsequently confirmed the entire demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand. The Tribunal first considered whether the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference could be treated as inadmissible ITC without examining the Appellant’s explanation concerning Financial Year 2017–18 invoices.
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the matter back for fresh verification in a case involving alleged excess input tax credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502 for financial year 2018–19. The disputed credit comprised ₹1,16,751 CGST and ₹1,16,751 SGST, and the department had also levied interest of ₹2,03,730 and penalty of ₹23,350, taking the total demand to ₹4,60,582. The taxpayer, M/s. N. R. Builders, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, argued that the apparent mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A was not wrongful ITC but credit on invoices pertaining to FY 2017–18 that was availed in FY 2018–19 within the time allowed under Section 16(4).  

On procedure, the taxpayer challenged the demand because no personal hearing was actually granted and no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 preceded the proceedings; the record instead showed a pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A dated 22.01.2024, followed by a show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 issued under Section 73. The show cause notice itself recorded the date, time, and venue of personal hearing as “NA,” and the proper officer then confirmed the demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority upheld that confirmation, but the Tribunal found that the lower authorities had not adequately examined the taxpayer’s explanation that the credit related to earlier-year invoices and therefore could have been admissible within the statutory time limit.  

The practical compliance outcome is that a GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch, by itself, was not treated as conclusive proof of inadmissible ITC in this case; the matter must be re-verified with reference to invoice dates and the Section 16(4) timing rules before disallowing credit and imposing consequential tax, interest, and penalty. The order also highlights that where the show cause notice does not provide an actual hearing opportunity and the case is decided ex parte, the taxpayer can successfully press for remand on procedural fairness grounds.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative and Judicial Developments – Period covered: September 2025 to September 2026 Summary: The period from September 2025 to September 2026 witnessed substantial changes in India’s GST framework across legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies and judicial interpretation. The Finance Act, 2026 amended provisions governing post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds and appellate arrangements, while omitting Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act concerning intermediary services. Commencement differs across provisions, and the amendments to Sections 15, 34 and 54 of the CGST Act await notification. Rate rationalisation was completed through the withdrawal of compensation cess and migration of specified tobacco and pan masala products to the 40 per cent slab. Risk-based provisional refunds were expanded, GSTAT benches became operational and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals. The return architecture increasingly requires verification and reconciliation before filing, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and the Invoice Management System. Judicial developments clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, statutory timelines for detention orders and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. With the 57th GST Council meeting scheduled for 12 September 2026, further proposals concerning ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds and small-business compliance remain under consideration but cannot be treated as operative law until formally implemented. The twelve months preceding the 57th meeting of the GST Council have produced the densest concentration of change since the levy was introduced in July 2017. Three distinct layers moved at once. The rate architecture recommended by the 56th Council was completed with the withdrawal of compensation cess and the migration of tobacco and pan mas
rows.summary:
The document reviews GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and says this was a high-change period spanning legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies, and case law. The Finance Act, 2026 amended the rules on post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds, and appellate arrangements, and it also omitted section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, which had dealt with intermediary services; however, the amendments to sections 15, 34, and 54 of the CGST Act are not yet operative because they still await notification. For rates, the earlier compensation cess regime was withdrawn and specified tobacco and pan masala products were moved into the 40% GST slab, completing the rate rationalisation recommended by the 56th GST Council; companies dealing in those products must therefore apply the new effective tax treatment rather than the prior cess structure.

On refunds, the framework for provisional refunds was expanded on a risk-based basis, meaning refund processing now depends more on risk assessment than a purely manual or uniform approach. For compliance and filings, the return architecture increasingly requires pre-filing verification and reconciliation, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System, so businesses must ensure invoice matching and internal review before submission to reduce mismatch and exposure. The document also notes that GSTAT benches became operational, and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals, which is important for taxpayers with pending or older dispute matters because appeal windows may now be governed by new cut-off dates.

The judicial developments highlighted by the document include rulings that clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, the statutory timelines applicable to detention orders, and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. In practical terms, this means compliance teams should not assume that supplier default eliminates buyer risk, and they should treat detention and penalty appeal deadlines as strictly time-sensitive. Finally, the document notes that the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026 and that proposals on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance were under consideration; these proposals are not law unless and until formally implemented, so they should be tracked but not relied upon as operative requirements.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. rows.summary:
The document summarizes a CESTAT Hyderabad ruling in the dispute between Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) and the Pr. Commissioner of Central Tax over Service Tax on fees collected for certifying SOFTEX forms and issuing No Objection Certificates (NoCs) under the STP Scheme. For compliance purposes, the material issue is that the Department’s position was that these certification/NOC charges are taxable service consideration, with exposure covering multiple years and continuing at least through June 2012, and involving tax, interest, and penalties. The summary indicates that the disputed amounts were not merely incidental administrative fees but were specifically linked by the Department to a taxable service classification under “Business Support Service,” so entities performing similar scheme-administered certification or approval functions should assess whether such charges may be treated as taxable service receipts.

The Tribunal also independently examined limitation. The Show Cause Notice dated 21.12.2018 was the fifth n
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that once a declarant receives an SVLDRS discharge certificate, the underlying dispute cannot be pursued further by the Revenue for the same tax period and issue. In this case, Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd. had been issued Show Cause Notice No. 20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018 alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during 2013-14 through June 2018; the adjudicating authority later confirmed service tax demand of Rs. 1,43,75,615/- only for the normal period and dropped the portion relating to the extended period. Big C then opted for the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019, its declaration was accepted, the determined amount was paid, and Form SVLDRS-4 dated 10.02.2020 was issued as a discharge certificate for full and final settlement.  

The Tribunal treated the discharge certificate as legally bringing finality to the dispute under Section 129 of the Finance Act, 2019, meaning proceedings could not continue on the same matter after settlement. It relied on the Bombay High Court’s decision in Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for the proposition that continuing proceedings after issuance of an SVLDRS discharge certificate is inconsistent with the purpose and statutory finality of the scheme. The Tribunal also noted, on its own examination of limitation, that the show cause notice issued on 21.12.2018 was the fifth notice in the relevant sequence, reinforcing the limitation issue, and on that basis dismissed the Revenue’s appeal.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that where a taxpayer has validly settled a legacy service tax dispute under SVLDRS and received Form SVLDRS-4, the Revenue is barred from maintaining an appeal on the same dispute and covered period. This decision is specifically relevant to legacy indirect tax matters, especially where notices, adjudication, and settlement overlap, and it confirms that a discharge certificate should be treated as conclusive settlement documentation for the issues and time period included in the declaration.

rows.summary:
The Patna High Court considered a regular bail application in Complaint Case No. 49 of 2026 involving allegations under Section 132(1)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The case arose from a CGST complaint alleging approximately ₹73.75 crore in tax evasion through issuance of tax invoices to multiple beneficiary firms without any actual movement or supply of goods, fraudulent availment of input tax credit without receipt of goods or services and without corresponding e-way bills, falsification of accounts and financial records, and operating/abetting shell entities by controlling GST credentials, banking operations, passwords, and compliance activities.

The immediate compliance significance is that the case illustrates enforcement risk under Section 132 of the CGST Act where invoice issuance, ITC claims, e-way bill mismatches, and control over filing credentials or bank operations are used as evidence of fraud; entities should ensure actual movement/supply documentation, support for ITC claims, segregation of access to GST and banking credentials, and accurate books and filings. The document provided does not state any new rule, deadline, or statutory amendment; it is a case-law summary focused on allegations and bail proceedings rather than a change in compliance requirements.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court in **Subhra Baral v. Deputy Commissioner of Revenue** held that a GST adjudication process can be vitiated where the **show cause notice is uploaded only under the GST portal’s “Additional Notice and Orders” tab without any separate intimation to the taxpayer**. The case involved a **Form GST DRC-01 show cause notice No. ZD190524017416E dated 12.05.2024**, which proposed **tax, interest, and penalty** under the **West Bengal GST Act and the Central GST Act, 2017**. The petitioner said he never received a meaningful notice because the document was not separately communicated, so he did not file a reply; he discovered the resulting **adjudication order dated 28.07.2024** only in **March 2025** when his accountant checked the portal.

The petitioner’s **appeal under Section 107** was later **dismissed solely as time-barred**, and the appellate order was dated **29.05.2025**. The High Court found the petitioner had made out a **prima facie case** that the notice procedure violated **natural justice**, because a notice hidden in the portal’s additional documents area, without further alert, did not provide a fair opportunity to respond. The Court therefore concluded that the matter could not be upheld merely on limitation where the underlying notice and order had not been effectively brought to the taxpayer’s attention. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that **GST notices must be actively monitored across all portal tabs, including “Additional Notice and Orders,” and portal-only posting without separate intimation can create a strong procedural challenge where the taxpayer is deprived of an opportunity to reply**.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Mayur Timber v. State of Rajasthan & Ors.** quashed a GST demand raised under **Section 74 of the CGST Act, 2017** because the entire proceeding was based on a **show-cause notice dated 13.06.2024**, a reminder, and an **adjudication order dated 15.10.2024** that were **not signed at all—neither digitally nor physically**. The demand that had been confirmed included **GST of Rs. 3,13,894**, **interest of Rs. 4,26,002**, and **penalty of Rs. 3,13,894**, arising from an allegation that the taxpayer had availed **input tax credit (ITC) without actual receipt of goods**.

The Court held that under **Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017**, merely generating a notice or order on the GST portal is not enough; **electronic issuance and authentication are separate, mandatory requirements**, and the document must be properly authenticated by signature. The Court emphasized that a signature is not a formality: it authenticates the document, identifies accountability of the issuing officer, and ensures the decision reflects actual application of mind. Because the notice and order lacked signatures, the Court treated them as **non-existent in law**, and held that the defect was **not a curable procedural irregularity** but one that went to the **root of the authority to initiate and complete proceedings**.

The Court also relied on the fact that the documents were uploaded only under **“Additional Notices and Orders”**, and the taxpayer became aware of the demand only when **bank recovery proceedings** were initiated. In addition, the Court found that the taxpayer had **not been afforded an effective personal hearing**, contrary to **Section 75(4) of the CGST Act**, which further vitiated the adjudication. On that basis, the Court rejected the State’s argument that the taxpayer should be relegated to an **alternative statutory remedy**, and allowed the writ petition, thereby invalidating the unsigned notice and consequential order.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12577 Case Name Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment.
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India & Ors.** held that **late deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) is not the same as non-payment of FTT**, and therefore a penalty cannot be imposed under **Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979** merely because the tax was deposited after the due date. The Court drew a distinction between **Section 38(3)**, which applies where an assessee **“fails to pay”** the tax, and **Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979**, which governs **delayed deposit**; in other words, a timing breach does not automatically trigger the same penalty provision as outright non-payment. The Supreme Court also made clear that **penalty under Section 38 is not automatic** simply because the statutory deadline was missed; the legal character of the default matters.

The facts involved **six delayed deposits of FTT by the airline**. In **five cases**, the delay was only **1 to 11 days**, and the airline stated that the relevant **demand drafts had been purchased before the due dates** but could not be deposited because of **security restrictions**. In the **sixth case (December 1995)**, the delay was **63 days**, which the airline attributed to the relevant employee being on **emergency leave**. An initial adjudication imposed a **penalty of Rs. 12,000** for the six late payments, but after remand the penalty was increased sharply to **Rs. 71,29,140**.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this decision protects taxpayers/collecting entities from being treated as having “failed to pay” FTT merely because of a delayed remittance, so long as the tax was in fact collected and the issue is lateness rather than non-payment. However, the case does **not** excuse delayed remittance; it only limits the penalty route under the specific provision applied here. Entities responsible for collecting and depositing FTT should therefore continue to follow the statutory deposit timelines under the Finance Act and Rules, but can note that the Supreme Court has said **delay alone is not equivalent to default in payment** for the purpose of **Section 38(3)**.

rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT allowed the taxpayer’s appeal on the deductibility of Portfolio Management Service (PMS) charges while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, reversing the disallowance upheld by the CIT(A). The dispute related to Assessment Year 2011-12 and arose from an assessment under section 143(3); the assessee had reported total income of Rs. 72,26,297 from salary, short-term capital gains, and income from other sources, and had claimed Rs. 8,42,360 as fees/charges paid to Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. for PMS.

The Assessing Officer had denied the deduction on the basis that PMS charges were not expenditure incurred “wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer” of a capital asset, and the CIT(A), by order dated 28.08.2025, sustained that view. The CIT(A) relied mainly on the Mumbai Tribunal’s earlier decision in ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah, which had held PMS fees and performance-linked charges not deductible under section 48.

Before the Tribunal, the assessee argued that the issue was unsettled because different coordinate benches had taken conflicting positions, and pointed to KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a capital-gains deduction. The assessee also noted that the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding before the Bombay High Court, but the document indicates that no contrary final court ruling was available at the time to settle the issue. On that basis, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s claim and allowed the PMS charges as deductible in computing capital gains under section 48.

For compliance purposes, this decision is relevant to taxpayers using PMS arrangements who seek to treat management fees and related charges as capital gains deductions; however, the document also reflects that there were divergent ITAT views at the time, so the position was not uniformly settled across benches. The key practical implication is that PMS fees of the type paid here—Rs. 8,42,360 to a portfolio manager—were accepted by this Mumbai ITAT as eligible section 48 expenditure for this assessment year, despite contrary precedent relied on by the tax authority.

rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court dismissed AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd.’s writ petition challenging the assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it denied refund of input tax credit reflected in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the SGST head. The company, an exporter of spice extracts and oleoresins, had earlier been registered under the Kerala VAT Act, 2003 and filed Form GST TRAN-1 in November 2017 to transition excess VAT input tax credit into the GST Electronic Credit Ledger; the transitional credit was reflected in the ledger on 27.12.2017. For the month of November 2017, it then claimed a refund of ITC, but the Department rejected the claim on the basis that transitional credit moved through TRAN-1 is not credit “earned” during the relevant tax period and therefore does not count as “Net ITC” for refund purposes under Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018.

On maintainability, the Court held that the writ petition could not be entertained because the petitioner had not pursued the statutory appellate remedy and had instead come to the High Court after the limitation period for filing an appeal had expired. The petitioner’s argument that appeal would be futile because the adjudicating authority had relied on a binding departmental circular was not accepted. In effect, the decision confirms that belated writ relief cannot be used to resurrect a time-barred GST refund challenge, and that taxpayers disputing refund rejections based on Rule 89(4) and the 15.03.2018 circular must pursue the ordinary GST appellate process within the prescribed time limits.

The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad in **Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Tax** held that a **time-share accommodation arrangement is not taxable as “Club or Association Service” merely because the contract uses member-style terminology**. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and sold time-share holiday rights under a scheme giving customers a **contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week each year for 12 years** in exchange for a **predetermined consideration**; the Tribunal said the real substance of the arrangement was a **customer-service relationship**, not a club/association membership.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that **taxability depends on the actual legal and commercial nature of the arrangement, not the labels used in the agreement**. The Tribunal found that the time-share purchasers had **no proprietary rights, voting rights, management rights, or shareholding rights** in the company, and they did **not become members of the company under the Companies Act, 1956** because they did not subscribe to the memorandum or become shareholders. On that basis, they could not be treated as “members” of a club or association for service tax purposes.

The appeal was **partly allowed**. The original order had confirmed **service tax of Rs. 1,63,15,458/-** with **interest** under Club or Association Service, along with penalties under **Sections 76, 77, and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994**, and smaller demands under **Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service, and Renting of Immovable Property Service**. The summary provided indicates the Tribunal set aside the Club or Association Service demand as based on an incorrect characterization, while leaving the case only **partly** allowed because other issues/demands were also in dispute.

For a corporate compliance team, this decision is relevant to businesses selling **time-share, vacation ownership, or similar accommodation-right schemes**: if customers only receive a contractual right to use property for defined periods and do not obtain any corporate or membership rights, the arrangement should not automatically be classified as a club/association service solely because the paperwork refers to participants as “members.” The practical compliance takeaway is to ensure contractual documents, billing treatment, and tax positions reflect the **true legal structure** of the offering, especially where there is **no ownership interest, no governance rights, and no statutory membership relationship**.

The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that customs authorities cannot keep an imported vehicle under prolonged detention without promptly issuing a lawful seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, and then later try to justify the delay retroactively. In this case, the petitioner imported a Toyota Land Cruiser from Japan, declared it through Bill of Entry No. 7472252 dated 26.12.2024, paid customs duty of Rs. 99,78,795, and obtained out-of-charge clearance on 02.01.2025; despite that, DRI searched his residence on 07.02.2025, prepared a panchnama, and orally directed him not to deal with the vehicle, but did not contemporaneously seize it. The DRI issued the actual seizure memo only on 17.04.2026—more than a year later—followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4), which the Court treated as an unjustified and improper sequence given the absence of timely statutory action.

The Court also criticized the Department’s provisional release conditions dated 18.05.2026, which required the petitioner to furnish a bond for Rs. 85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs. 1.20 crore by invoking paragraph 2 of Circular No. 35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The Court noted that the cited circular language had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex v. Union of India insofar as it restricted the adjudicating authority’s discretion, and the Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated continued reliance on that invalidated portion. For compliance purposes, the decision underscores that customs/DRI officers must act within the statutory framework when detaining goods, must not leave imported property in a prolonged state of informal restraint without a timely seizure order, and cannot rely on a circular provision that has been judicially curtailed to impose rigid bond/bank-guarantee conditions. The ruling is directly relevant to importers and customs enforcement actions involving detention, seizure, show-cause proceedings, and provisional release of imported assets, especially where the goods have already been cleared and duty has been paid.

The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. rows.summary:
The CESTAT Kolkata held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because an intermediary buyer was involved, where the manufacturer’s invoice clearly names the assessee as consignee and the statutory invoice requirements are otherwise met. In this case, Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. had taken credit of **Rs. 83,839** on the basis of **three invoices**—**two issued in 2011** and **one dated 22.01.2014**—and the Department proposed reversal on the theory that the goods had been purchased through **M/s Ashis Enterprise**, which allegedly did not have dealer registration. The Tribunal accepted the appellant’s explanation that the invoices from **M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal** expressly showed **Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee**, while **Ashis Enterprise** was only shown as the buyer and had separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment; the goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and entered in **RG 23A Part I** on receipt. The Tribunal found that all particulars required under **Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004** were present, and emphasized that there was **no allegation that the goods were not actually received** by the appellant. Because the Revenue could not establish any violation of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the demand for reversal was **set aside** and the appeal was **allowed**.

For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that credit should not be rejected solely due to the involvement of a non-registered intermediary if the core documentation shows direct receipt by the claimant, the manufacturer’s invoice identifies the claimant as consignee, and the goods are properly recorded in the receiving records. The key operational point is that businesses should be able to correlate the manufacturer’s invoice, any intermediary commercial invoice, and warehouse/store records to demonstrate actual receipt and eligibility of credit.

A show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 demanded service tax of Rs.43,86,471/- under Works Contract Service, which was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant challenged the order and sought waiver of pre-deposit. The Commissioner (Appeals) fixed the stay application for hearing on 12.06.2014; although the appellant sought an adjournment, the request was declined and, by order dated 13.06.2014, it was directed to deposit 50% of the service tax demand. The appellant subsequently requested a speaking order considering its legal submissions and precedents, but did not comply with the pre-deposit condition. Its appeal was consequently dismissed on 23.07.2014. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that its appeal had been dismissed without adjudication on merits and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had failed to consider its prima facie case, balance of convenience and financial hardship. It relied, inter alia, upon Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya P
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad ruling in **ECI BJCL JV v. Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax** holding that **non-compliance with a pre-deposit order is enough to justify dismissal of a service tax appeal**. The underlying dispute arose from EPC/works contract activity performed for the **Government of Andhra Pradesh** involving construction of **dams, reservoirs, canals, and allied structures** during **June 2007 to March 2012**; the department issued a **show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012** demanding **service tax of Rs. 43,86,471** under **Works Contract Service**, and the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on **09.01.2014**. When the assessee appealed and sought waiver of pre-deposit, the Commissioner (Appeals) heard the stay request on **12.06.2014**, declined an adjournment request, and on **13.06.2014** ordered deposit of **50% of the adjudged service tax demand** as a condition for proceeding with the appeal.

The appellant then asked for a speaking order that addressed its legal submissions and cited case law, but it **did not comply with the 50% pre-deposit requirement**; as a result, its appeal was dismissed on **23.07.2014**. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that dismissal without a merits decision was improper and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had not adequately considered **prima facie case, balance of convenience, and financial hardship**, relying on multiple precedents. The Tribunal, however, upheld the dismissal and treated the pre-deposit direction as a valid procedural requirement that had to be met before the appeal could be entertained.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that in service tax litigation, **failure to comply with a pre-deposit condition can by itself terminate the appeal**, even where the appellant believes it has strong legal arguments on classification or taxability. The case is specifically relevant to entities executing **works contracts / EPC projects** and shows that once an appellate authority orders a deposit condition—here, **50% of the demand**—the appellant must either comply or risk dismissal without the merits being examined.

rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court held that Vodafone Idea Limited was entitled to immediate release of long-pending TDS refunds totaling **Rs. 53,09,56,470**, along with **applicable interest**, for **Assessment Years 2003-04, 2008-09 to 2013-14**. The Court noted that these refunds had remained unpaid for about two years even after the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal’s orders and the subsequent **appeal-effect orders** passed by the Assessing Officer, which had already quantified the refundable amounts.

For **AY 2012-13**, the Tribunal order was dated **05.06.2024**, followed by an appeal-effect order dated **30.10.2024**; Vodafone Idea quantified the refund at **Rs. 11,06,37,172**, but its **Form 26B application dated 25.04.2025** was rejected. For **AY 2013-14**, the Tribunal order was dated **30.04.2024**, followed by an appeal-effect order dated **14.10.2024**; the refund was quantified at **Rs. 7,57,50,048**, and the **Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025** was also rejected. For **AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12**, the relevant Tribunal orders were dated **26.11.2024** and **03.02.2025**, and the appeal-effect order was passed on **15.05.2026**, with the refund quantified at **Rs. 34,45,69,250**.

A key compliance issue in the case was whether the taxpayer had to use **Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A, and Form 26B** to process the refunds. Vodafone Idea argued that those provisions govern the processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess or incorrect deduction/deposit, but **do not apply where the refund arises only after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order has crystallized the liability/refund**. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Procedure, but the High Court accepted the taxpayer’s position and directed release of the refund with interest, effectively holding that **Form 26B was not a precondition** in this circumstance.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where a refund becomes payable only after appellate or Section 201 proceedings, the department cannot insist on Form 26B as a procedural barrier to withholding payment once the amount has been determined in the taxpayer’s favor. Entities with similar pending TDS refund claims should review whether their refunds have already been quantified by appeal-effect orders and, if so, whether continued non-payment can be challenged for immediate release together with statutory interest.

The Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs has notified the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026** by **S.O. 4870(E) dated 2 September 2026**, issued under **clauses (aa) and (ab) of section 46(2) of FEMA, 1999**. The amendment takes effect **from the date of publication in the Official Gazette** and further amends the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019**.

This new provision expressly allows an **e-commerce entity** to operate an **inventory-based model of e-commerce solely for exporting goods or products manufactured or produced in India**. The permitted exports must be carried out in accordance with the **Foreign Trade Policy 2023**, the **Handbook of Procedures (HBP)**, and the **Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015**.

In practical terms, entities involved in India-origin product exports via e-commerce should review whether their model now falls within the newly permitted export-only inventory structure, while activities not tied to export of Indian-manufactured/produced goods remain subject to the earlier restrictions.

The notification also notes the regulatory history of the principal NDI Rules: they were originally published on **17 October 2019** and have been amended multiple times up to **S.O. 3030(E) dated 12 June 2026**. The PIB Backgrounder on **Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0**, posted on **5 September 2026**, explains a government-backed credit support scheme approved on **5 May 2026** and implemented by **NCGTC** to provide additional financing to businesses impacted by external disruptions. The scheme is designed to facilitate up to **₹2.55 lakh crore** of additional credit through **Member Lending Institutions** and applies to **MSMEs, eligible non-MSME business borrowers, and scheduled passenger airline companies**.

For **MSMEs**, the scheme provides **100% guarantee coverage** and permits additional credit generally up to **20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding during Q4 FY 2025–26**, subject to a maximum of **₹100 crore per borrower**. For **eligible non-MSMEs**, the coverage is **90%**, with the same general credit limit structure of up to **20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding in Q4 FY 2025–26**, also capped at **₹100 crore per borrower**. For **scheduled passenger airline companies**, the scheme provides **90% guarantee coverage** and allows additional credit up to **100%**, subject to a ceiling of **₹1,500 crore per borrower**; any borrowing above **₹1,000 crore** is tied to specified equity conditions.

The scheme remains operational until **31 March 2027** or until guarantees totaling **₹2.55 lakh crore** have been issued, **whichever occurs first**. Repayment terms differ by borrower type: **MSME and eligible non-MSME loans** have a **five-year tenure including a one-year moratorium**, while **airline loans** have a **seven-year tenure including a two-year moratorium**. As of **20 August 2026**, the scheme had already issued **6,73,979 guarantees** covering **₹2,50,024 crore**, with MSMEs accounting for **97.3% of guarantees by number** and **80.79% of the guaranteed amount**.

The Backgrounder also notes that the government has conducted outreach efforts and that applications/access are available through the **Jan Samarth Portal**. rows.title: Corporate Law | CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Dial4Trade for Online Listing and Sale of Ammonium Nitrate Without Mandatory Safeguards
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a ₹10 lakh penalty on Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited for facilitating the online listing, hosting, advertising and sale of Ammonium Nitrate without mandatory regulatory safeguards. The CCPA also directed Dial4Trade to immediately discontinue listing, hosting, advertising or facilitating the sale of Ammonium Nitrate or any other substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884. During its examination, the Authority found that the platform did not adequately disclose the seller’s valid PESO licence details, verify the buyer’s identity and licensed status, provide mechanisms for transaction traceability under the Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012, or caution users regarding legal restrictions and consequences of unauthorised possession. The listing also carried imagery depicting explosions and blast effects. The CCPA held that a product listing communicated to the public over the internet falls within the definition of an “advertisement” under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and that presenting a regulated explosive substance like an ordinary consumer product without required licensing disclosures constitutes a misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice. The Authority rejected Dial4Trade’s B2B marketplace and intermediary safe-harbour contentions, holding that marketplace e-commerce entities remain subject to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and prescribed due-diligence requirements. The action forms part of a sector-wide examination of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive substances. rows.summary:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a **₹10 lakh penalty** on **Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited** for **facilitating the online listing, hosting, advertising, and sale of ammonium nitrate** without the safeguards required for a regulated explosive substance. The CCPA also ordered the company to **immediately stop listing, hosting, advertising, or otherwise facilitating the sale of ammonium nitrate** and **any other substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884**. This is not just a narrow product-specific issue: the order is directed at the platform’s conduct in enabling sale of a hazardous substance through its marketplace.

In its review, the Authority found multiple compliance failures: the platform did **not adequately disclose the seller’s valid PESO licence details**, did **not verify the buyer’s identity or licensed status**, did **not provide traceability mechanisms** for transactions as expected under the **Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012**, and did **not warn users about the legal restrictions and consequences of unauthorized possession**. The listing also used **images depicting explosions and blast effects**, which the CCPA treated as aggravating the misleading nature of the presentation. The Authority held that an online product listing made available to the public qualifies as an **“advertisement” under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, and that presenting a regulated explosive as if it were an ordinary consumer product without the mandatory disclosures amounts to a **misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice**.

The CCPA rejected Dial4Trade’s argument that it was merely a **B2B marketplace/intermediary** and therefore not responsible for the content or sale. The Authority emphasized that **marketplace e-commerce entities remain subject to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020** and must comply with the prescribed **due-diligence obligations**, including the checks and disclosures relevant to regulated goods. The action is part of a broader **sector-wide examination of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive substances**, so other platforms handling similar products should expect scrutiny and should review whether they have the required licensing verification, buyer validation, traceability, and warning controls in place.

The Amnesty is available for six months from the notification date, up to 28 December 2026. In addition to retrospective regularisation of exempt status, PF Trusts may benefit from waiver of certain requirements under the CoSS, 2020, including minimum employee headcount, corpus size and the three-year compliance rule. After retrospective regularisation, an establishment may choose to comply either as an exempt or unexempt establishment. The Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is undertaking outreach among potential beneficiaries and stakeholders, including the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), professional bodies and establishments. rows.summary:
The Ministry of Labour & Employment has introduced a one-time amnesty under the EPF Scheme 2026 to allow retrospective regularisation of the exempt status of provident fund trusts that were recognised under the Income Tax Act, 1961 but never obtained a formal exemption order under section 17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 or section 143 of the Code on Social Security, 2020. The Bombay High Court (Pune Bench), Madras High Court and Kerala High Court have issued directions encouraging or requiring eligible establishments to avail the Scheme in specified proceedings. Employers must first clear outstanding interest on delayed PF contributions and then apply online through the EPFO Employer Portal using the VISHWAS, 2026 module. The system calculates the revised damages, and eligible employers are given 15 days for payment, with a further automatic 15-day extension where required. Upon payment confirmation, EPFO issues a digitally signed Settlement Certificate, after which the concerned court or tribunal proceedings stand closed. EPFO has established dedicated VISHWAS Cells and Helpdesks at its 153 Regional Offices. rows.summary:
The Government of India’s EPFO VISHWAS, 2026 Scheme is a one-time settlement mechanism for resolving long-pending disputes over damages/penalties for delayed Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) contributions at reduced rates. It applies only to eligible employer cases relating to delays in PF contributions arising before 14 June 2024, and the document says it can cover matters that are already pending before courts or tribunals, EPFO penalty orders where recovery is still pending, penalty notices that have been issued but no final order has yet been passed, and instances where payment delays were recorded but no penalty notice has yet been issued.

The scheme is open until 28 December 2026, and the document expressly says this deadline will not be extended. Under the settlement formula, damages are calculated at 0.25% per month for delays of up to two months, 0.50% per month for delays of more than two months but up to four months, and 1% per month for delays beyond four months; this is described as much lower than the normal penalty regime, which may reach 37% per year. Employers are first required to clear all outstanding interest on the delayed PF contributions before they can use the scheme.

The compliance process is: eligible employers must apply online through the EPFO Employer Portal using the dedicated VISHWAS, 2026 module, after which the system computes the revised damages. Once the calculation is generated, the employer is given 15 days to make payment, with an automatic additional 15-day extension available where needed. After payment is confirmed, EPFO issues a digitally signed Settlement Certificate, and the relevant court or tribunal proceeding is then treated as closed.

Operationally, EPFO has set up dedicated VISHWAS Cells and Helpdesks at all 153 Regional Offices to support applications and settlements. The document also notes that the Bombay High Court (Pune Bench), Madras High Court, and Kerala High Court have issued directions encouraging or requiring eligible establishments to avail themselves of the scheme in certain proceedings, which means employers with litigation in those jurisdictions should review whether they are covered and act before the 28 December 2026 cut-off.

IRDAI has issued Public Notice No. IRDAI/PPGR/BB/2026-27/25 dated 4 September 2026 warning that the website **“igmsirdai.online”** and its complaint-registration webpages are **not official IRDAI platforms** and appear to be impersonating IRDAI’s insurance grievance system/Bima Bharosa/IGMS. rows.summary:
The President’s message frames India’s financial-system evolution as a shift from basic financial inclusion to active financial participation and, ultimately, financial empowerment, and it ties that shift directly to the profession’s role in promoting financial literacy, trust, and informed decision-making. It notes progress such as a higher Financial Inclusion Index, expanded account ownership, and the continued reach of government and digital rails like Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Aadhaar-enabled services, UPI, digital payments, insurance, pensions, and investment products. It also signals continuing engagement on professional development and regulatory capacity-building, including ICAI’s international participation (such as the IFAC Board Meeting in India and the ICAI International Conference–ASEAN), professional pathways with ISCA, WOFA 2026, public-finance workshops, new IFSCA-related certificate courses, and the MoU with the Department of Higher Education, Government of Madhya Pradesh. Additional items mentioned include the All India Leadership Summit, financial-reporting and audit-quality initiatives, the revised Guidance Note on Tax Audit under Section 44AB, the I-Kar Pe Charcha mobile application, ICAI’s strategy meeting, and regional conferences.

The message does not announce a single new binding regulatory rule with a specific effective date, rate, or threshold in the text provided; instead, it functions as a strategic update and call to action. The core compliance takeaway for professionals is that ICAI is emphasizing stronger competence in financial literacy, fraud awareness, and digital-risk awareness, alongside continued attention to audit, tax-audit, reporting-quality, and public-finance capability. The closing appeal is to convert financial literacy from mere awareness into a sustained movement for financial empowerment in support of a more confident, resilient, and financially empowered Viksit Bharat.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); R Ramesha Vs Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (Karnataka High Court) When Compensation Arrives Six Years Late, the Return Cannot Travel Back in Time: Karnataka HC Directs Consideration of Condonation u/s 119(2)(b) for Refund of TDS on Exempt Land-Acquisition Compensation The Karnataka High Court has directed the PCIT, Bengaluru-3, to examine & decide the assessee’s application u/s 119(2)(b) seeking condonation of delay in filing the revised return for AY 2019-20, where compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land was actually received only in the year 2025 after resolution of a prolonged title dispute. The assessee claimed that the compensation was exempt from income tax u/s 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 & consequently sought refund of the TDS deducted by the KIADB. Background of the dispute The petitioner claimed title, as legal heir of the original owners, over land measuring 3 acres and 20 guntas situated in Survey Nos.87/3 & 87/4 of Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk. The lands, along with surrounding properties, had been acquired by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board – KIADB under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966. However, payment of compensation was delayed because of a dispute concerning the petitioner’s title to the acquired lands. According to the petitioner, the title dispute was ultimately resolved by a civil court decree in his favour. It was only thereafter that the KIADB deposited the acq
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that, where compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land was not actually received until years after the relevant assessment year because of a title dispute, the taxpayer’s inability to reflect that compensation in the original return should be addressed through condonation of delay under section 119(2)(b) of the Income-tax Act rather than by rigidly denying the refund claim. In this case, the petitioner, claiming as legal heir of the original owners, said he was entitled to compensation for 3 acres and 20 guntas in Survey Nos. 87/3 and 87/4 at Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk, which had been acquired by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966. The compensation payment was delayed for years due to a dispute over title, and only after a civil court decree resolved the title in his favor did the KIADB deposit/disburse the compensation; the petitioner then sought treatment of the compensation as exempt under section 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, and also sought refund of TDS deducted by KIADB.  

The court directed the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Bengaluru-3, to examine and decide the assessee’s application for condonation of delay in filing the revised return for Assessment Year 2019-20. The practical compliance point is that the refund claim depends on whether the delayed receipt of compensation can be brought into the tax computation through condonation under section 119(2)(b), because the compensation was received only in 2025 even though the return year at issue was AY 2019-20. For corporate or institutional compliance teams handling land acquisition payouts, the decision reinforces that where compensation is legally exempt and TDS has been withheld, late receipt caused by a bona fide dispute may justify a condonation-based revised return/refund route, and the tax authority must specifically consider that request rather than summarily rejecting the refund claim on timing grounds.

rows.title: Company Law | Annual ROC Compliance 2026: Beyond AOC-4 and MGT-7
rows.desc: Summary: Annual ROC compliance for FY 2025-26 should be approached as a complete corporate compliance closure exercise rather than merely filing AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. The process covers finalisation and audit of financial statements, Board approval, Board’s Report, AGM, annual financial-statement and annual-return filings, auditor-related filings, DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, related-party transactions and other event-based compliances. The FY 2025-26 cycle is particularly significant because the small-company thresholds were enhanced with effect from 1 December 2025 to ₹10 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover, while the director KYC framework moved from annual compliance to a three-year cycle effective 31 March 2026. Companies should therefore reassess MGT-7/MGT-7A applicability, XBRL applicability, MGT-8 requirements and the applicable DIR-3 KYC cycle rather than relying on older checklists. AOC-4 should reconcile with the signed financial statements, while MGT-7/MGT-7A should agree with statutory registers, share capital records and MCA master data. Similar reconciliations should be undertaken for borrowings and DPT-3, MSME dues and MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR and share capital. The article also highlights the distinction between additional filing fees and statutory penalties, potential director-disqualification consequences, the continuing obligations of companies with no business activity, and the increasing importance of consistency between books, GST returns, Income-tax filings and MCA records. The recommended professional approach is Review → Reconcile → Identify Exceptions → Rectify → Approve → File, ensuring that annual ROC filings are the final output of a broader annual corporate compliance review. rows.summary:
The document says FY 2025–26 annual ROC compliance should be treated as a full corporate compliance closure exercise, not just the mechanical filing of AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. It covers the entire sequence from finalisation and audit of financial statements, Board approval, Board’s Report and AGM, through annual financial-statement and annual-return filings, auditor-related filings, and event-based or periodic compliances such as DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, and related-party transactions. The key compliance message is that companies should first reconcile their internal records and statutory filings, then identify and rectify exceptions, and only then approve and file the annual ROC documents.

A major change highlighted is the revision of the “small company” thresholds effective 1 December 2025: the limits have increased to ₹10 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover. Because of this, companies need to re-check whether they qualify for MGT-7A instead of MGT-7, whether XBRL filing applies, and whether MGT-8 certification is required, rather than relying on older threshold-based checklists. The document also notes that director KYC has shifted from an annual filing requirement to a three-year cycle, effective 31 March 2026, so companies must determine which directors fall into the new DIR-3 KYC cycle and ensure the correct filing timing.

The summary emphasizes that AOC-4 must match the signed financial statements exactly, and MGT-7/MGT-7A must agree with statutory registers, share capital records, and MCA master data. Similar pre-filing reconciliations are required for borrowings reported in DPT-3, MSME dues reported in MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR disclosures, and share capital changes. The article also flags the continuing obligation to comply even where there has been no business activity, meaning inactive companies are not automatically exempt from annual ROC obligations. It additionally warns that failures can trigger additional filing fees, statutory penalties, and in some cases director-disqualification consequences.

The document further stresses the need for consistency across books of account, GST returns, Income-tax filings, and MCA records, indicating that annual ROC compliance should be validated against the company’s broader regulatory footprint. In practical terms, the recommended workflow is: review all applicable compliances, reconcile source records with MCA requirements, identify and correct mismatches, obtain approvals, and then file the forms. For a compliance team, the main takeaway is that FY 2025–26 filings should be managed as a coordinated year-end compliance closure exercise with updated threshold checks and cycle-based director KYC planning, rather than as isolated ROC forms filed at the deadline.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri, dealt with a writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy concerning entitlement to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 39 of the CGST Act, read with Section 16(5). The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court treated as being within the statutory cut-off contemplated under Section 16(5), and later submitted a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit. That rectification request was rejected by the revenue authority by order dated April 8, 2026 on the ground that it was not filed within the period said to be prescribed by a departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024, read together with a circular dated October 15, 2024.

A key point in the judgment is that the Court records an apparent drafting/correction issue: paragraph 3 referred to the applicable period as “six weeks,” but a later correction order dated August 21, 2026 stated that this should be read as “six months,” and also corrected the word “communication” to “circular.” The petitioner’s legal argument was that the rectification filing period could be extended because Section 16(5) itself does not prescribe a specific deadline for filing such a rectification application. The revenue’s position was that the original order dated March 6, 2024 had been served on the petitioner the same day by post, and it disputed the petitioner’s timing/entitlement on that basis.

For compliance purposes, the document is significant because it addresses whether an administrative time limit imposed through circulars can bar rectification-based ITC relief under Section 16(5) where the statute itself does not set a filing deadline. The operative dates and deadlines referenced in the dispute are March 6, 2024 (original order), April 8, 2024 and October 15, 2024 (departmental circular/notification framework), November 30, 2021 (return filing cut-off noted by the Court), January 12, 2026 (rectification application), April 8, 2026 (rejection order), and August 21, 2026 (correction order changing “six weeks” to “six months”). The document does not provide the final merits outcome beyond these facts, but it clearly indicates that the enforceability and length of the rectification window for Section 16(5) ITC claims was the central compliance issue.
