This document is a Madras High Court judgment dated 27.03.2017 in appeals filed by the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central 2, Chennai, against Ennore Cargo Container Terminal Pvt. Ltd. for Assessment Years 2007-08 and 2010-11, challenging a common ITAT order dated 12.05.2016. The Revenue’s main tax issue was whether the company was entitled to deduction under Section 80IA(4) for its Container Freight Station (CFS) operations after the statutory amendment to Section 80IA(4) inserted an Explanation with effect from 01.04.2002 that omitted the phrase “any other public facility of similar nature.” The Revenue also argued that the assessee was not actually “developing” infrastructure facilities and was only acting as a custodian handling and moving containerized import/export cargo at the CFS, rather than operating a qualifying infrastructure facility.

For AY 2007-08, the Revenue additionally questioned the ITAT’s treatment of a deemed dividend issue under the Income-tax Act. The document excerpt does not provide the full reasoning or the final outcome of the High Court’s decision on the substantive tax issues, but it does establish that the appeals were brought under Section 260A and that the core compliance issue for similarly situated businesses is the availability of Section 80IA(4) infrastructure deductions for CFS-related activities in light of the post-01.04.2002 wording of the provision. Entities operating CFS or similar logistics/infrastructure facilities should note that the dispute turns on whether their role is sufficiently “development” of infrastructure versus mere custody/handling services, and whether the amended statutory language supports deduction eligibility for their activity.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the tax treatment of a scientifically estimated provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd., a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction and toll collection under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) concession with the Government of Maharashtra. For Assessment Year 2015-16, the company had reported a book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467 and an income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672, but the Assessing Officer added back Rs. 7,47,00,000 by disallowing the provision created for future major repairs. The assessee argued that its 30-year concession agreement required major repairs throughout the concession period, with the first such repair due after seven years (in the eighth year) and the last in the 30th year, so the liability accrued over time and could be recognized through a reliable estimate rather than only when cash was actually spent.

The Court’s ruling matters for compliance because it confirms that, where a contractual obligation exists and the amount can be estimated scientifically, a provision may be deductible even if the repair cost has not yet been incurred in cash. The assessee relied on its BOT concession terms and on CBDT Circular No. 9/2014, which addresses expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT arrangements. The Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune, had already accepted the assessee’s position after reviewing the concession agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38, and 39, and the ITAT, Mumbai dismissed the Revenue’s appeal on 8 February 2023; the High Court then rejected the Revenue’s further appeal under Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

For taxpayers in similar BOT infrastructure arrangements, the key compliance takeaway is that the tax deductibility of a repair provision depends on the existence of a binding contractual repair obligation and supportable estimation methodology, not merely on actual payment timing. The decision does not announce a new filing deadline or rate change, but it reinforces that entities operating road concessions should maintain robust documentation showing why the liability has accrued, how the estimate was computed, and how the concession agreement specifically obligates the repairs over the life of the project.

The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal filed before the First Appellate Authority had passed its order is not maintainable under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017. In this case, Pankajam Plastics had filed an appeal in APL-01 before the First Appellate Authority and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, claiming that the department had already started recovery proceedings. However, the record showed that the First Appellate Authority’s order rejecting APL-02 was actually passed later, on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, meaning no appealable order under Section 107/108 existed when the GSTAT appeal was lodged. The Registry had flagged this as a defect, and the Tribunal agreed that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 was premature because Section 112(1) permits an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal only against an order already passed under Section 107 or Section 108.  

For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that a taxpayer cannot bypass the statutory sequence by filing a Tribunal appeal before the first appellate order exists, even if recovery action is being initiated. The operative procedural requirement is that an aggrieved person must first have an actual order from the First Appellate Authority before invoking the GSTAT under Section 112. No filing deadline or monetary threshold was set in this decision; the key requirement is timing and maintainability of the appeal, not the merits of the underlying tax dispute.

The petitioner referred
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court dealt with a GST recovery dispute involving Best Agrolife Limited after a notice dated 25/03/2025 required payment of tax and interest within seven days, warning that recovery proceedings under Section 79 of the Maharashtra GST Act, 2017 would begin if payment was not made. The company did not pay in response to the notice; instead, by email dated 11/04/2025, it said it had issued credit notes under Section 34 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for returned goods and rate differences, and that these credit notes were reflected through the e-invoice portal and used to adjust outward tax liability against earlier sales periods. It argued that this only reduced output tax liability and did not create any actual tax shortfall because the liability had already been discharged, and it supported that position with a GSTN-generated “Tax Liability Report” for April 2022 through February 2025 and a “NEGATIVE LIABILITY STATEMENT” for 01/09/2024 to 27/03/2025 showing negative sales/negative liability carried on the portal and automatically adjusted against later liabilities.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the court did not grant interim relief against recovery, and the existence of portal-based negative liability, credit-note adjustments, or retrospective set-off claims did not excuse the taxpayer’s failure to pay within the seven-day deadline in the demand notice. The matter shows that when a tax officer issues a demand notice under the MGST framework and expressly threatens Section 79 recovery, the taxpayer must respond promptly and substantively; simply asserting that credit notes were raised and that later portal adjustments offset the liability may not be enough to stop recovery action. The document therefore highlights a practical compliance risk: companies using credit notes for returns or rate differences should ensure that their GST returns, e-invoice reporting, and liability adjustments are fully aligned and promptly documented, because delays or unresolved mismatches can still trigger immediate recovery proceedings.

PAN : ABJFS4506M Appellant Respondent / ORDER PER INTURI RAMA RAO, AM: This is an appeal filed by the Revenue directed against the order of ld. Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)-8, Pune [‘the CIT(A)’] dated 13.12.2019 for the assessment year 2014-15. 2. Briefly, the facts of the case are that the assessee is a partnership firm engaged in the business of development of lands. The factual background of the issue was explained by the assessee vide his letter dated 30.11.2016, which is extracted by the Assessing Officer vide para no.4.1 of the assessment order, which reads as under :- “Sarsan Developers Private Limited (SDPL) and Kumar Housing Corporation Limited (KHCL) had entered into an agre
rows.summary:
This order concerns a penalty dispute under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2014-15 involving **M/s. Sarsan Developers, Pune**, a partnership firm engaged in land development. The firm filed its return on **29.11.2014** declaring **nil income**, but in the assessment completed under **section 143(3)** by the Assessing Officer on **23.12.2016**, an addition of **₹5,60,73,319** was made. That amount had been claimed as part of development expenses and represented a payment to a retiring partner, **Kumar Housing Corporation Limited**, which the department treated as a capital expenditure rather than a revenue business expense.

The key compliance issue is that the firm had originally **debited ₹13,40,50,885 as development expenses**, including the disputed **₹5.60 crore** payment. The Assessing Officer treated the payment to the retiring partner as not allowable in computing business income, and the assessment was finalized at **nil income** only after this addition. The order under discussion is not the assessment itself but the Revenue’s appeal against the **CIT(A)’s order dated 13.12.2019**, which had evidently deleted the penalty; the Pune ITAT has now **restored the penalty**.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position that the claim of this **capital expenditure** as a deductible development expense amounted to penalty-exposing conduct under **section 271(1)(c)**. The decision underscores that where a taxpayer claims a large payment to a retiring partner or similar structural payout as a revenue deduction, but the tax authorities view it as capital in nature, the claim can lead not only to disallowance but also to a concealment/inaccurate particulars penalty. The case therefore signals the need for careful tax characterization of partner retirement settlements, restructuring payouts, and development-project expense allocations, with supporting documentation and legal analysis robust enough to defend revenue-deduction treatment. The Tribunal’s order was pronounced on **10.10.2023**.

Following the jurisdictional Bombay High Court decision in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd., the Tribunal held that the AO could not independently assess an altogether different item after abandoning the very issue for which reassessment jurisdiction had been assumed. Reopening Triggered by Cash & Time Deposits The assessee was a co-operative credit society. It had not filed its return of income for AY 2018-19, reportedly because its audit report was not received in time. Information available on the Insight Portal indicated that the assessee had made cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 in The RDCC Urban Bank and had also invested ₹55,50,000 in time deposits. Since no return had been filed, the AO formed the view that these transactions aggregating to ₹1,47,36,100 represented income that had escaped assessment. After issuing a show-cause notice u/s 148A(b), the AO passed an order u/s 148A(d) on 07.04.2022. The AO recorded that the cash deposits & time deposits remained undisclosed and constituted information sug
rows.summary:
For AY 2018–19, the Pune ITAT held that the reassessment of Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit could not stand because the Assessing Officer reopened the case on one specific ground but ultimately made an addition on a completely different issue. The reopening was based on portal information that the assessee, a co-operative credit society, had not filed a return and had allegedly made cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 in The RDCC Urban Bank and time deposits/investments of ₹55,50,000, totaling ₹1,47,36,100, which the AO treated as escaped income. After issuing notice under section 148A(b), the AO passed an order under section 148A(d) on 07.04.2022 and proceeded with reassessment, but instead of taxing the alleged deposits, he made a disallowance of ₹7,06,146 under section 80P(2)(a)(i).

The Tribunal quashed the reassessment proceedings, relying on the Bombay High Court ruling in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd., which requires the AO, if reopening is based on a particular escapement issue, to actually assess that issue; the AO cannot “abandon” the original reason for reopening and then make a fresh addition on an unrelated matter. In practical terms, the decision means that where reassessment is initiated to examine alleged unexplained deposits or similar escaped income, the tax authority must either sustain an addition on that very issue or lose the jurisdictional basis for the reassessment if it shifts to a different disallowance, such as denial of a deduction under section 80P. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that reopening notices and resulting additions must match: a reassessment founded on one alleged item of escaped income cannot be lawfully used as a general opportunity to make unrelated adjustments.

rows.summary:
This GSTAT matter concerned an anti-profiteering allegation against M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. in its “Vertex Panache” real estate project, where the applicant alleged that the company did not pass on the benefit of additional input tax credit (ITC) that arose after GST came into force on 01.07.2017, which would amount to a violation of Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee referred the complaint to the DGAP, and the DGAP’s initial report alleged total profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as base profiteering plus Rs. 7,82,144/- as GST, said to be distributable among 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes defended itself by arguing that the increase in construction costs had substantially absorbed the ITC benefit, pointing to a budgeted construction cost of Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/- versus actual expenditure of Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, a difference of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost.

The company specifically said the cost escalation was driven by major input increases of 19.87% for Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% for sand, and 73.17% for bricks, and claimed that the additional expenditure attributable to these items alone was Rs. 3,49,87,499/- based on actual quantities and costs. It relied on the Delhi High Court’s reasoning in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, especially paragraph 118, to argue that genuine commercial cost increases can justify higher prices even where tax incidence changes or ITC becomes available. The respondent also supported its position with a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 issued by M/s Tukaram & Co.

On the material provided, the key compliance issue is the anti-profiteering rule under Section 171: businesses affected by GST transition, especially real estate project developers, must pass on the benefit of ITC to recipients unless they can substantiate that other bona fide cost escalations offset that benefit. The document does not provide the final GSTAT outcome or any new rule-making deadline; rather, it records the dispute and the company’s cost-escalation defense against the allegation that ITC benefits were not passed through.

This order concerns an anti-profiteering allegation against **M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd.** arising from the claimed failure to pass on the GST rate-cut benefit on **“MI LED Television 4A 80 cm”** after the GST rate was reduced from **28% to 18%**, effective **1 January 2019**, under **Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31 December 2018**. The complaint was filed by **Shri Rohit Kumar Agrawal** and referred to the **DGAP** by the Standing Committee under **Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017**. DGAP examined invoices and outward taxable supply records for the period **1 November 2018 to 31 December 2018** (pre-rate reduction) and **1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019** (post-rate reduction) and initially found profiteering of **₹7,79,947**.

During the proceedings, after the matter moved from the now-ceased National Anti-Profiteering Authority to the **GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)**, the Tribunal required the respondent to prove that the alleged profiteered amount had been returned to customers. The company relied on **Electronic Gift Voucher (EGV)** screenshots, an **Excel mapping** linking vouchers to customer orders/invoices, and later **credit notes**. DGAP’s initial objection was that the EGVs appeared **conditional, time-bound, and restricted**, and that the internal label **“Offers and cash back”** did not by itself show that the GST benefit had been passed on.

DGAP ultimately accepted **credit notes of ₹2,21,056** issued to **174 customers** whose orders had been cancelled or whose goods were returned, reducing the alleged profiteering amount to **₹5,58,891**. The respondent argued that the remaining benefit had also been passed on through EGVs and associated customer mappings, and the Tribunal assessed whether those vouchers constituted valid transfer of the GST benefit. The key compliance point from the decision is that the Tribunal treated **EGVs as a valid mode of passing on the GST rate-reduction benefit**, provided there is adequate traceability to the affected customer transactions and the benefit is demonstrably linked to the price reduction obligation.

The order results in a direction for a **₹10,241 fund deposit** (as reflected in the title), indicating a residual amount was required to be deposited rather than fully retained by the company. For compliance teams, the substantive takeaway is that when a GST rate cut applies from a specified effective date, businesses must ensure the benefit is passed on to end customers through a clearly documented mechanism—whether by price reduction, refund, credit note, or voucher—supported by transaction-level evidence; where vouchers are used, the company should maintain documentary linkage showing the voucher corresponds to the specific sale and the statutory benefit has been transferred.

rows.summary:
The document summarizes an ITAT Hyderabad decision in **Ravi Kumar Gollapudi v. DCIT** for **Assessment Year 2018-19** involving the tax treatment of **interest expense claimed against interest income under “Income from other sources.”** The assessee filed a return declaring **total income of ₹30,33,940**, and the case was selected for **limited scrutiny**, with a notice issued under **section 143(2)**. During assessment, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had claimed **interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089** against **interest income of ₹58,81,505** reported in the year; the prior year figures were also discussed, with **interest income of ₹65,26,481** reported in the earlier year, while the assessee stated that the remaining interest was received in later years.

The key issue was whether the expense could be disallowed simply because the interest paid in the year exceeded the interest received in that year. The ITAT held that, because the assessee regularly followed the **cash system of accounting**, recognition of interest income on an **actual receipt basis** is permissible under **section 145(1)**, so a year-to-year mismatch between interest paid and interest received cannot, by itself, justify outright denial of the deduction. However, the Tribunal made clear that deduction under **section 57(iii)** is not automatic: the assessee must establish a **direct nexus** between the borrowed funds, the interest-bearing advance, and the income actually offered to tax.

As a result, the Tribunal did **not** accept the disallowance as a matter of principle, but it also did **not** allow the full claim unconditionally; instead, it **remanded the matter** for verification of whether the necessary nexus exists. The amount in dispute discussed by the Tribunal was a **₹13.66 lakh disallowance**, and the compliance takeaway is that taxpayers using the cash system can defer recognition of interest income until receipt, but they still need contemporaneous evidence showing that the borrowed funds were used to generate the taxable interest income to support a deduction under section 57(iii).

Along with the Information, the Informant filed IA No. 178A of 2025 seeking interim relief under Section 33. The Commission noted that it had already considered the impugned agreements in its order dated 02.06.2026 and had formed a prima facie view that certain clauses raised concerns, resulting in a direction for investigation which remained pending before the DG. Granting them while the matter was under investigation would have the effect of pre-judging the issues requiring determination. The Commission therefore held that the interim reliefs were neither appropriate nor warranted at that stage. Having regard to the dictum of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Competition Commission of India v. Ste
rows.summary:
The Competition Commission of India refused to grant interim relief in the matter filed by Smt. Rinima Borah Agarwal against Mrs. India Inc., a sole proprietorship run by Smt. Mohini Sharma. The Informant had invoked Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002, alleging violations of Sections 3 and 4, and the Commission had already, by order dated 02.06.2026 under Section 26(1), directed the Director General to investigate the case.  

In the interim application (IA No. 178A of 2025), the Informant asked the Commission to stay specified clauses in the Participant Terms and Conditions dated 23.10.2024 and the Winner’s Terms and Conditions dated 27.10.2024, and also to restrain Mrs. India Inc. from issuing any communications that would restrict or discourage her from joining or participating in other competitions while the case was pending. The Commission held that these requests were effectively the same as final relief, and granting them before the DG investigation was completed would improperly decide issues that still needed to be investigated and adjudicated.  

Accordingly, the Commission found that interim relief was not appropriate or warranted at that stage and rejected the application. The key compliance implication is that the challenged contractual clauses were not yet stayed, but they had already been identified by the Commission as potentially raising competition concerns and remain under active DG investigation, so the underlying terms and communications are still exposed to scrutiny and possible future relief after investigation.

rows.title: Corporate Law | DNA Evidence Establishes Paternity, Not Consent: Delhi HC Upholds Acquittal
rows.desc: Summary: The Delhi High Court, in KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr., upheld the acquittal of Respondent No. 2 and dismissed the complainant’s appeal. The Court held that a DNA report establishing biological paternity proves the fact of sexual intercourse but does not, by itself, establish whether the relationship was consensual. It considered the allegations of repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion and administration of an intoxicating substance, along with the DNA evidence. The Court examined the Trial Court’s assessment of inconsistencies in the complainant’s testimony, the delay in disclosure and reporting, the surrounding circumstances and the defence of a consensual relationship. Relying on the principles governing appeals against acquittal, including the Supreme Court’s decision in Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors., the Court held that an acquittal should not be disturbed where the Trial Court’s view is reasonably possible. Interference requires patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading or omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons. The Court also cautioned that the conduct of a complainant in a sexual-offence case cannot be assessed through stereotypical assumptions. It ultimately held that the gravity of an accusation cannot substitute the requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr., CRL.A. 320/2026 and CRL.M.A. 10175/2026, Neutral Citation No. 2026:DHC:7451, considered an appeal against the a
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court, in **KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.** ( **CRL.A. 320/2026** and **CRL.M.A. 10175/2026**, Neutral Citation **2026:DHC:7451**), **dismissed the complainant’s appeal and upheld the respondent’s acquittal** in a sexual-offence prosecution. The Court reiterated that a **DNA report showing biological paternity only proves that sexual intercourse occurred**; it **does not, by itself, prove that the intercourse was non-consensual**, which remained the critical issue in dispute. The case involved allegations of **repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion, and administration of an intoxicating substance**, but the Court accepted the Trial Court’s evaluation that the evidence, including the complainant’s testimony and the surrounding circumstances, contained **material inconsistencies** and that there had been **delay in disclosure/reporting**.

For compliance purposes, the key legal standard reinforced here is the **limited scope of appellate interference with acquittals**: an acquittal should not be disturbed if the Trial Court’s view is a **reasonably possible view**. The High Court said reversal on appeal requires something materially more serious, such as **patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading of evidence, omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons**. The Court relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in **Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors.** for that standard.

The Court also emphasized that, in sexual-offence cases, a complainant’s conduct **cannot be judged through stereotypical assumptions**, and that the **seriousness or gravity of the allegation cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt**. In practical terms, the ruling underscores that investigators and litigants should not treat **DNA/paternity evidence as dispositive of consent**, and that prosecution must still independently establish the elements of the offence, especially lack of consent, through reliable and coherent evidence.

The Tribunal held that where the reassessment order constitutes the very foundation of the penalty, its validity can be examined even in collateral penalty proceedings. Finding that the notice u/s 148 had been issued with the approval of an incompetent authority, the Tribunal quashed both the reassessment order & the consequential penalty. The assessee, Shri Ahmed Altaf Sayeed, had filed the appeal against the order of the CIT(A) confirming a penalty of ₹2,13,664 u/s 270A for AY 2018-19. Delay caused by professional lapse condoned There was a delay of 110 days in filing the appeal before the Tribunal. The assessee explained that he had entrusted the matter to his Chartered Accountant before travelling to Saudi Arabia for pilgrimage. He genuinely believed that the appeal would be filed within the prescribed period. However, owing to pressure of audit work & return filing, the Chartered Accountant inadvertently lost sight of the limitation date. After returning from Saudi Arabia, the assessee contacted the Chartered Accountant & the appeal was filed immediately. The assessee supported his explanation with an affid
rows.summary:
The Hyderabad ITAT held that a penalty order under section 270A cannot survive where the underlying reassessment itself was initiated on a legally defective notice under section 148. In this case, the assessee challenged a confirmed penalty of ₹2,13,664 for AY 2018-19, and the Tribunal accepted that the validity of the reassessment proceedings could be examined even in an appeal against the penalty, because the reassessment was the foundation of the penalty. The key defect was that the notice under section 148 had been issued with approval from an authority that was not competent under section 151, so the reassessment order was quashed and the consequential penalty was also set aside.

For compliance purposes, the ruling underscores that reassessment action must be backed by approval from the correct “specified authority” under section 151; if the sanctioning authority is wrong or lacks jurisdiction, the notice and everything flowing from it are vulnerable to challenge. It also confirms that taxpayers may raise such a jurisdictional defect later, even in collateral proceedings against penalty, rather than being confined only to an immediate challenge to the reassessment notice. Separately, the Tribunal condoned a 110-day delay in filing the appeal because the assessee showed that the delay resulted from a professional lapse by the Chartered Accountant while the assessee was abroad for pilgrimage, indicating that bona fide, adequately explained filing delays may be excused where supported by an affidavit and credible facts.

It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of
rows.summary:
The document explains the GST input tax credit restriction in Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act as it applies to works contract services and to goods/services used for constructing immovable property, and notes that tax authorities are issuing notices demanding reversal of ITC claimed on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses. The core compliance issue is that ITC connected to “immovable property” is generally blocked, but the article emphasizes that not every item installed in a building is immovable, so credits related to separately identifiable plant, machinery, and other movable business equipment may still be eligible if the facts support that characterization. It specifically discusses how immovable property is determined using the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act, and judicial tests such as the purpose of annexation, the degree and permanency of attachment, functionality, intention, and marketability, which means compliance teams need to assess each asset or installation based on substance rather than simply treating all site work as ineligible.

The article highlights that items such as HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, cabling, security systems, and other business equipment can fall into the movable-or-eligible-credit analysis depending on how they are installed and used, rather than being automatically treated as blocked immovable property. It also notes the statutory exceptions under Section 17(5), including the carve-out for plant and machinery and situations where construction is not undertaken on the taxable person’s own account, which are key points for defending ITC positions. A practical compliance recommendation is to structure procurement and execution through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services, because combining them in a single contract increases the risk that otherwise eligible credit may be denied or disputed by the department.

For compliance purposes, the document does not introduce a new deadline, rate, or filing date; instead, it addresses ongoing eligibility rules and audit/litigation risk under existing GST law. The operational takeaway is that companies building or expanding business facilities should document the legal and functional nature of each installation, segregate billing where possible, and retain evidence supporting why an item is movable or qualifies as plant and machinery so they can justify ITC claims if challenged.

rows.title: Income Tax | Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebuyers
rows.desc: How Home Buyers Get Trapped into Paying TDS Interest When Builders Delay Telling Them About TDS on Installments Summary: Homebuyers purchasing property from builders through construction-linked installments may incur substantial interest liability if tax is not deducted at source from each payment. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer acquiring qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% at the time of payment or credit, whichever is earlier. For transactions governed by the 1961 Act, the buyer must furnish Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction and issue Form 16B to the seller. From 1 April 2026, the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with Form 141 replacing Form 26QB for applicable transactions. Problems arise when builders raise installment demands without informing buyers about TDS and communicate the requirement only near possession or final payment. Earlier installments may consequently remain subject to delayed deduction. Interest is then payable from the date on which tax should have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the obligation. Under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest applies at 1% per month or part thereof for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part thereof for delayed deposit after deduction. Buyers should independently monitor every installment, deduct TDS within the applicable timeline and complete the prescribed statement and certificate requirements without waiting for instructions from the builder. Table of Contents▸ Introduction What the Law Actually Says Where the Problem Starts Why This Creates an Interest Liability What Buyers Should Actually Do Final Thought Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction Buying a flat or property from a builder is usually done in installments—some amount at booking, some at various construction stages, and the balance near poss
rows.summary:
The document explains that homebuyers paying builders through construction-linked installments can face TDS noncompliance if they do not deduct tax from each installment when due. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer of qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% on each payment or credit, whichever occurs earlier, and for covered transactions must file Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month in which deduction is made; the buyer must also issue Form 16B to the seller. The document warns that builders may ask for installment payments without mentioning TDS until later, often near possession or the final payment, but that delay does not excuse earlier non-deduction: if TDS was not deducted when required, interest is still charged from the date the tax should originally have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the rule.

It specifically states that under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest is 1% per month or part of a month for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part of a month for delayed deposit after deduction. It also notes a law change effective 1 April 2026: the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, and Form 141 will replace Form 26QB for applicable transactions. The compliance takeaway is that buyers should track every installment independently, deduct and deposit TDS on time for each payment, and complete the required statement and certificate filings without waiting for builder instructions; otherwise, they may accrue avoidable interest even where the builder did not inform them promptly.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by using the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts” in a conclusory way. In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the company challenged an **SCN dated 13.06.2025** for **FY 2018–19** involving a demand of **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, arguing that the normal limitation period under **Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025** and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without stating any concrete facts showing fraud or suppression. The Court agreed that the **notice itself must disclose the foundational facts** that justify using the extended period; the legal validity of the SCN is judged on its face, and later explanations cannot cure a jurisdictional defect.

The Court found the SCN deficient because it contained only a vague reference to **“fraud or concealment of facts”** without explaining **what conduct amounted to fraud, how concealment was detected, or what specific facts were allegedly suppressed**. It also noted that the use of the word **“or”** reflected uncertainty as to the exact allegation being made, which further undermined the validity of the invocation of Section 74. The department attempted to justify the notice through its counter affidavit, but the Supreme Court refused to rely on those post hoc explanations, reiterating that a defective notice cannot be repaired through later pleadings in court.

As a result, the Supreme Court **set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order and quashed the SCN itself**, and it **restrained the department from taking further action on the basis of that notice**. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that when GST authorities seek to proceed under **Section 74** rather than **Section 73**, the notice must contain **specific, stated reasons and factual particulars** supporting fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression; a bare label is not enough to sustain the extended limitation period or the demand.

rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench restored a **Section 129 penalty under the UPGST Act, 2017** for a consignment of **iron goods/scrap moved without an E-Way Bill**, holding that the surrounding facts supported an inference of attempted tax evasion. The case arose from transport of **132.90 cubic feet of iron goods** by **M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly** under **Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018**; the vehicle was intercepted by the **Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018**, and the driver did **not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception**. On that basis, the authorities imposed **tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- under Section 129(3)**.

The first appellate authority had earlier **set aside both the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018**, but the Tribunal reversed that outcome. The Department’s position was that movement without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated **Rule 138 of the GST Rules**, and that later production of the **tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment** did not erase the original compliance failure. It argued that the interception circumstances, the nature of the goods, the route, and the subsequent documentary production together indicated an **intention to evade tax**.

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the Tribunal treated **absence of an E-Way Bill during transport as a serious statutory breach that can trigger detention and penalty even if supporting sales/tax documents exist later**. The decision reinforces that businesses moving taxable goods must ensure the **E-Way Bill is generated and available with the vehicle/driver before or during transit as required**, because post-event document submission may not prevent **Section 129 tax and penalty exposure**. The source text also notes an internal **party-description inconsistency** in the order, where the cause title and paragraph references do not align on which side was appellant/respondent, but that inconsistency does not change the substantive holding that the **Section 129 penalty was restored**.

rows.summary:
The Tribunal considered three connected appeals involving developers/construction companies in Chennai and Coimbatore: Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd., Ceebros Property Development, and Prime Developers. The department had issued show cause notices alleging short-payment of service tax on their construction projects under **Commercial or Industrial Construction Service** and disputing the assessees’ use of the **Works Contract Service composition scheme** after **1 June 2007**. For Real Value Promoters, the dispute specifically covered four projects, with the department objecting to the tax treatment adopted for **Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, and Surya Skanda** on the ground that the activity was not a valid works contract and that the appellants had not properly exercised the option required for the composition scheme.

The common legal issue was whether these development/construction arrangements should be treated as **separate supply/construction arrangements plus ECIS-related activity** rather than as a single **works contract** for service tax purposes. The Tribunal’s order addresses the classification dispute that affected how service tax was to be computed, including whether the assessees could lawfully pay tax under the **works contract composition scheme** after **1.6.2007** instead of under the general construction-service category. The order indicates that the department’s demand was based on a view that the contract structure and the nature of the services did not satisfy the requirements for works contract classification.

This decision matters for compliance because it highlights that real estate developers and contractors cannot assume that all construction-linked service arrangements automatically qualify as works contracts merely because they involve construction activity and some material supply. The key compliance point is that tax treatment depends on the actual contractual structure and whether the statutory conditions for the composition route were properly met, including any required election/option formalities. The relevant tax periods are those after **1 June 2007**, when service tax under the works contract composition scheme was being claimed by the appellants, and the order arose from original adjudication orders dated **16.8.2010**, **6.1.2010**, and **10.5.2010** for the respective appellants.

The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in a GST-fraud-related criminal case involving an allegedly non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The applicant’s name reportedly surfaced only through the statement of Sakeel Khan, and he claimed to have no criminal history other than the present case. The disputed period was 2009-10 to 2014-15, covering both the pre-negative-list and post-negative-list service tax regimes. The appellant had received Rs. 3,06,738/- from hoarding rent during April 2009 to June 2012 and Rs. 3,39,22,974/- as rent from various immovable properties during April 2009 to July 2014. The Department proposed service tax of Rs. 39,22,945/- together with interest, penalties and late fee for non-filing of ST-3 returns. The demand was confirmed by the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals), leading to the appeal before the Tribunal. The appellant contended that the expression “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been incorrectly interpreted. It argued, relying particularly on Cuddalore Municipality Vs Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise, that the expression “any other person” meant a person other than the owner. It also argued that vacant land was excluded from the relevant definition and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect service tax rate. On advertisement receipts, the appellant maintained that it merely collected statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than selling advertisin
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi decision examines service tax exposure of a municipality for two separate streams of receipts during the period 2009-10 to 2014-15: (1) amounts collected for allowing advertisers to use municipal land/space for hoardings, and (2) rent/licence fees received from leasing or licensing municipal immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons, and traders. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding-related receipts between April 2009 and June 2012, and Rs. 3,39,22,974 from immovable-property rent between April 2009 and July 2014; the Department demanded service tax of Rs. 39,22,945, plus interest, penalties, and late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns. Both the adjudicating authority and the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand before the matter reached the Tribunal.

On the renting issue, the municipality argued that “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been wrongly applied, that the phrase “any other person” in the relevant definition should be read to mean someone other than the owner, that vacant land was outside the taxable definition, and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect rate. On the hoarding issue, it contended that it was only collecting statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than providing advertising services in the commercial sense. The Tribunal accepted the municipality’s position on the hoarding receipts and held that the municipal collection for allotment/licensing of space for hoardings was not taxable as an advertising service in the manner alleged by the Department.

At the same time, the Tribunal held that the municipality’s renting/licensing of immovable property was taxable service, meaning the activity of allowing use of municipal immovable property did fall within the service tax net. However, it quashed the extended-period service tax demand, so the Department could not sustain the longer look-back invocation on the facts of the case. The decision therefore leaves municipal bodies exposed to service tax on taxable renting/licensing of immovable property for the relevant period, but it also confirms that hoarding-space collections made as statutory municipal licence fees were not to be treated as the disputed taxable advertising service in this case, and it relieves the assessee from the extended-period demand, along with the associated penalties and late-filing consequences to the extent tied to that extended demand.

rows.title: Income Tax | MEIS Rewards Taxable as Revenue Receipt from AY 2016-17: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12628 Case Name DCIT Vs Aarti Drugs Ltd. (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The ITAT Mumbai Special Bench was constituted to decide whether the amount received by the assessee under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 is taxable as a revenue receipt in view of the amendment to Section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act by insertion of clause (xviii) with effect from Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee, engaged in manufacturing specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had initially claimed the MEIS assistance as a revenue receipt, but subsequently contended before the CIT(A) that it was a capital receipt. The CIT(A) accepted the assessee’s contention for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, leading to the Revenue’s appeals. The Revenue argued that MEIS constitutes government assistance and falls within the amended definition of income under Section 2(24)(xviii), irrespective of the nomenclature of the benefit as a “reward”. It relied upon the objective of the Foreign Trade Policy, the expression “by whatever name called”, the Supreme Court’s decisions in Sahney Steel Press Works Ltd. and Ponni Sugars & Chemicals Ltd., and various Tribunal decisions. The assessee, on the other hand, contended that MEIS was a reward intended to improve the export competitiveness of the country and did not constitute the forms of assistance contemplated by Section 2(24)(xviii). It relied, among others, upon Ponni Sugars, CIT v. Chaphalkar Brothers, DCIT v. Munjal Auto Industries and Shree Balaji Alloys. The Special Bench first examined the “purpose test” laid down by the Supreme Court. In Sahney S
rows.summary:
This ITAT Mumbai Special Bench decision holds that receipts under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 are taxable as revenue receipts under the Income-tax Act from Assessment Year 2016-17 onward because of the amendment to section 2(24) inserting clause (xviii). The key statutory change is that, effective AY 2016-17, “assistance in the form of a subsidy or grant or cash incentive or duty drawback or waiver or concession or reimbursement by the Central Government or a State Government” is included in the definition of income “by whatever name called,” so the tribunal treated MEIS rewards as falling within this expanded income definition. The assessee, Aarti Drugs Ltd., a manufacturer of specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had originally treated the MEIS benefit as revenue, then argued before the CIT(A) that it was capital in nature; the CIT(A) accepted that view for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, but the Revenue appealed, and the Special Bench reversed that position.

The Tribunal’s reasoning was that the character of MEIS depends on the “purpose test” and the scheme’s operation, not on the label “reward.” It found that MEIS is government assistance linked to exports and meant to incentivize and support export activity, which places it within section 2(24)(xviii) for the relevant years, regardless of whether the benefit is described as a reward or incentive under the Foreign Trade Policy. The Revenue had relied on Supreme Court authorities such as Sahney Steel and Ponni Sugars, along with the statutory phrase “by whatever name called,” while the assessee argued MEIS was intended to improve export competitiveness and therefore should be treated as capital; the Special Bench did not accept that characterization for income-tax purposes after the AY 2016-17 amendment. Practically, the ruling means companies receiving MEIS benefits for export transactions from AY 2016-17 onward should treat those receipts as taxable revenue income and not as capital receipts, and should ensure their tax computations, return positions, and any past appellate positions for the relevant years align with this treatment.

rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s section 260A appeal in **PCIT v. NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd.** concerning **A.Y. 2009-10**, where the reassessment notice under **section 148** had been issued on **09.03.2015**, i.e. **more than four years after the end of the relevant assessment year**. The assessee was a manufacturing company dealing in edible and non-edible oil products and by-products, and its original assessment under **section 143(3)** had been completed on **29.12.2011**. The recorded reasons for reopening referred to two alleged issues: a supposed short disallowance under **section 14A read with Rule 8D**, and alleged income of **Rs. 244.98 crores** said to have been received from **National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL)** through a paper trade arrangement.  

In the reassessment, however, the Assessing Officer did **not** make any addition on either of those recorded grounds; instead, he made a disallowance of **Rs. 13,89,08,810/-** under **section 43(5) read with section 73 and section 40A(2)(b)**, plus an additional **Rs. 1,04,652/-** as an excess disallowance under **section 14A**. The assessee challenged the reopening before the CIT(A), arguing that the reassessment was invalid because no addition arose from the very reasons recorded for reopening. The CIT(A) accepted that position, noting that the **Rs. 244.98 crore NSEL figure** related to an addition made in the assessee’s case for **A.Y. 2011-12**, not the year under appeal, and that the assessee had **not undertaken NSEL transactions in A.Y. 2009-10**; the CIT(A) also held that the original **section 14A** disallowance had already been deleted.  

The High Court upheld the CIT(A) and the Tribunal, effectively confirming that where reassessment is initiated on specific recorded reasons but the final reassessment does not make any addition on those reasons, the reopening cannot be sustained on the basis of unrelated additions made later in the reassessment order. For compliance purposes, the decision is significant for tax audit and reassessment risk management: where reopening is beyond four years and is founded on particular alleged escapement items, the Revenue must be able to connect the final reassessment to those recorded grounds; otherwise, the reassessment is vulnerable to being quashed.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 272A(2)(e) Penalty Cannot Continue Beyond Section 139(4): Chennai ITAT
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12626 Case Name Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2013-14 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Swamy Vivekanandha Vidhyala Trust Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The appeal concerned levy of penalty under section 272A(2)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for failure by a charitable trust to furnish its return of income. The assessee, a charitable trust running an educational institution and registered under section 12A, had not filed its return for AY 2013-14. The Assessing Officer received information that the assessee had deposited cash of Rs. 75,55,200/- into its bank account. Consequently, assessment proceedings were reopened by issuing notice under section 147. In response, the assessee filed a return declaring Nil income after claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad). The assessment under section 147 accepted the returned income. Subsequently, penalty proceedings under section 272A(2)(e) were initiated. The assessee explained that the return had not been filed because of a bona fide belief that no return was required where the income was exempt. It also contended that there was no loss to the Revenue and no intention to conceal income. The Assessing Officer rejected these submissions and levied penalty of Rs. 3,04,300/-. The CIT(A) confirmed the penalty, holding, among other things, that the assessee had failed to comply with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was not an acceptable excuse, absence of revenue loss and mens rea was irrelevant, and that the penalty was mandatory in the absence of reasonable cause under section 273B. At the hearing before the Tribunal, the assessee pressed only ground No.8 and did not press the remaining gro
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a penalty for failure to file a return under section 272A(2)(e) cannot keep running indefinitely for a charitable trust once the statutory extended-filing period under section 139(4) has expired. The assessee in this case was a registered charitable trust running an educational institution, and for AY 2013-14 it had not originally filed a return; the Assessing Officer later reopened the matter after noticing cash deposits of Rs. 75,55,200 in the trust’s bank account. In response to the reopening, the trust filed a return declaring nil income and claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad), and the assessment under section 147 accepted that returned income.

Penalty proceedings were then initiated under section 272A(2)(e) for the original failure to furnish the return. The Assessing Officer imposed a penalty of Rs. 3,04,300, and the CIT(A) upheld it, reasoning that the trust had not complied with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was no defense, that no revenue loss and no mens rea were irrelevant, and that penalty was mandatory absent reasonable cause under section 273B. Before the Tribunal, the assessee ultimately pressed only one ground, and the ITAT accepted the core legal principle that while penalty may be leviable for failure to file, the default period cannot extend beyond the last date permitted for belated filing under section 139(4). In practical compliance terms, the ruling means that for entities covered by section 139 obligations—here, a charitable trust—the exposure to section 272A(2)(e) penalty is limited to the period of actual default up to the section 139(4) deadline, rather than being calculated as an open-ended continuing default after that point.

No. 1242 of 2026; that earlier writ was disposed of on 09.02.2026 with a direction to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and submit a reply to the section 148 notice. In this later petition, she asked the Court to quash the demand and direct reopening of the income-tax e-filing portal because she claimed she could not upload the return due to technical problems on the portal.

A key compliance-relevant fact is that the petitioner had already deposited Rs. 5 lakhs in purported compliance with the earlier High Court order, and she produced documentary evidence supporting that payment and other filings. She also submitted a screenshot to demonstrate the portal upload failure, and the Court accepted that screenshot as sufficient evidence of the technical issue. The Revenue had notice of the petition and did not disprove the inability to upload.

The Court held that, in the interests of justice, the petitioner must be given another opportunity to comply with the earlier direction to file the return. Accordingly, the writ petition was disposed of with a direction that portal access be restored/reopened so she could file the return of income, rather than treating the failure to upload as a default on the merits. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where a taxpayer can substantiate a bona fide e-filing portal failure with evidence such as screenshots and show partial compliance with a prior court direction, the High Court may permit later filing instead of letting the demand or non-compliance stand uncorrected.

Bank of Baroda were required to be adjusted between the interest component and the principal tax component. The consolidated order covered AYs 2003-04, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2016-17 and 2005-06, with ITA No.5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 taken as the lead case. The Revenue challenged the order of the CIT(A), NFAC, contending that where a refund comprised both tax and interest under section 244A, any refund payment should first be appropriated towards the principal tax component rather than the interest component. According to the Revenue, section 244A contained no express provision prescribing that interest should be adjusted first. It was also argued that adjusting the refund against interest would result in further interest liability on the unpaid tax component and would effectively amount to charging interest on interest. The assessee contended that the issue had already been settled by various judicial decisions and by decisions of the Tribunal in its own case. It relied on the principle of consistency and submitted that, in the absence of any change in facts or circumstances, the earlier view should be followed. The assessee also relied upon decisions concerning Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India and Tata Sons Limited, among others. The Tribunal noted that section 244A provides
rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT dismissed the Revenue’s appeals and upheld the CIT(A), NFAC view on how income-tax refunds must be adjusted when the refund amount includes both principal tax and interest under section 244A. The dispute arose in consolidated appeals involving Bank of Baroda for AYs 2003-04, 2005-06, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2016-17, with ITA No. 5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 treated as the lead case. The Revenue argued that, because section 244A does not expressly say otherwise, any refund should be first appropriated against the principal tax component rather than the interest component, and that doing the reverse would create additional interest exposure on the unpaid tax and effectively amount to charging “interest on interest.”

The assessee relied on prior judicial rulings, including decisions in its own case, and argued that the issue was already settled and should be followed on consistency grounds absent any change in facts or law. It also cited supporting rulings involving other taxpayers such as Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India, and Tata Sons Limited. The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position and confirmed that the refund adjustment under section 244A must be made interest-first rather than tax-first, rejecting the Revenue’s contrary contention. For compliance purposes, this means that where the department issues a refund under section 244A that includes both tax and statutory interest, the refund amount is to be applied first toward the interest component before being applied to the principal tax liability, and the Revenue cannot insist on a tax-first set-off in these circumstances.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017. As a result, the customs demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068/- along with consequential interest was quashed, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-appellants, were held unsustainable.

The dispute arose from a DEEC licence obtained under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002, which allowed duty-free import of 5350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue’s allegation was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that maize had been fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the required steel products. The Tribunal rejected the demand because the department did not produce reliable, corroborative evidence to sustain the fraud allegation.

In reaching that conclusion, CESTAT relied on multiple pieces of supporting evidence: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga land customs station, customs examination of the export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, confirmation from DRI Chennai regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, actual realization of export proceeds, and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. The Tribunal also noted that the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report indicating that the available evidence did not support the allegation of fraud. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that customs duty demands and associated penalties based on alleged diversion or sham exports must be supported by solid, corroborated evidence, and that documented export clearance, certification, foreign buyer permission, receipt of export proceeds, and DGFT discharge evidence can be decisive in defeating such allegations.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside a customs penalty of **₹425,27,99,100 (about ₹425.28 crore)** that had been imposed on **Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya** by the **Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat** under **Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962**. The underlying allegation was that a consignment of **natural diamonds** had been wrongly declared as **lab-grown diamonds** in order to secure a **lower customs tariff**, but the Supreme Court did **not** decide that merits issue.

Instead, the case turned on the integrity of the materials relied on in the customs adjudication. The appellant argued that several judgments and articles cited in the **Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025** were generated using **artificial intelligence**. The Supreme Court independently checked the authorities used by the second respondent and found that some cited case laws were **non-existent** or had **fake citations**, while others existed but **did not support the legal propositions** attributed to them; the Court described this as appearing to be an **AI “hallucination.”**

The matter had already been taken to the **Gujarat High Court**, which dismissed the challenge on **20.01.2026** before the case reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court relied on its recent ruling in **Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd.**, reiterating a **zero-tolerance approach** to producing, citing, or relying on **AI-generated precedents without verification**. For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that adjudicating authorities and litigants must **independently verify all case law and legal authorities before using them in orders or pleadings**, because reliance on fabricated or misrepresented authorities can lead to the order being undermined or set aside.

The petitioner sought a direction to the respondent to lift the blockage and permit free utilisation of the Input Tax Credit available in the electronic credit ledger. An assessment order dated 17.03.2023 had been issued for the assessment period 2017-2020. Primarily challenging the clubbing of assessments relating to multiple assessment periods, the petitioner had filed W.P.No.41890 of 2025. An interim stay concerning recovery measures was granted on 25.02.2026. The electronic credit ledger, however, had already been blocked on 04.02.2025, and that blocking order was challenged in the present writ petition. The petitioner contended that the blocking could not survive in view of the interim order dated 25.02.2026. It was further argued that the blocking travelled beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act. Comparing Section 79 with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, learned counsel contended that negative blocking was impermissible under Section 79. The Revenue submitted that there was no infirmity in the blocking. It also contended that the interim order dated 25.02.2026 merely directed that recovery proceedings be kept in abeyance and did not affect the earlier blocking order. The Court accepted the Revenue’s inter
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court upheld the blocking of M/s. Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions’ electronic credit ledger, rejecting the petitioner’s challenge to reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025. The company had asked for the blockage to be lifted so it could freely use the input tax credit reflected in its electronic credit ledger, arguing that the blockage was beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act and that “negative blocking” is not permitted under that section when compared with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The petitioner also relied on an interim stay order dated 25.02.2026 in a separate writ petition (W.P. No. 41890 of 2025), but that stay related only to recovery proceedings arising from an assessment order dated 17.03.2023 for the 2017–2020 assessment period.

The Court accepted the Revenue’s position that the 25.02.2026 interim order did not undo or invalidate the earlier 04.02.2025 electronic credit ledger blocking, because the stay only kept recovery proceedings in abeyance and did not address the ledger freeze itself. As a result, the blocking of the electronic credit ledger remained in force, and the petitioner was not granted free utilisation of the input tax credit. For compliance teams, the practical point is that a stay on recovery measures does not automatically解除 or override a separate ledger-blocking action; if the department has already imposed a block on the electronic credit ledger, it may continue independently unless specifically challenged and set aside.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kerala HC Remands Medical PG Stipend vs Salary Dispute for Fresh Assessment
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12620 Case Name Nahas Kakkattummal Vs ITO (Kerala High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Kerala High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. The dispute concerned amounts received by the appellant while pursuing postgraduate medical studies. According to the appellant, the amounts were stipend and not salary. The appellant’s counsel contended that the assessment order had been issued by relying “blindly” on documents supplied by the University where the appellant was studying and drawing stipend, in which the sums were shown as salary. It was submitted that the appellant was admittedly a postgraduate student and that the amount received was stipend statutorily paid under law and in accordance with mandatory guidelines of the National Medical Commission. On that basis, it was argued that the Assessing Authority could not assess the receipts as salary. Alternatively, the appellant sought liberty to produce additional documents before the Assessing Authority. Counsel pointed out that even the University communication relied upon by the Assessing Authority categorically certified that the appellant had been admitted to an MD/MS postgraduate course as a Junior Resident. It was submitted that such students were covered by the regulations of the NMC, which prohibited payment of salary but mandated stipend. The appellant also relied upon Ext.P5, which certified that he was a bona fide PG student of the University, and contended that the letters relied upon by th
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court considered a writ appeal by a medical postgraduate student, Nahas Kakkattummal, challenging an income-tax assessment that treated amounts he received during his MD/MS studies as **salary** rather than **stipend**. The appellant argued that he was an admitted postgraduate medical student, that the payments were **statutorily mandated stipend** under the **National Medical Commission (NMC)** regulations, and that the Assessing Officer had wrongly relied on university documents “blindly” because those documents referred to the payments as salary even though the same communications also certified that he was a **bona fide PG student / Junior Resident**. He also relied on an additional certificate (Ext. P5) supporting his student status and asked, at minimum, for permission to place further documents before the tax authorities.

The High Court noted that the Single Judge had declined to exercise writ jurisdiction and sent the petitioner to the ordinary statutory remedy under the Income Tax Act, 1961, but the appellate court found it appropriate to intervene to ensure the factual issue was properly examined. The court therefore **remanded the matter for fresh assessment** so the Assessing Authority could reconsider whether the receipts were actually stipend or taxable salary, rather than simply accepting the university’s description at face value.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that payments made to **medical postgraduate trainees/junior residents** may need to be evaluated based on the governing **NMC rules** and the person’s actual training status, not merely by how an employer/university labels the payment in correspondence or records. The decision underscores a need to maintain documentation showing the recipient’s enrollment/status, the legal basis for the payment, and whether the payment is stipend under mandatory medical education regulations, because those facts may determine the income-tax characterization. The document does **not** state a new general tax rate or threshold; the operative change is the court’s direction for **fresh fact-finding/assessment** on the true nature of the receipts.
