rows.summary:
The Kolkata ITAT’s SMC Bench dealt with an AY 2015-16 reassessment of Sandhya Roy arising from a Joint Development Agreement dated 22.01.2015. The assessee had not filed an original return of income and also did not file any return in response to the section 148 notice issued on 31.03.2022, after which the Assessing Officer completed reassessment under sections 147, 144 and 144B. The AO treated the JDA as a “transfer” under section 2(47), computed the alleged sale consideration at ₹48,68,542 based on fair market value plus cash consideration, assumed a nil cost of acquisition, and assessed long-term capital gains of ₹48,68,542 as total income.

Before the CIT(A) (NFAC order dated 16.02.2026), the assessee challenged both the reopening and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the assessee relied on the Supreme Court’s reassessment-transition rulings in Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajeev Bansal, but the CIT(A) rejected the argument because the section 148 notice was issued on 31.03.2022, i.e., before 01.04.2022, and therefore was not within the category of notices the Department had accepted as time-barred in the Supreme Court proceedings. The CIT(A) accordingly upheld the reassessment framework under the Ashish Agarwal directions.

On the substantive capital-gains issue, the ITAT noted that the dispute required fresh examination on the merits rather than summary affirmation. The Tribunal therefore remanded the matter back for reconsideration, meaning the capital-gains computation arising from the JDA is not finally sustained as decided below and must be re-adjudicated in light of the facts and applicable law. For compliance purposes, the case highlights that JDAs can be treated as transfer events for capital-gains purposes, that reassessment notices issued on 31.03.2022 are being tested against the Supreme Court’s transitional regime, and that taxpayers facing such notices must be prepared to substantiate both the validity of reopening and the correct valuation/capital-gains computation.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Allahabad HC Quashes GST Order for Notice Served Only Through Portal After Cancellation
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12618 Case Name Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Allahabad High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ved Enterprises Unnao Vs State of U.P (Allahabad High Court) Summary: The petitioner challenged the order dated May 28, 2022 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao under Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The writ petition was filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The petitioner’s registration under the Act had been cancelled on 16.11.2021. Thereafter, the petitioner did not carry on any business. A show cause notice was uploaded on the GST portal and, subsequently, the impugned order was passed under Section 74. The Court held that once the registration had been cancelled, the petitioner was not obligated to check the GST portal. The Court observed that the mode of service of any show cause notice had to be by way of alternative means to the petitioner. The petitioner relied upon the coordinate Bench decision in M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB. The Court stated that it was essentially in agreement with the principle enunciated by the coordinate Bench. Finding a violation of the principle of natural justice, the Allahabad High Court quashed and set aside the impugned order dated May 28, 2022. The Department was left at liberty to issue a proper notice to the petitioner and act in accordance with law. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P. and others, Neutral Citation No.2024:AHC:23697-DB FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT 1. Heard Sri Mukesh Kumar Tewa
rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court quashed a GST demand order passed under **Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh GST Act, 2017** against **Ved Enterprises, Unnao**, holding that the Department violated natural justice by serving the show-cause notice only through the GST portal after the taxpayer’s registration had already been cancelled. The petitioner’s GST registration had been **cancelled on 16 November 2021**, and the petitioner stated it was no longer carrying on business; in that situation, the Court said the taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to keep checking the portal for notices. The impugned order was dated **28 May 2022** and had been issued by the **Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao**.

The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on the coordinate Bench decision in **M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P.** and agreed with the principle that, where registration has been cancelled, service of notice must be made through **some alternative effective mode** rather than only by portal upload. Because the notice was not properly served, the resulting order was invalid and was **quashed and set aside**. The Department was expressly given liberty to **issue a proper notice** and proceed again **in accordance with law**, meaning any fresh action must comply with valid service requirements and procedural fairness. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that once a taxpayer’s GST registration is cancelled, portal-only communication may be insufficient for adverse proceedings, and authorities must use a service method reasonably calculated to reach the person before passing a demand order.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three related writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited by a common order dated 24.04.2026. All three matters arose from the same GST dispute for the tax period 2019–2020 and centered on the legality of limitation extension under the GST laws: one petition challenged an impugned order/reply dated 29.05.2024, another challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the consequential State Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the GST enactments extending limitation periods, and the third challenged a show cause notice dated 31.05.2024 issued in Form GST DRC-01 for the same tax period. The Court had earlier granted interim protection on 13.08.2024, and after that the jurisdictional State Tax Officer submitted a detailed report dated 27.01.2026.

Based on that report, the Court noted that the officer’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. In light of the later developments and the 27.01.2026 report, the Court closed the writ petitions rather than continuing to adjudicate the limitation challenge. For compliance teams, the practical point is that this decision does not announce a new general GST filing or reporting requirement; instead, it shows that limitation-extension actions under Section 168A, Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023, and related DRC-01 proceedings for the 2019–2020 period were central to the dispute, but the Court ultimately disposed of the matter after the departmental report. Entities with similar limitation-related GST notices, especially DRC-01 proceedings tied to extended limitation periods, should treat this as a reminder to verify whether the underlying extension mechanism and the factual basis asserted by the department remain defensible in their own cases.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court permitted Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. to pursue a delayed GST appeal and set aside the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the appeal as time-barred. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to hear and decide the appeal on merits, but only after the petitioner deposits the late fees, penalty, and any other statutory deposits that are legally payable. This means the Court treated the delay as excusable in the circumstances, rather than allowing a limitation-based dismissal to stand.

The petitioner had challenged the underlying order dated 07.02.2024 and also sought restoration of its GST registration, so the practical compliance impact is that cancellation/restoration disputes can still be revived through writ proceedings where the taxpayer shows circumstances beyond its control. The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on prior Rajasthan High Court decisions, especially the Division Bench ruling in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., where a 99-day delay was condoned after granting relaxation of the 120-day appellate window under Section 107 of the CGST Act, and the appeal was required to be entertained if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also cited other cases supporting condonation in appropriate facts, including M/s. Molana Construction Company, Man Singh Tanwar, RPC PSIPL JV (two decisions), and M/s. Kakar Automobiles.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that while Section 107 limitation issues remain important, the High Court has recognized that medical reasons and similar circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control can justify judicial relief against a strict limitation rejection. Entities facing GST cancellation or adverse orders should document such reasons carefully and be prepared to make all required statutory deposits, because the Court’s relief was conditional and did not eliminate the underlying payment obligations.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Jagdish Prasad Agrawal v. Union of India** dealt with the blocking of a taxpayer’s **Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger** under **Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. The petitioner, a partnership firm, had challenged the blocking of its **IGST ITC**, including the allegation that the credit had been blocked with a **negative balance**, and sought a declaration that the blocking was illegal, void, and inoperative, along with re-credit of any ITC that had been wrongly set off against the demand. By the time of hearing, the petitioner said the blocking had already **ceased automatically after one year**, as contemplated by the statute, and the ledger had been reactivated, so the only remaining issue was whether the department had complied with the mandatory safeguards under Rule 86A before blocking the credit.

The respondents admitted that the **Electronic Credit Ledger was now operational** again, but they **could not show that Rule 86A had been followed before the block was imposed**. They also conceded that, although the officer may have had reasons to act, **no proper reasoned order** had been passed and **no opportunity of hearing** had been given to the taxpayer before the blocking. The department characterized the failure to follow the rule as a **bona fide mistake** and assured the Court that **future blocking would be done only in accordance with law**. The key compliance takeaway is that **ITC blocking under Rule 86A is not a free-form administrative action**: the department must be able to demonstrate **pre-blocking compliance with the rule’s mandatory conditions and procedural safeguards**, including a reasoned basis for action, and it should not block credit without following the prescribed process.

For taxpayers and compliance teams, the case is important because it confirms that **blocking of ITC can be challenged if the department cannot prove Rule 86A compliance**, and that the blockage is not meant to continue indefinitely—here the Court noted that it had ended by **operation of the statute after one year**. Companies should therefore maintain documentation showing the status and use of their electronic credit ledger, promptly review any sudden ITC blockage notices or ledger freezes, and be prepared to question whether the authorities had recorded reasons and followed the required legal procedure before restricting credit.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The company was a 100% export unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers, and it exported those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had sought a refund under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, but the department rejected ₹78,79,939 of the claim on the ground that CENVAT credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services had no nexus with the exported output services.

Before the Tribunal, the taxpayer argued that taking credit, using credit, and claiming refund are legally separate steps, and that once the department had not disputed the availment of credit under Rule 14 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, it could not later deny the refund under Rule 5 by re-litigating the eligibility of those credits. It also argued that the disputed services qualified as “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on prior case law, and that a direct one-to-one nexus with the exported service was not required for refund eligibility. The Tribunal accepted the appeal and held that the refund could not be denied on the basis of the same credit’s alleged ineligibility when the credit itself had never been challenged or reversed under Rule 14. For compliance purposes, the case supports the position that exporters claiming refund of unutilised CENVAT credit should be prepared to substantiate input-service eligibility, but that an established, unchallenged credit availment record materially strengthens a Rule 5 refund claim and limits the department’s ability to reject the refund later on nexus grounds alone.

Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad considered an appeal by M/s Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. against an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014 confirming Service Tax demands, interest and penalties principally under “Banking and Other Financial Services” and “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” for 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The first dispute concerned charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from foreign buyers through banking channels. The appellant, a manufacture-exporter of pharmaceutical products, contended that the foreign buyers remitted consideration through their banking arrangements and that the foreign/intermediary banks deducted charges before the balance reached the appellant’s Indian bank. The Department proceeded on the basis that, because the deductions economically reduced the amount received by the appellant, the appellant was the recipient of banking services and was liable to Service Tax under Reverse Charge Mechanism. The Tribunal rejected that approach. It found no evidence that the appellant had engaged the foreign banks, entered into contractual arrangements with them, or was otherwise obliged to pay consideration to them for services rendered to it. Merely bearing the economic impact of deductions did not establish a service provider-service recipient relationship. The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier decision, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020,
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. was not liable to service tax under reverse charge merely because foreign or intermediary banks deducted charges while transmitting export proceeds from overseas buyers to the company’s Indian bank account. The Tribunal rejected the Department’s theory that the company became the recipient of “Banking and Other Financial Services” simply because the net amount received was reduced by bank deductions; it found no evidence that Aurobindo had contracted with those foreign banks, engaged them, or agreed to pay them consideration for any service. In other words, an economic burden created by deduction from export remittances was not enough to create a taxable service-provider/service-recipient relationship.

The second issue concerned “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” in relation to regulatory approval support for pharmaceutical products. The Tribunal set aside the service tax demand on this count as well, concluding that the assistance taken for obtaining regulatory approvals in foreign jurisdictions was not taxable in the manner asserted by the Department on the facts of the case. The order under appeal was an Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014, and it had confirmed service tax, interest, and penalties for the periods 2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012. The Tribunal relied in part on its own earlier decision in Aurobindo Pharma’s favour, Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that export-related bank deduction charges do not automatically become reverse-charge service-tax liabilities absent a real contractual and consideration-based relationship with the bank, and regulatory approval support for pharma products was not sustained as taxable “scientific or technical consultancy” on these facts. This is an appellate tribunal decision in the service tax regime, so it addresses historic pre-GST liabilities rather than creating a new ongoing tax filing procedure, but it is relevant to defending similar historical demands and to documenting whether any foreign bank or regulatory support provider was actually engaged by the Indian entity and paid by it.

rows.summary:
This CESTAT Mumbai decision concerns a deceased Customs Hawaldar, Rajendra Bane, whose widow appealed against personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalties arose from a 16.08.2018 smuggling case involving gold recovered from the gentlemen’s toilet at Pune International Airport after passengers arrived from Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52, with the department alleging that Bane had facilitated the smuggling and assisted the smugglers despite being on sanctioned leave at his native place near Ratnagiri.

The tribunal record shows the department relied on Section 108 statements, including statements of co-accused/accomplices, call records obtained from the telephone operator, and the seizure of gold from the airport toilet and from a passenger. The defence denied any involvement and maintained that Bane was in fact on leave at the relevant time; it further argued that he had merely passed intelligence to the Superintendent on duty at the airport, and that the source of that information could not be disclosed because it was protected as privileged informer communication.

The Commissioner (Appeals) had rejected that explanation, but the tribunal ultimately found that the evidence was insufficient to establish Bane’s participation in the smuggling operation. On the facts described, the tribunal deleted the penalties under Section 112(a), holding that the department had not proved the charge against the customs official.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that personal penalty exposure under Section 112(a) still requires proof linking the individual to the unlawful import or facilitation; suspicion, association, or uncorroborated statements were not enough on the facts of this case. The decision is also relevant to customs personnel and internal enforcement teams because it underscores the need for corroborated evidence before imposing personal penalties, especially where the accused employee asserts that he was off duty/on leave and claims to have acted as an intelligence source rather than as an accomplice.

rows.summary:
The Patna High Court did not decide the substantive GST exemption issue itself; instead, it remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority for fresh consideration because the exemption question had not been addressed on the merits. The petitioner, M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, is a registered GST taxpayer engaged in conducting Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness programmes, mainly on assignments from Government Departments, and the dispute related to FY 2022–23. The tax department had issued proceedings under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 based on gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100 received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya, and the Adjudicating Authority ultimately imposed tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452 by order dated 20.08.2025.

The petitioner appealed under Section 107(1) of the CGST Act, but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on 28.02.2026 solely because it was filed with a 21-day delay. The petitioner then pointed to Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025, which it said stated that GST was not applicable on receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak and that Nukkad Natak teams consisting of 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from GST. On that basis, the petitioner argued that the issue was a substantive exemption question and not just a late-filing problem.

The High Court accepted that the Appellate Authority had not examined the exemption claim and directed it to reconsider the appeal on the merits in light of the cited memo. Practically, this means the tax demand of Rs. 1,63,452 was not finally upheld by the High Court at this stage, and the exemption/zero-liability argument remains open before the appellate forum. For compliance purposes, the case highlights that entities performing Nukkad Natak for government public-awareness work should review whether any local administrative memo or exemption position is being relied upon, but they should also note that the court did not itself declare a blanket GST exemption for all such activities.

rows.summary:
This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns a penalty dispute for Assessment Year 2014-15 arising from a Section 54 capital gains exemption claim, not a change in law or a general compliance rule. The assessee sold a residential house for Rs. 1,35,00,000 and computed long-term capital gain of Rs. 72,19,588, then claimed exemption for the full gain in his return filed under section 139(1). He had invested Rs. 68,25,500 with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers toward a proposed residential project and deposited Rs. 10,00,000 in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme with SBI; when the developer’s project stalled for reasons beyond his control, he entered into a compromise and purchased another residential property for Rs. 49,95,000, leaving a shortfall of Rs. 24,40,579 that he offered to tax.

The Assessing Officer taxed that Rs. 24,40,579 in AY 2014-15 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5,25,923 under section 271(1)(c), calculated at 100% of the tax sought to be evaded. The CIT(A)/NFAC, by order dated 19.02.2026 under section 250, upheld the penalty on the theory that the assessee had furnished inaccurate particulars by claiming the Section 54 exemption. The Tribunal deleted the penalty, holding that the shortfall in investment was not taxable in the original year in the manner sought by the Revenue and that, on these facts, the assessee’s claim did not amount to furnishing inaccurate particulars or concealment warranting penalty under section 271(1)(c). For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that where a taxpayer has made a bona fide Section 54 claim, invested amounts through a developer and CGAS, and later faces a project failure beyond control with a subsequent replacement purchase, the mere existence of a taxable shortfall may support assessment taxability but does not automatically justify concealment/accuracy penalty if the claim was transparently disclosed.

According to the Appellant, the disputed credit related to Financial Year 2017–18 invoices but was availed in Financial Year 2018–19 within the permissible period under Section 16(4). rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the matter in **N. R. Builders v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes** after finding that the authorities had not properly verified the taxpayer’s explanation for an alleged **GSTR-3B vs GSTR-2A input tax credit mismatch**. The case involved a proprietary concern engaged in **quarrying and sale of crushed stones**, and the disputed credit was **₹2,33,502 in total ITC** for **FY 2018–19**, split equally between **CGST ₹1,16,751 and SGST ₹1,16,751**; the department also levied **interest of ₹2,03,730** and **penalty of ₹23,350**, taking the total demand to **₹4,60,582**. The taxpayer’s key defense was that the credit was not excess ITC at all, but related to **FY 2017–18 invoices** that were **claimed in FY 2018–19 within the time permitted under Section 16(4)** of the CGST Act, so the mismatch required substantive verification rather than automatic disallowance.

The document also highlights procedural defects that mattered to the Tribunal: the assessee said **no personal hearing was granted**, and **no FORM GST ASMT-10 notice** had preceded the proceedings. The department issued a **pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A on 22.01.2024**, followed by a **show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73**; the show-cause notice itself listed the personal hearing particulars as **“NA”**, and the Proper Officer then confirmed the full demand **ex parte**. The **First Appellate Authority upheld the demand**, but the Tribunal found that the revenue should not have treated the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference as inadmissible ITC without first examining the taxpayer’s invoice-level explanation and Section 16(4) timing claim.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that businesses facing ITC mismatch notices should be prepared to substantiate whether mismatched credits relate to prior-year invoices legally availed within the statutory deadline, rather than assuming the mismatch will be accepted as wrongful credit. The decision also reinforces the importance of **procedural fairness in Section 73 proceedings**, including a meaningful opportunity of hearing and proper notice workflow, because an ex parte confirmation based only on reconciliation differences may not survive appellate scrutiny when the taxpayer has a plausible documentary explanation.

rows.summary: The Gujarat High Court held that a charitable trust was entitled to exemption under Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act on capital gains arising from sale of a charitable asset, where the sale proceeds were reinvested in a fixed deposit pursuant to charity-regulator conditions, and it quashed the Commissioner’s order dated 19.11.2020 passed under Section 264 that had rejected the trust’s request for relief. The assessee, Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar, was a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and registered under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007; it sold immovable property for Rs. 4,87,50,000 under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011 and invested the entire sale proceeds in a two-year Fixed Deposit Receipt with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, as required by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the trust had inadvertently not claimed the Section 11(1A) exemption even though the capital gains were fully disclosed and tax was paid, and the return was processed under Section 143(1), creating a demand of Rs. 19,44,180. The Court emphasized that Section 264 revision is broad enough to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a mistake or omission, and relied on earlier precedents such as C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports, and S.R. Koshti to support correcting an inadvertent non-claim of exemption when the underlying facts show eligibility. Practically, the ruling confirms that charitable trusts that sell capital assets and reinvest the proceeds in a permitted manner should examine whether Section 11(1A) relief is available even if the exemption was not claimed in the original return, and that a Section 264 revision can be used to seek correction of such an omission where the assessment has resulted in an unjust tax demand.

Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Delhi ITAT partly allowed the assessee’s appeal for AY 2012-13. The Tribunal first upheld the validity of reassessment proceedings initiated after four years, holding that the subsequent survey conducted on 30.11.2018 revealed information regarding allegedly bogus transactions which had not been examined in the original assessment. The original assessment order itself recorded that the assessee had no business activity, despite substantial purchases, sales and disclosed profit. The Tribunal therefore found that the reopening was based on subsequent information and was not merely a change of opinion. On merits, however, the Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer could not simply treat the entire purchases of Rs.5,81,57,000/- as undisclosed income when the corresponding sales of Rs.5,94,91,966/- had also been treated as bogus. The Tribunal rejected the assessee’s contention that banking-channel transactions alone established genuineness, since physical movement of goods and existence of the parties had not been established. Considering the totality of circumstances, it directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs.5,94,91,966/-, while giving credit for the profit already disclosed by the assessee. rows.summary:
For AY 2012-13, the Delhi ITAT held that reassessment proceedings initiated after four years were valid because they were based on later information from a survey conducted on 30.11.2018, which allegedly exposed bogus transactions that had not been examined in the original assessment. The Tribunal noted that the original assessment itself recorded that the assessee had no business activity despite reporting substantial purchases, sales, and profit, and therefore the reopening was not treated as a mere change of opinion.

On the merits, however, the ITAT rejected the Assessing Officer’s approach of adding the entire purchase amount of Rs. 5,81,57,000 as undisclosed income simply because the related sales of Rs. 5,94,91,966 were also treated as bogus. The Tribunal also rejected the assessee’s argument that payments routed through banking channels were enough to prove genuineness, stating that this did not establish actual physical movement of goods or the existence of the counterparties. Instead of taxing the full purchases, the Tribunal directed the AO to apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966, while allowing credit for profit already disclosed by the assessee.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the ruling confirms reopening can be sustained where fresh post-assessment information arises, especially from a survey, but it also limits the quantum of addition in bogus purchase/sale cases where both sides of the transaction are considered non-genuine. The decision signals that companies should not rely solely on banking-channel documentation to defend purchase genuineness; they should be able to evidence actual movement of goods, vendor existence, and underlying business activity, particularly where the books show substantial trading volume but the business substance appears doubtful.

rows.summary:
The Ahmedabad ITAT dismissed the Revenue’s appeals in **ITA Nos. 1569 and 1570/AHD/2026** involving **DCIT vs. Nirma Limited** for **AY 2018-19 and AY 2020-21**, upholding the CIT(A)’s orders dated **09.02.2026** passed under **Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**; the Tribunal heard the matters together and issued a common order on **21.08.2026** because the issues were identical. For **AY 2018-19**, the Revenue’s challenge to the deletion of **Rs. 4,09,94,465** for depreciation on **goodwill** arising from the amalgamation of **Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.** was rejected: the Tribunal accepted the CIT(A)’s reliance on earlier Tribunal rulings in the assessee’s own case for **AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17** and did not accept the argument that the goodwill was only an accounting entry because the amalgamating company was sick, loss-making, and had negative net worth. The summary indicates that the same pattern of relief continued for the other disputed item involving **electricity and steam valuation**, meaning the Tribunal did not accept the Revenue’s attempt to rework the valuation for internal transfers between units where earlier precedent in the assessee’s case had already been established. For compliance purposes, this decision is significant mainly for taxpayers with **amalgamations, demergers, captive electricity generation, and intra-group/intra-unit transfer pricing positions**, because it reaffirms that, at least on these facts, depreciation claims on goodwill/brands created through restructuring and the assessee’s valuation approach for internal electricity transfers were sustained when supported by earlier favorable orders.

rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai disposed of a consolidated set of income-tax appeals involving DCIT and IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited (formerly Reliance General Insurance Company Limited) for assessment years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21. Although the underlying appeals concerned various additions and disallowances, including issues related to payments made to motor vehicle dealers, the Tribunal did **not** decide those merits; it resolved the matter on a threshold legal issue arising from the later insolvency proceedings of the assessee’s parent company, Reliance Capital Limited (RCL).

RCL, which held about **99.83%** of the assessee’s equity, was admitted into the **Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)** under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The **NCLT, Mumbai Bench** admitted the insolvency petition on **06.12.2021** and imposed the statutory **moratorium under Section 14**. A resolution plan proposed by **IndusInd International Holdings Limited** was approved by the Committee of Creditors in **June 2023** and then approved by the NCLT on **27.02.2024** under **Section 31** of the IBC, making the plan binding on stakeholders covered by it.

The Income-tax Department had participated in the NCLT proceedings and had raised objections there, particularly around the **carry forward of losses under the Income-tax Act**. In the ITAT proceedings, the assessee argued that, because the resolution plan had been approved under Section 31, any tax disputes or claims that were pending and not specifically preserved before approval could not continue independently. The Tribunal accepted the effect of the resolution plan as overriding the pending proceedings, so it **disposed of the appeals without adjudicating the merits** of the tax additions/disallowances.

For compliance teams, the key practical point is that once an IBC resolution plan is approved by the NCLT under Section 31, unresolved pre-approval claims or disputes that were not preserved can be barred from further pursuit, even in income-tax litigation. The case therefore underscores the need for tax authorities and other stakeholders to timely assert and protect their claims in CIRP/NCLT proceedings, because post-approval litigation may be cut off by the binding resolution plan.

The assessee was engaged in manufacturing and trading agricultural products, principally guar gum and its by-products, Churi and Korma. During the relevant year, its factory and stock were taken over by the bank after the assessee’s Phalodi bank account became an NPA. The assessee subsequently found that its stock of guar gum had been damaged due to rain, germs, bacteria and alleged negligence while the premises remained under the bank’s possession. The damaged stock could not be sold as normal guar gum and was processed into Churi/Korma. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s valuation of the closing stock and adopted an NRV of Rs. 82.58 per kg based on an internet website, resulting in an addition of Rs. 2,79,03,981/-. The assessee contended that it had consistently followed Accounting Standard-2 (AS-2), under which inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. TaxGuru’s publication on AS-2 confirms that inventories are required to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value and explains that the cost may not be recoverable where inventories are damaged or their selling prices have declined. [Accounting Standard 2: ‘Valuation of Inventory’](htt
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur, in **ITO v. Varsha Mills** for **Assessment Year 2017-18**, dismissed the Revenue’s appeal and upheld deletion of two additions made by the Assessing Officer. First, the Tribunal agreed that the assessee’s damaged guar gum inventory had to be valued under **Accounting Standard 2 (AS-2)** at the **lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV)**, rather than at an internet-derived rate adopted by the AO; the AO’s revaluation led to an addition of **₹2,79,03,981**, which the Tribunal found unsustainable because the stock had allegedly deteriorated due to rain, germs, bacteria, and negligence while in bank possession after the assessee’s Phalodi bank account became an NPA and the factory/stock were taken over by the bank. The assessee’s case was that the damaged guar gum could not be sold as normal guar gum and had instead been processed into **Churi/Korma**, and the Tribunal accepted the deletion of the stock valuation addition.

Second, the Tribunal also upheld deletion of the **₹3,36,49,500 addition under Section 69A** relating to **cash deposits made during the demonetization period**. The Revenue’s position was that these cash deposits represented unexplained money, but the Tribunal did not sustain that addition, meaning the assessee was not treated as having unaccounted cash merely because deposits were made during demonetization. For compliance purposes, the case reinforces that inventory write-downs need support from consistent accounting treatment and credible evidence of damage/NRV impairment, and that cash deposits during demonetization can be challenged under Section 69A if the source is not explained—although in this case the assessee succeeded in overturning the addition.

rows.summary:

The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Delhi ruling in favor of PNB Gilts that removes a ₹4.26 crore disallowance made under Section 14A of the Income Tax Act. rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corruption Controls
rows.desc: Summary: Audits are a quiet but essential safeguard for bank deposits, investments, provident funds, companies and cooperative societies. However, the effectiveness of this safeguard is being weakened by declining real audit fees, market concentration and inadequate time for completing complex assignments. Between FY2018 and FY2023, the market value of Nifty 500 companies reportedly increased by about 92%, while their audit fees rose by only 28%. At the same time, six large audit networks handle around two-thirds of Nifty 500 companies, concentrating both influence and systemic risk. The problem is even sharper in cooperative societies, rural branches and local bodies, where auditors may have only a few days to examine cash-heavy, paper-based records. Professional restrictions also affect smaller practitioners: chartered accountants are generally restricted from undertaking business activities without ICAI permission, while the revised tax-audit ceiling treats assignments of widely different sizes as one audit each. Strengthening audit as an anti-corruption mechanism requires disclosure of the actual time available for an audit, scrutiny of abnormally low fees, development of capable mid-sized firms, risk- and complexity-based audit ceilings, and fair remuneration and timelines for rural and cooperative audits. Higher fees alone cannot guarantee quality, but persistent underpricing, rushed work, market concentration and conflicted incentives can collectively weaken independence and reduce the depth of scrutiny. N U M B E R S T E L L S T O R I E S The Underpriced Watchman Why fixing audit is one of the simplest ways to fight corruption — from an auditor’s chair Your salary lands in a bank. Your savings sit in a fixed deposit, a mutual fund, maybe a cooperative society your family has trusted for years. Your provident fund is invested in companies you have never heard of. The company you work for reports its numbers every year, and your job depends on those numbers be
rows.summary:
The document argues that underpriced audit engagements can undermine anti-corruption controls by reducing audit quality, because very low fees, limited auditor time, and concentration of work in a small market can all weaken the independence, depth, and effectiveness of audits. Its core compliance message is that when audits are priced too cheaply, auditors may not devote sufficient resources to properly test controls, scrutinize transactions, or identify warning signs of corruption and misuse of funds, which in turn increases risk for companies, investors, and depositors. It emphasizes that stronger, better-resourced audits are important for protecting savings and improving India’s broader anti-corruption environment.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical implication is that audit pricing and scope should not be treated as a purely commercial issue: if an audit is materially underpriced, management should consider whether the fee level could impair audit quality or signal that planned procedures may be too shallow to detect control failures. The document does not appear to announce a new legal deadline, filing requirement, numerical threshold, or formal regulatory rule; rather, it is a policy-oriented warning about the compliance risk created by low-fee audit arrangements and market concentration. Organizations using external auditors should therefore ensure the engagement is resourced adequately for the complexity and risk profile of the business, and should be alert to whether budget pressure could compromise the auditor’s ability to perform a credible anti-corruption review.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why Does the GST Department Chase Bona Fide Buyers Under Section 16(2)(c) Instead of Defaulting Sellers Under Section 76? Summary: Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act makes a recipient’s entitlement to Input Tax Credit conditional upon the tax charged by the supplier having actually been paid to the government. Consequently, even a bona fide buyer who possesses a genuine invoice, receives the goods or services, pays the entire consideration including GST and files returns correctly may be required to reverse ITC if the supplier defaults. Section 76, however, independently empowers the GST department to recover tax collected but not deposited from the person who collected it, together with applicable interest and penalty. Despite this direct remedy, enforcement action is frequently taken against compliant buyers because they are easier to trace, possess identifiable assets and remain active within the GST system, whereas defaulting suppliers may have closed operations, disappeared or operated through shell entities. Automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch identification also makes buyer-side proceedings administratively easier than investigation and recovery against sellers. The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), recognising ITC as a statutory benefit subject to legislative conditions, including supplier payment of tax. Nevertheless, questions of fairness and enforcement sequencing remain. A balanced approach would prioritise recovery under Section 76 from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for transactions involving collusion, fraud or failure to establish genuineness. Until legislation or binding precedent clarifies the sequencing of these provisions, buyers should maintain comprehensive evidence of supplier verification, invoices, receipt of supplies, e-way bills, transport records, banking payments and return reconciliation. Anyone who has dealt with a GST department notice in the las
rows.summary:
The document is a commentary on a recurring GST compliance issue rather than a new statutory amendment: it examines why bona fide purchasers can be denied input tax credit (ITC) when their suppliers collect GST but fail to deposit it with the government. The discussion focuses on the interaction between Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, which conditions ITC on tax actually being paid to the government, and Section 76, which allows recovery of tax from a person who has collected it but not remitted it. The key compliance message is that, under this framework, the tax department may target the buyer’s ITC claim even where the buyer acted in good faith, if the seller did not discharge the tax liability.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that invoice possession and payment to the vendor are not enough to secure ITC unless the supplier has also properly reported and paid the tax. Businesses therefore need stronger vendor-due-diligence and invoice-validation controls, because the risk of ITC denial can arise from counterparty non-compliance rather than the buyer’s own error. The document’s emphasis is on the policy and legal rationale behind this enforcement approach, namely that GST law prioritizes tax actually reaching the exchequer and gives the department a route to recover from the person who collected the tax but defaulted on payment. No new filing deadline, rate change, or numerical threshold is set out in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: Income Tax | Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS 2026)
rows.desc: Summary: The Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme, 2026 (FAST-DS) provides a one-time, time-bound route for eligible taxpayers to declare specified foreign assets and foreign income omitted from earlier returns. The Scheme operates under Chapter IV of the Finance Act, 2026, comprising sections 130 to 144, together with the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers–Disclosure Scheme Rules, 2026. Form 1 may be filed electronically up to 31 December 2026. Section 133 creates two separate declaration routes: Row 1 covers undisclosed foreign assets or foreign income, subject to an aggregate ceiling of ₹1 crore and payment equal to 30% tax plus an amount equal to 100% of that tax, producing an effective burden of 60%; Row 2 covers specified foreign assets acquired from foreign income earned while non-resident or from income already offered to tax but omitted from Schedule FA, subject to a ₹5 crore ceiling and a flat ₹1 lakh fee. Rule 3 prescribes valuation as on 31 March 2026, including special rules for foreign bank accounts, sold assets, reinvestment and currency conversion. Rule 5 operationalises electronic filing and provides a 20% valuation-variance safeguard for assets other than bank accounts. The Scheme also prescribes Forms 2 to 4 for determination, payment intimation and certification. Full and timely payment is essential for immunity under the Black Money Act; false particulars, excluded cases, excess-value declarations and payment defaults may invalidate or bar relief. Section 133 — “Amount payable by declarant” (the core) Row 1 (Sl. No. 1) — Genuinely undisclosed money Row 2 (Sl. No. 2) — Clean money, just not reported 5. Why pay tax even if I’m voluntarily declaring? 6. Rule 5 — Declaration of asset/income located outside Indi

Because the excerpt is truncated and does not include the underlying operative text, it does not provide the actual numeric thresholds, payment rates, filing dates, or the exact scope of immunity. The CIT(E) had rejected the application principally on the grounds that Form No. 10AB was incomplete and that the assessee had not furnished registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959. The CIT(E) had relied upon section 12AB(1)(b)(i), observing that compliance with other laws material for achieving the objects of the institution was required to be examined. The assessee submitted that it was an Urban Improvement Trust, Pali, constituted under the statutory framework of the State Government and functioning as a statutory/public authority for urban improvement and development. It therefore could not be treated like an ordinary private public trust requiring registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959. Reliance was placed on section 77 of the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, which provides that the Act does not apply to a public trust administered by an agency acting under the control of the State Government or by a local authority. The Tribunal accepted that the legal character of the assessee was material. It held that before drawing an adverse inference from non-registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, the CIT
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that an assessee’s failure to obtain registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, by itself, cannot be used as a ground to reject renewal of registration under Section 12AB of the Income-tax Act. The case concerned Urban Improvement Trust, Pali, whose Section 12AB renewal application had been rejected; the Tribunal did not finally grant renewal on the merits but directed the tax authorities to conduct a fresh examination of the application.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that renewal under Section 12AB must be evaluated on the statutory income-tax criteria, and a separate state-law registration deficiency cannot automatically defeat the application. Any authority reviewing a Section 12AB renewal request must therefore base its decision on the requirements of the Income-tax Act and the relevant facts of the trust’s activities and eligibility, rather than relying solely on absence of Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration.

The dispute arose because the University had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), while the Assessing Officer and CIT(A) considered the specific exemption contemplated under section 11(1)(d) unavailable under that provision for the relevant year. Mewar University, Chittorgarh, was constituted under the Mewar University Act, 2009 enacted by the Rajasthan State Legislature. It was registered under section 12AA and also had approval under section 10(23C)(vi). It filed its return for AY 2017-18 declaring nil income. Assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 30.12.2019 determining total income at ₹15,61,58,900 after various additions and disallowances. The CIT(A) granted relief on the other substantive issues, but sustained the addition relating to the corpus contribution of ₹26,50,000. The disputed amount consisted of two donations: ₹1,50,000 received from Shri Ramesh Chandra Baser through NEFT and ₹25,00,000 received from Mundra International through cheque. The Assessing Officer took the view that because the assessee had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi), rather than under section 11, there was no question of allowing the corpus contrib
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur held that corpus donations totaling ₹26.50 lakh cannot be treated as taxable income merely because the recipient institution had claimed exemption under section 10(23C)(vi) of the Income-tax Act. In other words, the tax authority cannot deny corpus-donation treatment or automatically tax these receipts solely on the basis that the entity is claiming a particular exemption provision.  

For compliance purposes, this ruling is relevant to educational or other institutions receiving donations intended to form part of their corpus, because it confirms that the tax characterization of the receipt depends on the nature and purpose of the donation, not just on the fact that the institution has sought exemption under section 10(23C)(vi). The decision does not announce a new filing deadline, rate, or numeric threshold beyond the specific amount involved in the case, but it reinforces that corpus contributions documented as such should not be added to taxable income simply due to the exemption claim.

The Tribunal treated the section 80G appeal as consequential to the section 12AB appeal and therefore first adjudicated the registration issue. ISKCON had been registered as a charitable institution under section 12A since 11.06.1975 and had enjoyed section 80G approval since 16.01.1971. The Tribunal recorded that its objects and activities had not undergone change and that it operates more than 270 centres across India. Its activities include free food distribution, education, yoga, medical relief, environmental projects, maintenance of goshalas, agricultural and rural-development work, devotional publications, broadcasting and accommodation for spiritual seekers. The CIT(E) treated activities including meditation camps, scriptural courses, devotional books and articles, satvik food distribution, broadcasting and royalty, agriculture and farm operations, and accommodation as falling within the residuary limb of section 2(15), namely advancement of any other object of general public utility. He consequently invoked the proviso to section 2(15), relied upon selected data from the ISKCON Juhu centre,
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai ruled in favor of ISKCON, holding that its charitable activities do not fall within the restrictive proviso to section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, which is often used to deny charitable status where an organization is seen as carrying on “advancement of any other object of general public utility” with commercial elements. As a result, the tribunal set aside the tax authority’s rejection of ISKCON’s registration under section 12AB, meaning ISKCON’s charitable registration should not be denied on that ground. The tribunal also directed renewal of ISKCON’s approval under section 80G, which is the provision that allows donors to claim tax deduction benefits for contributions made to the organization.  

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the tribunal found ISKCON’s activities to remain within the charitable framework and not to be disqualified merely because of the nature of its operations. The decision affects entities with similar religious/charitable structures that seek or rely on section 12AB registration and section 80G approval, especially where the tax department has challenged charitable status by invoking the section 2(15) proviso. rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court dealt with a GST detention case involving M/s. TPJ Carriers, the owner of a 14-wheeler tanker (No. KL-40/S-7040) hired to transport bulk bitumen for M/s. SVP Petro Products. The State GST authorities intercepted the conveyance and initiated proceedings under Section 129(3) of the CGST/KSGST Act, 2017, ultimately imposing a penalty of Rs. 23,86,590. The transporter sought release of the vehicle by paying the lesser amount contemplated in the first proviso to Section 129(6), namely Rs. 1,00,000, and the Court noted that this amount had in fact been paid.

The compliance issue arose because, even after about two and a half months from the penalty order, the authorities had not taken steps to sell the seized goods or otherwise dispose of them. The authorities argued that sale had not yet been pursued because the appeal period may not have expired. The Court examined Section 129(6) and emphasized that where the person transporting the goods or the owner does not pay the penalty within 15 days from receipt of the Section 129(3) order, the detained or seized goods or conveyance become liable to be sold or otherwise disposed of to recover the penalty.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the statute creates a 15-day payment deadline after a Section 129(3) order, after which the goods/conveyance may be sold to realize the penalty; the Court’s discussion indicates that authorities should not indefinitely wait merely because an appeal window may still be running. The first proviso to Section 129(6) also provides a specific release mechanism for the conveyance: if the transporter pays the penalty or Rs. 1,00,000, whichever is less, the conveyance may be released. The second proviso was referenced in the summary but the text provided cuts off before its full content, so no further operative detail can be reliably extracted from this excerpt.

Following discrepancies noticed during the survey, the assessee declared additional income of Rs. 1,15,16,100 towards excess cash, Rs. 1,75,98,542 towards excess stock and Rs. 2,27,29,200 towards undisclosed investment in furniture and fixtures, aggregating to Rs. 5,18,43,842. After considering that amount, its gross profit worked out to Rs. 8,42,95,900, or 10.79%. The Assessing Officer, however, treated the excess-stock surrender as income from other sources and excluded it while computing the business gross profit. rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi in **GRP Auto v. JCIT** allowed the taxpayer’s appeal for **AY 2010-11** and deleted the **Rs. 1,08,51,505** addition that the Assessing Officer had made by applying a different gross profit rate. The assessee, a firm trading in auto parts, had filed a return declaring **total income of Rs. 4,36,31,310** and was part of a group of auto-part concerns with substantial purchases from sister entities such as **Swiss Auto Products, Swiss Lamps Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Auto Pvt. Ltd., Swiss Devices (1), and Taruna Auto Pvt. Ltd.** A **survey under section 133A** was conducted on **21-01-2010**, during which the assessee surrendered a total of **Rs. 5,18,43,842** on account of **excess cash (Rs. 1,15,16,100)**, **excess stock (Rs. 1,75,98,542)**, and **undisclosed investment in furniture and fixtures (Rs. 2,27,29,200)**.

A key compliance issue in the case was how the surrendered **excess stock** amount should be treated. The assessee credited the **Rs. 1,75,98,542** excess-stock surrender to the profit and loss account under **“Sales and Other Income,”** which resulted in a gross profit of **Rs. 8,42,95,900**, or **10.79%** of turnover. The Assessing Officer instead treated that surrender as **income from other sources**, removed it from business results, and computed gross profit at **Rs. 6,66,97,358**, or **8.53%** of turnover. On that basis, the Assessing Officer rejected the books under **section 145(3)** and applied a differential gross profit rate, which produced the disputed addition of **Rs. 1,08,51,505**.

The Tribunal held that this approach was not justified and that the **rejection of the books of account under section 145(3)** was improper on the facts. It accepted the assessee’s treatment of the surrendered excess-stock amount as part of the business results for gross profit computation and held that the **gross profit rate could not be applied uniformly across the pre-survey and post-survey periods** in the manner adopted by the Assessing Officer. For compliance purposes, the case underscores that where a survey leads to disclosed stock discrepancies and the taxpayer recognizes the amount in the trading/profit-and-loss account, tax authorities may not mechanically reclassify it outside business income and then use that reclassification to justify a book rejection or a revised GP estimate without adequate basis.

rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that the dispute over the proposed sale of assets linked to Byju’s K3 Education Private Limited should be addressed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), not through parallel writ proceedings before the High Court. The petitioner, the Resolution Professional of Byju’s K3, had challenged the NCLT’s order dated 13.08.2026 in I.A. No. 768/2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 29/2025 and sought to quash the public announcement dated 02.08.2026 for sale of certain assets at the IndoSpace Logistics Complex, Bommasandra, Bengaluru, alleging that the Resolution Professional of Think and Learn Private Limited (described as a subsidiary or related company) was attempting to sell property that actually belonged to Byju’s K3. The High Court noted that the matter was already pending before the NCLT and that the assets of both companies were in the Tribunal’s custody, so the appropriate course was for the parties to proceed before the NCLT rather than litigate the same issue separately in the High Court, especially since the dispute was between two resolution professionals.

The Court also allowed the petitioner to place before the NCLT any documents that came into his possession after the original filing, which means the evidentiary record could be supplemented in the tribunal proceedings. No new substantive corporate-law rule, filing threshold, or sale procedure was announced by the High Court itself; the key point is that any challenge to the ownership or saleability of the assets must be pursued in the insolvency forum already seized of the matter.

It was established, inter alia, to administer and facilitate implementation of the Software Technology Park Scheme. STPI was separately registered with the Service Tax Department and admittedly paid Service Tax on various services including renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services and project consultancy. The controversy was confined to charges connected with activities under the STP Scheme, particularly SOFTEX certification and issuance of NoCs. The appellan
rows.summary:
This CESTAT Hyderabad decision concerns whether charges collected by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) for certification of SOFTEX forms and issuance of No Objection Certificates (NoCs) are liable to Service Tax, and the Department’s position was that these receipts fall under **“Business Support Service”** under the Finance Act, 1994. Two appeals were involved: **ST/20226/2014** covered **2007–08 to 2011–12** and involved a Service Tax demand of **Rs. 5,15,53,520** plus interest and penalties; **ST/30531/2016** covered **April 2012 to June 2012** and involved a Service Tax demand of **Rs. 2,06,792** plus interest and penalties. In the second matter, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already upheld the demand but granted **cum-tax benefit**.

STPI argued that it is an **autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860**, functioning under the administrative control of the **Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India**, and that it was set up to administer and facilitate the **Software Technology Park Scheme**. It also pointed out that it was separately registered under Service Tax and had already been paying tax on other services such as **renting of immovable property, bandwidth services, co-location services, and project consultancy**; however, it contended that the disputed SOFTEX certification and NoC activities were part of its scheme-related regulatory functions, not taxable business support. The dispute was therefore limited specifically to whether these STP Scheme-related certification/approval charges constitute a taxable service or are exempt/ बाहर the tax net due to their nature as governmental/scheme facilitation functions.

For compliance purposes, the key issue is that the tax exposure identified by the Department was substantial and arose over multi-year and short-period windows, with the Department seeking tax, interest, and penalties on those charges. The document does not provide the final outcome of the appeal in the excerpt shown, but the material compliance point is that STPI’s SOFTEX certification and NoC fee receipts were under active challenge as potentially taxable “Business Support Service,” while the taxpayer maintained they were scheme-administration activities performed by a government-linked body already registered for and compliant with Service Tax on its other taxable services.

The Court held that although the Revenue’s investigation could give rise to strong suspicion regarding manipulation in the prices of PFL Infotech Limited and Risa International Limited shares, suspicion, however grave, could not substitute proof. The Court noted that the shares had been purchased and sold through recognised stock exchanges, Securities Transaction Tax had been paid, sale consideration had been received through banking channels, and there was no positive material establishing that either assessee had paid unaccounted cash to an operator or participated in an arrangement to manipulate share prices. The Court further held that the Tribunal’s findings of fact could not be interfered with under Section 260A in the absence of perversity. The Supreme Court decisions in CIT v. Durga Prasad More and Sumati Dayal v. CIT, dealing with the test of human probabilities, were distinguished on facts. The Court emphasised that the test of human probabilities does not dispense with the requirement of positive material connecting the assessee with an alleged tax-evasion design. Relying also on the principles stated in Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CIT, Omar Salay Mohamed Sait v. CIT and Umacharan Shaw and Brothers v. CIT, the Cour
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court dismissed the Revenue’s appeals in T.C.A. Nos. 714 and 721 of 2018 and left standing the Tribunal’s deletion of additions of Rs. 32.90 crore and Rs. 38.05 crore made under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The additions had been made on the basis that the assessees’ exempt long-term capital gains under Section 10(38) from shares of PFL Infotech Limited and Risa International Limited were allegedly bogus or part of a penny stock manipulation scheme.  

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that the Court found the Revenue had raised serious suspicion about share-price manipulation, but suspicion alone cannot replace proof of actual accommodation entries or unaccounted cash circulation. The Court relied on the factual findings that the share purchases and sales were carried out through recognized stock exchanges, Securities Transaction Tax was paid, and sale proceeds were received through banking channels; critically, there was no positive evidence showing that either assessee paid cash to an operator or knowingly participated in a scheme to rig prices. The Court also held that, in an appeal under Section 260A, the High Court would not interfere with the Tribunal’s factual findings unless they were perverse.  

The Court distinguished the Supreme Court’s human-probability cases, including CIT v. Durga Prasad More and Sumati Dayal v. CIT, stating that those decisions do not eliminate the need for positive material linking the taxpayer to an alleged tax-evasion design. It also referred to the principles in Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CIT, Omar Salay Mohamed Sait v. CIT, and Umacharan Shaw and Brothers v. CIT. There is no new operational filing deadline or procedural requirement announced in this decision; its compliance significance is evidentiary: where a taxpayer has exchange-traded trades, STT payment, and banked consideration, the tax department still must produce concrete evidence of the taxpayer’s involvement before treating capital gains as unexplained cash credits under Section 68.

The appeal arose from the order dated 22.10.2025 passed by the Ld. Addl./JCIT(A)-5, Kolkata, in relation to the assessment framed under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2016-17. The assessee was an individual engaged in retail trading of medicines and also derived income from operation of a sonography machine. A survey under section 133A was conducted at the business premises on 20.09.2016, during which ₹6,25,000 was surrendered. The assessee subsequently filed a return declaring total income of ₹14,81,960, including the surrendered amount, and paid tax at the normal applicable rate. During assessment, the Assessing Officer issued a show-cause notice proposing application of section 115BBE. The assessee contended that section 115BBE could apply only where the income fell within sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C or 69D, and that none of those deeming provisions applied to the surrendered business income. The AO rejected the explanation and taxed ₹6,25,000 at 30% under section 115BBE. Significantly, the AO did not invoke any particular provision from sections 68 to 69D or record a finding that the statutory requirements of any such provision were satisfied. The CIT(A) upheld the AO’s action, reasoning that the assessee had not explained the exact source of the surrendered income and that the deeming provisions would consequently apply. According to
rows.summary:
In **Dhukha Ram v. ACIT (ITAT Jodhpur)** for **AY 2016–17**, the Tribunal held that the **special tax rate under section 115BBE could not be applied to ₹6,25,000 surrendered during a survey** merely because the amount was disclosed during proceedings. The assessee, an individual carrying on **retail medicine trading and sonography machine operations**, had a **section 133A survey on 20.09.2016** at the business premises, after which he surrendered the ₹6,25,000, filed his return showing **total income of ₹14,81,960** including that amount, and paid tax at the **normal applicable rate**.  

During assessment under **section 143(3)**, the AO issued a show-cause notice proposing taxation under **section 115BBE**, which imposes a **30% tax rate** on certain categories of unexplained income. The assessee argued that **section 115BBE applies only where income is assessable under the deeming provisions in sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C, or 69D**, and that the surrendered amount was **business income**, not unexplained cash/investment/expenditure income covered by those provisions. Despite this, the AO taxed the ₹6,25,000 at 30% under section 115BBE.  

The Tribunal emphasized that the AO had **not identified or invoked any specific deeming provision under sections 68 to 69D** and had **not recorded any finding that the factual prerequisites of any such section were met**. The CIT(A) had upheld the addition on the theory that the assessee had not explained the exact source, but the Tribunal rejected that approach and allowed the appeal. The practical compliance takeaway is that **survey surrender alone does not automatically trigger section 115BBE**; for that rate to apply, the department must be able to place the amount within one of the specific deeming provisions and satisfy their conditions.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Co-operative Bank Conversion Mid-Recovery: Forum, Composite Notice & Cost of Delay
rows.desc: When a Co-operative Bank Changes Its Registration Midway Through Recovery – The forum, the composite notice and the cost of delay Summary: A State co-operative bank’s conversion into a multi-State co-operative bank during recovery can materially affect the forum, limitation and enforceability of proceedings against borrowers and guarantors. The article examines whether pre-conversion members automatically become members under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002; whether claims against sureties fall within Section 84; and how the six-year limitation under Section 85 interacts with acknowledgments made only by the principal borrower. It also analyses whether a composite SARFAESI demand notice adequately identifies borrower-wise liabilities and secured assets, and whether prolonged delay after possession can reduce a guarantor’s liability under Sections 139 and 141 of the Contract Act where security loses value. Parallel SARFAESI and arbitration proceedings may be permissible, but multiple references arising from one composite secured transaction require transparent appropriation and consolidated accounts to prevent duplication. Conditional attachment before award must satisfy the statutory requirement of intent to defeat or delay execution, while indiscriminate freezes involving non-parties may exceed arbitral authority. The article further highlights objections concerning the Central Registrar’s appointment power, delegation, tribunal constitution and the distinction between the place and seat of arbitration. It concludes with a practical defence sequence: challenge constitution and membership promptly, raise limitation early, contest attachment within the appeal deadline, demand complete account and valuation records, and obtain independent evidence of security value and sale consideration. Table of Contents▸ Brief Introduction The law as it stands The present position Conversion does not carry the members across Is a claim against a surety arbitrable u
rows.summary:
This article explains the compliance and litigation risks when a State co-operative bank is converted into a multi-State co-operative bank while recovery proceedings are already underway. The central point is that the conversion can change the **proper forum**, **limitation analysis**, and **enforceability** of actions against borrowers and guarantors, so parties cannot assume that a proceeding initiated before conversion will simply continue unchanged under the new statutory framework. It questions whether members of the pre-conversion State co-operative bank automatically become members of the multi-State co-operative bank, and notes that this membership issue matters for jurisdiction and standing; it also raises whether claims against sureties fall within **Section 84** and how the **six-year limitation period under Section 85** applies when only the principal borrower has made an acknowledgment.

The document also addresses **SARFAESI demand notice compliance**, stating that a **composite demand notice** must still clearly identify the liabilities of each borrower and the secured assets tied to the transaction; otherwise, the notice may be vulnerable for lack of specificity. It further warns that when possession is taken but sale or realization is delayed for a long period, a guarantor may argue that its liability should be reduced under **Sections 139 and 141 of the Contract Act** if the value of the security has deteriorated in the meantime. In parallel recovery tracks, the article says **SARFAESI and arbitration can proceed at the same time**, but where multiple references arise from one composite secured transaction, the creditor must maintain **transparent appropriation and consolidated accounts** to avoid double recovery or duplication of claims.

On the arbitration/enforcement side, the document says that any **conditional attachment before award** must meet the statutory standard that the respondent acted with intent to defeat or delay execution; broad freezes affecting **non-parties** may exceed the tribunal’s authority. It also notes procedural objections that may be available concerning the **Central Registrar’s appointment power**, delegation, tribunal constitution, and whether the relevant location is merely the place of arbitration or the actual legal seat, because those issues can affect validity and jurisdiction. The practical compliance advice is to challenge the tribunal’s constitution and membership issues **promptly**, raise limitation defenses **early**, contest any attachment **within the appeal deadline**, and insist on complete **account statements and valuation records**, including independent evidence of security value and the actual sale consideration, so liability and enforcement can be tested accurately.

rows.summary:
For AY 2023-24, the ITAT Chennai allowed the appeal of Sri Balaji Shopping World and deleted an addition of ₹48,08,962 that the Assessing Officer had made after treating the entire ₹76,38,827 reflected in Form 26AS (reported by BSNL and India 1 Payments Ltd.) as commission income. The assessee was carrying on mobile recharge services for BSNL and was also an authorised BSNL dealer; it argued that the gap between the Form 26AS gross receipts and the income shown in its books arose because BSNL allowed trade discounts on recharge vouchers, which had been netted off in the accounts rather than shown as separate income. The AO rejected the reconciliation, taxed the full gross receipts as commission, and after allowing expenses plus partner remuneration/interest, made the additional ₹48.09 lakh addition and also initiated penalty proceedings under section 270A.  

The CIT(A) had sustained the addition mainly because the assessee did not furnish revised TDS certificates, a correction to Form 26AS, confirmation from BSNL, or other independent corroboration. The Tribunal reversed that view, observing that the assessee had filed a detailed reconciliation with invoice-wise particulars showing the face value of recharge vouchers, the discounted purchase price, and the margin retained, and that the figures substantially matched the difference between the gross amount reported in Form 26AS and the income recognized in the books. The key compliance point from this ruling is that Form 26AS entries alone do not determine the true character of income; where gross receipts include trade discounts or similar adjustments, a taxpayer can rebut the presumption with a credible reconciliation and underlying transaction details. This decision does not create a new filing deadline or rate change, but it reinforces that businesses dealing in BSNL recharge vouchers or similar agency/distribution arrangements should maintain invoice-level documentation and a clear reconciliation between third-party reporting statements and book income to defend the accounting treatment in assessment or penalty proceedings.
