rows.summary:
This Gujarat High Court decision in **PCIT v. Cadila Healthcare Ltd.** concerns the Revenue’s appeal for **Assessment Year 2013–14** under **Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961**. The Court admitted questions relating to several tax issues raised by the Revenue, including **guarantee fee, interest on convertible loan, product registration expenditure, trademark registration and patent fees, research and development expenditure, and computation of book profit under Section 115JB**. The summary states that issues concerning **guarantee fee, interest on convertible loan, product registration expenditure, trademark registration and patent fee, expenses incurred outside the approved R&D facility under Section 35(2AB), and exclusion of Section 14A disallowance while computing book profit under Section 115JB** had already been admitted in another appeal, and therefore **questions A, B, C, D, F, and H** were admitted here as well.

The most important compliance point is the Court’s ruling on **Section 35(2AB)** weighted deduction for in-house R&D. Relying on its earlier decision in **Banco Products India Ltd. v. DCIT**, which followed **Claris Lifesciences Ltd.** and the Delhi High Court’s ruling in **Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Union of India**, the Court held that **once the prescribed authority approves/recognizes the R&D facility, the deduction cannot be denied merely because DSIR approval came in a later year**. In other words, the timing of the formal DSIR recognition letter does not by itself defeat the deduction if the company had already applied and the facility is otherwise eligible.

On the facts mentioned, the assessee **applied to the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) for recognition on 21 June 2012**, and the recognition was **approved on 9 October 2013**. The Court’s position is significant for companies claiming **Section 35(2AB)** deductions: if the R&D facility was duly applied for and later approved, tax authorities should not reject the claim solely because the approval was issued in a subsequent year. This ruling is relevant for corporate tax compliance teams tracking **R&D deduction eligibility, DSIR approval timing, and defensibility of claims in assessments and appeals**.

In AY 2013-14, the Tribunal deleted the addition of Rs. 3,59,22,304 under section 56(2)(viib), holding that the provision could not apply where shares were allotted as consideration other than cash pursuant to acquisition of a business undertaking. The Tribunal also allowed deduction of Rs. 11,61,86,712 written off as irrecoverable from Career Launcher Education Foundation under section 36(1)(vii), deleted the Rs. 1,41,71,192 disallowance under section 14A in the absence of exempt income, deleted the Rs. 1,88,42,329 addition relating to liabilities no longer required, and allowed Rs. 19,04,795 of loan processing charges as revenue expenditure. rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT partly allowed C. L. Educate Limited’s appeals for AY 2013-14 and AY 2017-18 and, most importantly for tax compliance, held that section 56(2)(viib) did **not** apply to shares issued as consideration for acquiring a business undertaking where the consideration was not paid in cash. On that basis, the Tribunal deleted the **Rs. 3,59,22,304** addition made under section 56(2)(viib) for AY 2013-14, which is a significant clarification for share issuances tied to business acquisitions rather than capital-raising transactions.

For AY 2013-14, the Tribunal also allowed a number of deductions and expense claims: it permitted a bad-debt/write-off deduction of **Rs. 11,61,86,712** under section 36(1)(vii) for amounts written off as irrecoverable from Career Launcher Education Foundation; deleted the **Rs. 1,41,71,192** disallowance under section 14A because there was no exempt income; deleted the **Rs. 1,88,42,329** addition relating to liabilities no longer required; and allowed **Rs. 19,04,795** of loan processing charges as revenue expenditure. It further deleted a **Rs. 14,33,356** royalty disallowance under section 40(a)(ia) because the recipient had already included the amount in taxable income. However, the Tribunal sustained the **100% disallowance** of advertisement/business promotion expenses and upheld the disallowance of prior-period expenses of **Rs. 32,87,466**.

For AY 2017-18, the Tribunal deleted an ad hoc bad-debt disallowance of **Rs. 34,10,731**, holding that the Assessing Officer could not simply disallow **1/11th** of the claim based on sample verification without a proper basis. It restricted the disallowance of commission paid to non-executive directors to **30%** under section 40(a)(ia), rather than sustaining a larger disallowance. The issue of the **Rs. 1,18,75,095** provision for expenses was sent back to the Assessing Officer for fresh verification, so that item remains unresolved and must be re-examined in assessment.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12587 Case Name Innovative Microfinance for Poverty Alleviation and Community Transformation Vs CIT (Exemptions) (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year NA Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. The assessee was a social impact organisation incorporated under section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956. It had initially undertaken rehabilitation of livelihood activities for families affected by the 2004 tsunami in Tamil Nadu and subsequently provided micro credit to marginalised sections of society in remote areas. It was holding registration under section 12A and approval under section 80G since incorporation. On 15.06.2022, the Reserve Bank of India informed the assessee that it was required to cease microfinance operations as a condition for registration under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The assessee stopped disbursement of microfinance loans from 15.06.2022 and thereafter only collected outstanding dues, which was completed on 31.10.2023. Its Board, in a meeting held on 26.10.2023, resolved that microfinance operations would cease with effect from 31.10.2023. The assess
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a delay in changing an entity’s stated objects does **not, by itself, justify denial of registration under section 12AB** or approval under **section 80G** when the organization has already stopped the impugned activity in substance. The taxpayer, Innovative Microfinance for Poverty Alleviation and Community Transformation (now Innovative Social Impact Foundation), was a charitable/social impact company incorporated under **section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956**, and it had held **section 12A registration and section 80G approval since incorporation**. Its original work included rehabilitation and livelihood support for families affected by the **2004 tsunami in Tamil Nadu**, and later microcredit activities for marginalized groups in remote areas.

The key triggering event was a communication from the **Reserve Bank of India dated 15.06.2022**, informing the assessee that it had to **cease microfinance operations** as a condition relevant to registration under **section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934**. In response, the assessee **stopped disbursing microfinance loans from 15.06.2022** and thereafter only recovered outstanding dues, which it states was fully completed by **31.10.2023**. The Board passed a resolution on **26.10.2023** recording that microfinance operations would cease **with effect from 31.10.2023**.

Despite this operational cessation, the CIT(E), Chennai issued orders dated **30.03.2026** and **31.03.2026** rejecting the assessee’s applications for **fresh registration under section 12AB** and **approval under section 80G**. The Tribunal found that the authorities should look at the **actual conduct and cessation of the activity**, not deny relief merely because the object clause or formal documentation had not been updated immediately. The practical compliance takeaway is that where a charitable organization changes its business/activity profile or is required by another regulator to stop a line of activity, the organization should document the cessation clearly, but a lag in amending objects should not automatically defeat tax registration if the underlying non-charitable or restricted activity has in fact stopped.

The Tribunal allowed both appeals **for statistical purposes**, meaning the rejection orders were not sustained on the reasoning adopted by the CIT(E). For compliance teams, the case underscores the need to maintain contemporaneous evidence of board resolutions, regulator communications, and the exact date an activity stopped, especially when seeking or renewing **12AB/80G** status after a change in operations.

The respondent, Big C Mobiles Pvt. Ltd., was engaged in sale of mobile phones through retail outlets in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Proceedings had been initiated through Show Cause Notice No.20/2018-19 dated 21.12.2018 alleging non-payment of service tax on insurance coverage charges collected from customers during 2013-14 to June 2018. After adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand only for the normal period and dropped the extended-period demand. Thereafter, the respondent opted for settlement under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme, 2019. Its declaration was accepted, the amount determined was paid and Form SVLDRS-4 dated 10.02.2020 was issued as a discharge certificate for full and final settlement. It relied upon Astute Valuers and Consultants Pvt. Ltd. Vs Union of India (Bombay High Court), where continuation of proceedings after issuance of a discharge certificate was held inconsistent with the object and statutory finality of the Scheme. The Tribunal also independently examined limitation. The Show Cause Notice dated 21.12.2018 was the fifth n
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad decision holding that once a taxpayer has received a valid discharge certificate under the Sabka Vishwas (Legacy Dispute Resolution) Scheme (SVLDRS), the Revenue cannot continue or revive an appeal on the same settled dispute. In this case, the Tribunal dismissed the Department’s appeal because the underlying tax dispute had already been resolved through SVLDRS, and the discharge certificate operated as final settlement for that matter. For compliance teams, the key point is that an SVLDRS discharge certificate has binding finality with respect to the covered issue, so any later departmental challenge on the same demand should be barred.

The decision also addresses limitation in a fifth show-cause notice (SCN): the Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s attempt to invoke the extended period of limitation for that notice. This means the Department could not justify the additional time window for raising the demand, which is important where allegations depend on suppression, wilful misstatement, or similar grounds typically needed to extend the normal limitation period. The appeals were filed with a delay of six days, which the Tribunal condoned after finding reasonable cause. The dispute concerned the computation of the permissible assessment block under Section 153C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the case of a person other than the person searched. The original search on the Alankrit Group took place on 18 October 2019; according to the assessee’s submissions recorded in the order, the Assessing Officer of the searched person recorded satisfaction on 14 June 2022, while reasons for initiating proceedings and issuing notice under Section 153C were recorded on 30 June 2022. The Revenue argued that the block period should be calculated with reference to the year of the original search and challenged the CIT(A)’s reliance on PCIT v. Ojjus Medicare (P.) Ltd., pointing out that an SLP had been filed against that decision. The assessee contended that the date relevant to a non-searched person was the date on which the seized material was handed over to its jurisdictional Assessing Officer or the date on which satisfaction was recorded, and that the impugned years consequently fell outside Section 153C. Relying principally on CIT v. Jasjit Singh and PCIT v. Ojjus Medicare (P.) Ltd., the Tribunal held that AYs 2010-11 and 2011-12 were outside the scope
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi ruling on **Section 153C of the Income-tax Act** concerning the **time limit for completing assessments** in cases involving seized material belonging to “the other person” (i.e., a person other than the one searched). The key holding is that the **limitation period for Section 153C proceedings starts from the date the Assessing Officer (AO) of the other person receives the seized material**, not from the date of the original search or seizure. Based on that rule, the Tribunal held that the assessments for **Assessment Years (AYs) 2010-11 and 2011-12** were **outside the permissible Section 153C limitation period** and therefore could not be sustained.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that when a company or related entity becomes subject to Section 153C proceedings because materials were found in someone else’s search, the department must be able to show **when the receiving AO actually got the seized material**, since that date governs the statutory block-period timeline. If the notice or assessment is issued beyond the limitation calculated from that receipt date, the assessment may be vulnerable to challenge as time-barred. The decision underscores the need to preserve records of the **date of transfer/receipt of seized documents between AOs**, because that date can determine whether the income-tax department’s action is valid.

The petitioner stated that the adjudication order dated 28.07.2024 came to his knowledge only when his accountant checked the common portal in March 2025. The State contended that ample opportunities had been granted and the appeal was correctly rejected as time-barred. The High Court, however, found that the petitioner had made out a prima facie case. rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court held that a GST adjudication order and the related appellate order could not stand where the department uploaded the show cause notice (SCN) only under the “Additional Notices” tab on the GST portal and did not separately intimate the taxpayer. The court found this mode of service violated natural justice because the taxpayer was deprived of a proper and effective opportunity to see and respond to the notice before adverse orders were passed. As a result, the HC quashed both the adjudication order and the appellate order.

For compliance purposes, the key point is procedural: GST authorities cannot rely on a buried portal upload alone if it does not reasonably alert the registered person to the SCN. Taxpayers should therefore monitor the GST portal carefully, including the “Additional Notices” section, and maintain internal controls to detect portal communications promptly. At the same time, if an SCN or order was issued without separate intimation and the taxpayer can show it was not effectively brought to its attention, this decision supports a challenge on natural justice grounds. The document does not state any new tax rate, threshold, or substantive GST liability change; it is a service/procedure ruling affecting how notices and orders must be communicated.

rows.summary: The Rajasthan High Court held that a GST show cause notice and the resulting order were invalid because they were unsigned, emphasizing that either digital authentication or physical signature is mandatory under Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules. In practical terms, the court found that GST notices/orders issued without proper authentication do not satisfy the legal requirement for validity, so taxpayers can challenge such documents on the ground that they were not duly signed. This ruling directly affects GST-registered entities that receive departmental notices or adjudication orders, because they should verify that any SCN, demand notice, or order is properly authenticated before treating it as enforceable. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is to check every GST communication for valid signature or digital authentication and to preserve a copy of any unsigned document as a potential ground for objection or appeal.

It further observed that approval under section 151 was granted by relying on the same old stateme
rows.summary:
This document reports an ITAT Delhi decision holding that a reassessment under the Income-tax Act cannot be sustained where it is based on stale investigation material that was already available to the tax department in earlier proceedings. In the case described, the tribunal found that the reassessment was improperly initiated because the “reasons to believe” did not rest on fresh, live information or a valid new basis; instead, the department attempted to reopen an assessment using the same information it had previously possessed and could have acted on earlier.

A key compliance takeaway is that the tribunal also held the approval under Section 151 to be mechanical, meaning the sanctioning authority had not applied independent, meaningful scrutiny before approving the reopening. That matters because reassessments require proper statutory approval, and the decision reinforces that such approval cannot be a rubber-stamp exercise; it must reflect real consideration of the facts and legal basis for reopening.

For companies and tax teams, the practical implication is that if the department issues a reassessment notice relying on old investigation material or information already on record, the notice may be challengeable as invalid, especially if the approval process appears perfunctory. This is not a substantive change in tax rates or filing deadlines, but a procedural ruling affecting the validity of reassessment actions under the Income-tax Act and the standards for Section 151 approval.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Penalty Not Automatic for Delayed Foreign Travel Tax Payment: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12577 Case Name Saudi Arabian Airlines Vs Union of India & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment.
rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court holding that a **delay in paying Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) does not amount to “non-payment” under Section 38(3)** of the relevant law, and therefore **penalty cannot be imposed automatically solely because the tax was paid late**. In other words, the Court distinguished between **late payment** and **failure to pay**, limiting the automatic use of penalty provisions where the tax was eventually paid rather than wholly omitted.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that entities responsible for collecting/remitting Foreign Travel Tax should still **pay on time to avoid disputes**, but a delayed remittance by itself is **not treated as an outright default equivalent to non-payment** under Section 38(3). Any penalty action must be assessed in light of this ruling rather than assumed to follow mechanically from lateness. The document does not specify any new filing deadline, rate change, or revised procedure; it is primarily a **judicial clarification restricting automatic penalty imposition** for delayed FTT payment.

rows.summary:
The document reports a Madras High Court ruling on reassessment procedure under the Income-tax Act: where the Income Tax Department had issued a Section 148 reassessment notice in the name of a deceased assessee, the court directed that a fresh notice must be issued to the deceased person’s legal representatives instead. The key compliance point is that a notice addressed only to a deceased individual is not sufficient to validly initiate or continue reassessment proceedings; the department must instead serve the legally responsible representatives of the deceased taxpayer.

For taxpayers and their estates, this means reassessment proceedings cannot be pursued mechanically against a dead person’s name, and legal heirs/executors must be properly identified and notified before the reassessment can proceed. The ruling is specifically relevant to notices under Section 148, i.e. notices for income escaping assessment, and it reinforces that procedural validity depends on issuing the notice to the correct legal person. The document does not mention any new monetary thresholds, tax rates, filing deadlines, or substantive tax changes; its significance is procedural and relates to proper service of reassessment notices after a taxpayer’s death.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the allowability of Portfolio Management Service (PMS) charges while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal arose from the order of the Ld. CIT(A), dated 28.08.2025, which had sustained the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2011-12. The assessee had returned total income of Rs. 72,26,297/- from salary, short term capital gain and income from other sources. In computing capital gains, the assessee claimed Rs. 8,42,360/- towards fees and charges paid to Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. for portfolio management services. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount on the ground that the expenditure could not be regarded as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of the capital asset within the meaning of section 48. The CIT(A) sustained the disallowance, relying principally upon the Mumbai Tribunal decision in ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah, where PMS fees and performance-linked charges had been held not deductible under section 48. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the issue was unsettled because different coordinate Benches had adopted divergent views. Reliance was placed upon KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a deduction while computing capital gains. The assessee also submitted that although the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding and Trading before the Bombay High Court, th
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai has held that portfolio management service (PMS) charges of Rs. 8.42 lakh are deductible while computing capital gains under Section 48 of the Income-tax Act. In this case, the Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position and allowed the PMS fees to be treated as an expenditure incurred in connection with the transfer of capital assets, despite the fact that there have been divergent views among different Tribunal decisions on this issue. The practical effect is that taxpayers who have incurred PMS charges in relation to managing investments and then realized capital gains may be able to claim those charges as a deduction from capital gains, reducing taxable gains, subject to the facts of their case and the applicable judicial view.  

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this is a favorable appellate ruling, but it is not described as a statutory amendment or a universal rule change; rather, it reflects a tribunal-level interpretation in a contested area. Entities or individuals using PMS should therefore preserve documentation showing the PMS fees paid, the link between those charges and the management/transfer of capital assets, and the basis on which the deduction is claimed under Section 48, because the deductibility position may still depend on jurisdictional precedent and case-specific facts.

Ltd. challenging an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it disallowed refund of input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the head SGST credit. The petitioner, engaged in export of spice extracts and oleoresins, was earlier registered under the Kerala Value Added Tax Act, 2003 and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 for transitioning excess input tax credit from its VAT ledger to its Electronic Credit Ledger. According to the petitioner, TRAN-1 was filed in November 2017 and the transitional credit was reflected in the Electronic Credit Ledger on 27.12.2017. For November 2017, the petitioner sought refund of ITC. The Department rejected the claim on the ground that transitional credit was not credit earned during the relevant period and therefore did not qualify as “Net ITC” under Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No.37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018. rows.summary: The Kerala High Court held that a taxpayer cannot use a delayed writ petition under Article 226 to resurrect a GST refund challenge that has already become time-barred. The case involved rejection of a transitional input tax credit (ITC) refund, and the court dismissed the writ on the ground that the claimant had missed the legally available time to pursue the remedy. In practical compliance terms, the decision reinforces that GST refund and transitional credit disputes must be raised within the prescribed limitation period, because courts may refuse to entertain stale challenges even if the underlying grievance concerns tax credit or refund denial. The ruling does not announce a new GST filing requirement or change any statutory deadline, but it is an important procedural warning: once the statutory or otherwise available challenge window closes, Article 226 will generally not be available as a fallback to reopen the matter.

For assessment year 2020-21, the petitioner’s return was subjected to scrutiny and the assessment was finalised. Subsequently, the petitioner received a notice under Section 148A proposing reassessment on the ground that certain income had escaped assessment. The basis of the proposed reassessment was an amount of Rs.8,05,92,988/- claimed as a deduction towards “Marked to Market valuation of hedge reserve”. According to the proposed basis, deduction was not allowable under Section 40A(13) in respect of marked-to-market valuation of hedge reserve computed in accordance with ICDS VI. The petitioner initially sought an adjournment. Thereafter, by email dated 07.11.2024, it explained that the sum of Rs.8,05,92,988/- deducted in the computation for AY 2020-21 had already been included in its tax computation for AY 2019-20. The petitioner furnished computation statements for AYs 2019-20 and 2020-21 in support of its explanation. According to the petitioner, the amount had already been included in taxable income for AY 2019-20 and had suffered tax, and its deduction while preparing the computation for AY 2020-21 was an accounting consequence. The petitioner also requested that, if its explanation was not accepted, it be given an opportunity to submit a further reply and be heard. The Assessing Authority nevertheless passed an order under Section 148A(3). Though the petitioner’
rows.summary: The document reports a Kerala High Court ruling on an income tax reassessment matter in which the court quashed an order passed under Section 148A(3) because the assessing authority did not properly consider the taxpayer’s claim that the disputed amount had already been taxed in Assessment Year (AY) 2019-20. In practical terms, the court held that before initiating or sustaining reassessment proceedings, the department must meaningfully examine the assessee’s explanation and tax history, especially where the taxpayer asserts that the same income has already been offered to tax in an earlier year. The decision appears to affect taxpayers facing reassessment notices under Section 148A and the tax authorities handling them, reinforcing that a reassessment order cannot be sustained if it ignores a material factual contention raised by the assessee. No specific tax rate, monetary threshold, or filing deadline is mentioned in the excerpt, but the compliance takeaway is that companies should preserve and be prepared to produce prior-year tax computations, return disclosures, and supporting records whenever the department questions whether an amount has been taxed already.

Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The CESTAT Hyderabad partly allowed the appeal of Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. against an Order-in-Original confirming service tax of Rs.1,63,15,458/- with interest under “Club or Association Service”, besides penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 and smaller demands under Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and had introduced a Time Share Holiday Scheme under which customers acquired a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week every year for 12 years against predetermined consideration. The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and that the time-share customers did not become members of the company in accordance with that Act. They neither subscribed to the memorandum, became shareholders, nor had the
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that service tax could not be levied on time-share accommodation by treating it as a “club or association” service, and it set aside the tax demand. The tribunal’s reasoning was that the customers using the time-share accommodation were not members of a club or association in the legal sense required for that tax category, so the arrangement did not fit the taxable service definition relied on by the department. As a result, the related penalties were also struck down as unsustainable.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this decision narrows the department’s ability to classify time-share accommodation receipts as club/association service merely because customers pay for access or use over time; the legal form of the relationship matters. The ruling indicates that businesses offering time-share accommodation should review how their service is categorized for indirect tax purposes, especially where the tax position was based on the customers being treated as members. No effective date, rate change, or prospective compliance deadline is stated in the text provided; the document reflects a judicial determination on a disputed tax classification and penalty exposure.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed a writ petition challenging the prolonged detention and subsequent seizure of a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan. The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings
rows.summary:
The document reports a Gujarat High Court ruling that Customs authorities cannot avoid the statutory seizure framework under Section 110 of the Customs Act by simply keeping imported goods under prolonged detention without issuing a proper seizure order. The specific case involved an imported Land Cruiser that had been held by Customs, and the court directed its release, indicating that indefinite retention of imported goods is not permissible when Customs has not lawfully completed the seizure process.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that once Customs takes possession or control of imported goods, it must act within the legal limits and cannot continue detaining the property indefinitely as a substitute for seizure. The ruling reinforces that Customs enforcement actions must follow the prescribed statutory procedure, including timely issuance of a seizure order where required, rather than relying on open-ended detention. No specific monetary thresholds, deadlines, or rate changes are mentioned in the provided text, but the decision is significant for importers, customs brokers, and compliance teams handling detained shipments because it strengthens the ability to challenge prolonged detention that is not backed by formal seizure action.

(CESTAT Kolkata) Summary: CESTAT Kolkata allowed the appeal filed by Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. and set aside the demand for reversal of CENVAT credit of Rs.83,839. The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set as
rows.summary:
The document reports a CESTAT Kolkata ruling on excise/CENVAT credit, holding that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely because the manufacturer’s invoice named the assessee as the **consignee**, so long as the goods were actually received by the assessee and properly entered in its records/accounts. In other words, the tribunal recognized that the invoice description and consignee designation were sufficient to support credit when the underlying transaction was genuine and the receipt of goods was evidenced.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that credit eligibility should be evaluated based on **substance and documentation of receipt/use**, not only on rigid invoice-form terminology, where the assessee is clearly identified as the consignee and the goods are traced into inventory or accounting records. The ruling does not announce a new rate, threshold, or filing deadline; it is a judicial interpretation affecting how manufacturers and recipients defend CENVAT credit claims in excise audits or disputes. Firms should still retain invoices, goods receipt evidence, stock/accounting entries, and any supporting transport or inward records to substantiate that the goods were received and accounted for, because those facts were central to the credit being allowed.

The appellant had executed EPC/works contracts relating to construction of dams, reservoirs, canals and allied structures for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012. A show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 demanded service tax of Rs.43,86,471/- under Works Contract Service, which was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant challenged the order and sought waiver of pre-deposit. The Commissioner (Appeals) fixed the stay application for hearing on 12.06.2014; although the appellant sought an adjournment, the request was declined and, by order dated 13.06.2014, it was directed to deposit 50% of the service tax demand. The appellant subsequently requested a speaking order considering its legal submissions and precedents, but did not comply with the pre-deposit condition. Its appeal was consequently dismissed on 23.07.2014. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that its appeal had been dismissed without adjudication on merits and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had failed to consider its prima facie case, balance of convenience and financial hardship. It relied, inter alia, upon Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya P
rows.summary: The document reports a CESTAT Hyderabad ruling that upheld dismissal of a service tax appeal because the appellant did not comply with a pre-deposit direction. The tribunal had ordered a deposit of 50% of the disputed amount under the **unamended Section 35F**, and the appeal was dismissed when that condition was not satisfied. For compliance purposes, the key point is that, at least for appeals governed by the pre-amendment regime, failure to make the required pre-deposit can be a complete bar to appellate relief and can result in dismissal of the case without a merits hearing. The decision reinforces that companies contesting service tax demands must strictly track and meet any court/tribunal-ordered pre-deposit requirement within the prescribed time, because non-compliance can forfeit the appeal.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vodafone Idea Limited Vs ACIT (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court allowed the connected writ petitions filed by Vodafone Idea Limited, seeking release of pending TDS refunds with applicable interest for Assessment Years 2003-04, 2008-09 to 2013-14. The petitions stated that the refunds had remained unpaid for about two years even after orders of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and subsequent orders passed by the Assessing Officer giving effect to those appellate decisions. For AY 2012-13, the Tribunal’s order dated 05.06.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 30.10.2024, with refund quantified by the assessee at Rs.11,06,37,172; the Form 26B applications dated 25.04.2025 were rejected. For AY 2013-14, the Tribunal’s order dated 30.04.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 14.10.2024, with refund quantified at Rs.7,57,50,048; the Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025 was rejected. For AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12, the relevant Tribunal orders were dated 26.11.2024 and 03.02.2025, followed by an appeal-effect order dated 15.05.2026, with refund quantified at Rs.34,45,69,250. The total amount found payable by the Assessing Officer was Rs.53,09,56,470. The petitioner argued that Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A and Form 26B address the processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess or incorrect deduction/deposit. According to the petitioner, they do not govern a refund that crystallises after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Pr
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court has directed the income tax department to refund **Rs. 53.09 crore of TDS, together with applicable interest**, and held that the department could not insist on **Form 26B** or rely on **Rule 31A** in this situation. The key point is that, **after a Section 201 assessment has already been completed**, the court treated the request as one that did not require the payer to go through the usual Form 26B process for correction or refund processing.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this ruling limits the tax department’s ability to reject or delay a TDS refund merely because **Form 26B was not filed**, where the liability issue has already been determined under **Section 201**. The decision appears to affect **deductors/payers seeking TDS refund after an adverse or completed Section 201 proceeding**, and it reinforces that procedural requirements under **Rule 31A** should not be applied mechanically to defeat a refund once the substantive assessment has been concluded.

The document does not provide any broader statutory amendment, rate change, or general new filing deadline; it is a **court-directed refund order** with interest, based on the facts of the case. Compliance officers should read it as a signal to review refund positions in Section 201 matters, especially where the department may attempt to insist on Form 26B even though the assessment record already resolves the tax position.

rows.summary:
The CBI has registered a criminal case against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and three others — Pankaj Suroliya, Amish Pandya, and Rajeev Dholakia — based on a complaint from LIC Housing Finance Ltd. One specifically identified facility was a Rs 500 crore loan to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd. and Pan India Infra Projects Pvt Ltd. as co-borrower, described as a home entity loan for takeover, top-up, and business expansion under Loan Account No. 610700003341.

The document reports that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) withdrew more than ₹6 trillion of liquidity from the banking system through cash absorption operations after a sharp surge in surplus funds. Specifically, on Monday the RBI received ₹3.53 trillion in offers at an overnight auction, following a separate 30-day auction in which banks parked ₹2.59 trillion, bringing the total absorbed amount to just over ₹6 trillion. The article ties this action to a record banking-system liquidity surplus of ₹11.6 trillion on September 6, which it says was nearly 4% of total banking system deposits.

The document does not announce a new regulatory requirement, deadline, or compliance filing obligation, and it does not identify a specific class of institutions beyond the Indian banking system generally. However, the scale and tenor of the RBI’s absorption operations—overnight and 30-day placements—are relevant for treasury and liquidity-risk teams because they affect available system liquidity, short-term rates, and banks’ ability to place excess funds with the central bank.

rows.summary:
ARCIL said its fastest portfolio growth is now coming from retail assets originated by NBFCs, even though bank-originated retail, corporate, and other retail portfolios continue to grow as well. Management said it expects retail and SME assets to take a larger share of the overall portfolio over time because those segments are growing faster than corporate assets; as of FY26, retail and SME together made up a little over 31% of ARCIL’s portfolio, while corporate assets were around 69%. The company also said its retail and SME portfolio has grown at a CAGR of close to 56% over the last couple of years.

Operationally, ARCIL said it currently handles about 32 lakh NPA accounts on the retail side and operates across roughly 24 states. It resolves close to 25% of its opening AUM each year, which it attributed to low leverage and cash flows generated through resolutions. The management also noted that about Rs 5.5 lakh crore of corporate assets written off by banks and NBFCs are returning to the resolution ecosystem, which is relevant to its future business pipeline.

From a strategic and regulatory/business development standpoint, ARCIL said it is set to become the first standalone asset reconstruction company to list in India. It said it is open to acquiring smaller ARCs, but only where there is a willing seller, appropriate valuation, and strategic fit. Management also described NARCL as both a competitor and a complement, with NARCL focused mainly on very large-ticket stressed assets.

The document reports that the one-year median marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) for scheduled commercial banks in India rose to **8.70% in August** from **8.60% in July**, and for the first time in **14 months** this moved **above its year-ago level** of **8.60%**. This increase occurred even though the **repo rate stayed unchanged at 5.25%**, and despite a sharp improvement in banking system liquidity, suggesting persistent funding-cost pressure rather than a broad rate cycle driven by monetary tightening.

The rise was **not broad-based**: it was driven **entirely by foreign banks**, whose one-year median MCLR increased to **7.33% in August from 7.20% in July**. By contrast, the one-year median MCLR for **public sector banks** remained unchanged at **8.80%**, and for **private sector banks** remained unchanged at **9.35%**. For compliance and treasury teams, this means the rate movement is concentrated in a subset of banks and does not reflect a uniform market-wide repricing.

The article also notes that system liquidity improved materially, with **surplus liquidity rising to around Rs 6.7 lakh crore by August 31**, compared with **Rs 2.5 lakh crore at the end of July** and **Rs 1.4 lakh crore at the end of June**. This improvement was largely attributed to the **conversion of Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits into rupees**, which eased near-term funding pressure on banks. A related point in the article is that banks’ **fresh spreads recovered in July**, with the spread for scheduled commercial banks **widening by 8 basis points**. There are no explicit new regulatory deadlines, filing requirements, or compliance procedures announced in the text; the document is primarily a market update indicating that lending-rate pressure persists for some banks despite easier liquidity conditions.

rows.summary:
This article does **not** describe a new regulation or compliance obligation; it is a discussion of India’s reported **7.8% real GDP growth** for **April–June (Q1 FY27)** and the methodology behind the revised national accounts series. The main issue raised is whether the combination of a **new 2022–23 base year**, **changes in price measures**, and **revisions to prior estimates** may be making real growth appear stronger than it would under the earlier series. The reported figures in the article are that **nominal GDP grew 10.3% year-on-year**, **real GDP grew 7.8%**, and **real GVA grew 8.2%**; the growth rate also exceeded the **RBI’s 7.0% forecast** and market expectations of roughly **7.1%**.

The article explains that the controversy centers on the **GDP deflator**, which is the implicit price index derived by comparing GDP at current prices with GDP at constant prices. Because the deflator is used to strip out inflation and convert nominal output into real output, changes in the price measure can materially affect the headline real growth number. For a compliance or finance team, the practical takeaway is limited to monitoring: if your organization relies on Indian macro indicators for forecasting, valuation, treasury planning, budgeting, or covenant models, this article signals that the **latest GDP series is still being debated and may be revisited in market commentary**. No filing, reporting, or operational action is mandated by the document itself.

rows.summary:
India’s central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), took liquidity-draining action on September 7, 2026 by absorbing more than 6 trillion rupees of excess banking system funds through cash withdrawal operations after bank liquidity had surged to a record high. Specifically, banks placed 2.59 trillion rupees into a 30-day operation and the RBI received another 3.53 trillion rupees of offers in an overnight auction; the central bank had targeted withdrawal of 7 trillion rupees through the 30-day operation, but participation was described by market traders as weak. One source close to the process said there were no technical issues and that bids were submitted through the RBI’s e-Kuber system, although the RBI itself did not comment.

For compliance and treasury teams, the key regulatory signal is that the RBI is actively and substantially tightening surplus liquidity conditions, which can affect short-term funding, money-market rates, and internal liquidity management assumptions. The article states that India’s banking system liquidity surplus reached 11.6 trillion rupees on September 6, equal to nearly 4% of banking system deposits, and that the spike followed India receiving $136 billion under special one-off schemes intended to improve external balances. The piece also notes the RBI had recently signaled that rate hikes could be ahead as inflation and growth firm up, and a treasury official expected another long-duration reverse repo later in the week, indicating further liquidity absorption could follow.

The article does not describe a new compliance rule, filing obligation, or reporting deadline, but it does document a material change in operating conditions for banks and other market participants: sustained surplus liquidity is being withdrawn, the total RBI liquidity withdrawal actions have exceeded 8.5 trillion rupees, and the central bank appears prepared to continue using reverse-repo style operations if excess cash remains elevated. For affected institutions, the practical obligation is to monitor RBI auction notices and funding conditions closely, ensure treasury systems and access to e-Kuber are functioning, and be prepared for continued volatility in overnight and term liquidity management.

India’s foreign-exchange reserves reached a new all-time high of **$740.80 billion** in the week ended **August 28, 2026**, rising by **$11.475 billion** from **$729.328 billion** on **August 21**. The article frames this as a materially stronger external buffer for India at a time when wars are disrupting global capital flows, making investors more cautious, keeping oil prices elevated, and increasing pressure on currencies.

That means the reserve accretion is paired with a second-order policy issue: **managing the rupee liquidity created by these inflows and the future dollar repayment obligations they generate**. The piece also notes that this reserve strength gives the RBI “unprecedented firepower” to intervene in foreign-exchange markets and absorb external shocks, while simultaneously complicating liquidity management in the domestic financial system.

Its material takeaway for regulated entities is strategic: Indian corporates with foreign-currency exposures, importers, borrowers with dollar obligations, and financial institutions active in FX or offshore funding should expect the RBI to have greater capacity to smooth volatility, but also to continue balancing reserve accumulation against domestic liquidity conditions. For any entity relying on external funding or exposed to oil and currency volatility, the environment described here suggests heightened attention to FX risk management, funding costs, and policy signals from the RBI.

The article says the Reserve Bank of India is facing a large liquidity-management challenge because FCNR(B) scheme inflows have created an estimated ₹10.5 lakh crore of system liquidity, far above earlier expectations. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India is reconsidering its draft proposal to impose a blanket ban on revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders/NBFCs, after industry feedback suggested the measure would affect far more of the NBFC sector than the RBI initially expected. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu met with NBFC representatives and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the central bank has already received about 350 industry feedback submissions on the draft proposal.

The main compliance issue under discussion is whether the RBI will proceed with a full prohibition on revolving credit or instead move to a partial restriction. Industry participants say the RBI originally believed the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but the consultation response indicates that a much broader set of lenders could be caught by the rule. One specific carve-out drawing repeated attention is an exemption for supply chain financing, which the industry has urged the RBI to preserve.

No final contours have been issued yet, so there is no confirmed operative rule to implement at this stage. However, sources cited in the article suggest the final guidelines may be issued in roughly two months, which is the only timeline provided. For compliance teams at NBFCs and other non-bank lenders, the key takeaway is that revolving credit products remain under active regulatory review, and firms offering such facilities should be prepared for either a narrower restriction or a broader ban depending on the RBI’s final decision, with supply chain financing potentially treated differently.

Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s leadership has changed after managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal retired early on health grounds, creating a continuity watchpoint for the bank’s long-term FY30 strategy. rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.
rows.summary:
The article says NBFCs have asked the Reserve Bank of India to clarify whether loan recovery calls qualify as “service calls” that may be made using the TRAI-mandated 1600 numbering series. Industry representatives raised the issue with RBI Deputy Governor S. C. Murmu, arguing that while sales calls should clearly remain outside the 1600 series, it is still unclear whether recovery calls are covered; this matters because customers are increasingly blocking calls originating from the 1600 series.

The underlying regulatory framework is that the Department of Telecommunications had allocated the 1600 series for service and transactional voice calls by government and BFSI entities, and TRAI later made migration to this series mandatory in a phased manner for RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities. TRAI’s objective was to help consumers distinguish legitimate regulated-financial calls from spam, promotional, and potentially fraudulent calls. For RBI-regulated entities, the compliance deadlines were staggered: commercial banks had to move to the 1600 series by January 1, 2026; large NBFCs with assets above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks, and small finance banks by February 1, 2026; and remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks, and other covered entities by March 1, 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key unresolved point is whether debt collection/recovery outreach can be treated as a permissible service call under the 1600 framework or whether it must be handled outside that series. The document does not indicate that any rule has changed yet; rather, it reports an industry request for RBI guidance because the current implementation is creating operational uncertainty and call-blocking risk for regulated lenders.

rows.summary:
This circular operationalises the freezing of promoter holdings at the ISIN level for companies undertaking a share buy-back under Regulation 24(i)(ea) of the SEBI (Buy-back of Securities) Regulations, 2018. For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that the holdings of the promoter and promoter group, including associates, must be **frozen at the ISIN level**, meaning the securities identified under the specific International Securities Identification Number involved in the buy-back cannot be transacted in a way that would defeat the freeze mechanism. This is a procedural implementation measure under the buy-back regime, so affected entities need to ensure their depository and custodial arrangements support the freeze and that internal records correctly identify all covered promoter-related holdings. Any company proposing a buy-back, along with its promoters/promoter group and associated intermediaries, should treat this as an operational control requirement that must be activated for the duration and scope prescribed under the buy-back framework.

The document does not state a separate monetary threshold, pricing formula, or new substantive buy-back eligibility condition in the title/content provided; instead, it establishes the mechanism for enforcing the existing regulatory freeze requirement under Regulation 24(i)(ea). Compliance teams should therefore focus on implementation readiness: identifying the relevant ISIN, mapping all promoter and promoter-group holdings (including associates), and ensuring the freeze is reflected in depository systems and transaction controls before and during the buy-back period.

rows.summary:
SEBI’s Nodal Co-ordination Cell issued an informal guidance response to Share India Securities Limited on August 17, 2026, in answer to a June 22, 2026 request concerning whether securities bought under Discretionary Portfolio Management Services (D-PMS) may be pledged. The firm explained that, under its D-PMS setup, clients maintain demat accounts with an approved custodian, trades are executed through empaneled brokers, and the securities purchased remain in the client’s beneficial ownership and are held in the client’s name in the demat account; the specific practical question was whether a client can pledge those securities, either directly or by routing instructions through the portfolio manager to the custodian.

The applicant, which is a SEBI-registered portfolio manager (**registration no. rows.summary:
This consultation paper proposes a framework for **devolving in-the-money (ITM) single-stock option contracts into futures one day before expiry**, specifically to reduce the risks created when **out-of-the-money (OTM) options can suddenly move into ITM near expiry** in a market that uses **physical settlement** for derivatives. In practical terms, the proposal is aimed at the **derivatives segment** and would affect **single-stock option contracts** that are close to expiry, especially where sharp price movements could create settlement and risk-management issues.

Because the document title indicates a **consultation paper**, it is not itself a final rule; rather, it is seeking feedback on whether this conversion mechanism should be adopted and how it should operate. The key operational concept is that **ITM option positions would be converted into futures contracts one trading day before expiry**, presumably to reduce settlement stress and manage the risks associated with last-day price volatility and exercise/assignment in physical settlement. The title does not provide the exact conversion mechanics, eligibility thresholds, conversion ratios, timelines for submission, or whether the process would be mandatory or automatic, so a compliance team should treat this as a **potential change to expiry/settlement handling for single-stock options** and watch for the detailed consultation text or final circular.

For compliance purposes, the material point is that firms trading, clearing, broking, or risk-managing **single-stock options in the derivatives segment** may need to adjust their **expiry-day controls, client communications, margin/risk systems, and settlement workflows** if the framework is implemented. Since the document is framed as a proposal to mitigate risks from sudden ITM shifts near expiry under physical settlement, affected firms should expect possible requirements around **pre-expiry position monitoring, automated conversion processes, and operational readiness for futures settlement instead of option exercise**.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021  Addendum- Executive Summary
rows.desc: Page 1 of 2 Addendum to Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting Norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 The following is the executive summary of consultation paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting placed on the website of SEBI on August 14, 2023 for seeking public comments. 1. Review of the Counter-Offer Mechanism  As per the Delisting Regulations, an acquirer can make a counter-offer only after the cumulative shareholding of the shares held by acquirer and shares tendered by public shareholders in Reverse Book Building (“RBB”) mechanism reaches at least 90% of the paid-up capital of the company.  In order to facilitate cases where cumulative shareholding of the shares held by acquirer and shares tendered by public shareholders does not reach 90%, it is proposed to reduce the threshold for counter-offer to below 90% but equal to or more than 75% (75%-90%) of the paid-up capital of the company.  The floor price of such counter-offer shall be the Volume Weighted Average Price of the shares tendered by the willing shareholders in the delisting offer wherein the acquirer failed to reach 90%. 2. Review of “Floor Price” under the Delisting Regulations-  In addition to the current parameters for computing floor price, it is suggested to introduce an additional parameter i.e. Adjusted Book Value which will be applicable for delisting of frequently traded and infrequently traded shares. 3. Alternatives to the Reverse Book Building Process  Presently, exit price is determined by way of RBB mechanism only.  It is proposed to introduce delisting at fixed price as an alternative to RBB for companies whose shares are frequently traded. 4. Review of the Reference Date for Determination of the Floor Price-  Presently, the reference date for computing the floor price is the date of approval of the board meeting.  It has been proposed in the consultation paper to change the reference date to the date of the initial public announcement.  F

rows.summary:

The DP must keep all beneficial-owner information from the account-opening form and supporting documents strictly confidential and may disclose it only where required by statutory, legal, or regulatory authority, while the beneficial owner must immediately notify the DP in writing of any change in the details previously provided in the account-opening form or later furnished to the DP.

rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), and it indicates that SEBI is **not accepting several requests to relax the compliance framework**. On the proposal relating to **identification/validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs**, commenters asked that existing FPIs not be required to provide additional proof because it would increase burden and paperwork; SEBI **disagreed**, saying the verification requirements will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry has already implemented. In practical terms, FPIs seeking the relevant status will still need to demonstrate the required conditions—such as diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios—but SEBI’s stated approach is to use a familiar verification model rather than introduce an entirely new process.

On **re-KYC and fee/payment periodicity**, commenters wanted the current periodicity to remain unchanged and opposed additional re-KYC requirements, arguing that material changes such as UBO updates would be caught through ordinary monitoring and that longer fee blocks would reduce SEBI’s flexibility. rows.title: Adjudication Order in the matter of trading activities of certain entities in the scrip of Veer Global Infraconstruction Limited.[Corrigendum]
rows.desc: RG/2026-27/32369-32379 1. Whereas, an Adjudication Order no. Order/SM/RG/2026-27/32369-32379 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Order’) has been passed in the matter of trading activities of certain entities in the scrip of Veer Global Infraconstruction Limited. 2. It is noted that under para 31.2 and 32.2 of the Order, synchronised trades of Patch 1 were inadvertently mentioned instead of synchronised trades of Patch 2 and Patch 3 respectively. Accordingly, para 31.2 and 32.2 of the Order may be read as under: Para 31.2: Synchronised trades The details of synchronised trades by suspected entities in the scrip during patch 2 was as below: Buyer Name Seller Name Synchronized Quantity Sum Of LTP Diff Number Of Days Number Of Trades %Market Volume Mrs Bhavana Sahay Mr Ranjan Sahay 1000 -17.90 1 1 0.64% Total 1000 -17.90 1 1 0.64% Market Total 1000 -17.90 1 1 0.64% It was observed that suspect group entities, through 1 synchronized trade among themselves, contributed 0.64% to market volume and Rs.-17.90 to net LTP. Para 32.2: Synchronised trades The details of synchronised trades by suspected entities in the scrip during patch 3 was as below: Buyer Name Seller Name Synchronized Quantity Sum Of LTP Diff (Rs) Number Of Days Number Of Trades %Market Volume Mrs Bhavana Sahay Mrs Rita Kumar 2000 0.00 2 2 0.52% Mr Ranjan Sahay Mrs Bhavana Sahay 2000 -5.05 2 2 0.52% Mrs Shahnaj Khatoon Mrs Rita Kumar 4000 13.70 4 4 1.04% Mrs Rita Kumar Mrs Bhavana Sahay 4000 -12.45 4 4 1.04% Total 15000 13.15 11 15 3.89% It was observed that through 11 synchronized trades among themselves, they contributed 3.89% to market volume and Rs.13.15 to LTP. 3. The order bearing Ref. No. Order/SM/RG/2026-27/32369-32379 shall always be read with this ‘Corrigendum’ and other contents of the Order shall remain unchanged. 4. A copy of this Corrigendum shall be served upon the Noticee, and also to the Securities and Exchange Board of India. DATE: April 27, 2026 PLACE: MUMBAI SUDEEP MISHRA ADJUDICATING OFFICER
rows.summary:
This corrigendum amends an Adjudication Order concerning trading activity in the scrip of Veer Global Infraconstruction Limited, specifically correcting the description of synchronized trades in paragraphs 31.2 and 32.2 of the original order. The substantive correction is that the original order mistakenly referred to “Patch 1”; it must instead be read as referring to “Patch 2” in para 31.2 and “Patch 3” in para 32.2.

For para 31.2, the corrected finding states that during patch 2, the suspected entities executed one synchronized trade: Mrs Bhavana Sahay bought from Mr Ranjan Sahay 1,000 shares, with a sum of LTP difference of Rs. -17.90, across 1 day and 1 trade, representing 0.64% of market volume. The order states that this single synchronized trade by the suspect group contributed 0.64% to market volume and Rs. -17.90 to net LTP.

For para 32.2, the corrected finding states that during patch 3, the suspected entities executed 11 synchronized trades among themselves, involving 15 trades in total and 15,000 shares, with a total sum of LTP difference of Rs. 13.15 and a contribution of 3.89% to market volume. The table lists the specific matched trades: Mrs Bhavana Sahay/Mr Ranjan Sahay for 2,000 shares with Rs. 0.00 LTP difference over 2 days and 2 trades; Mr Ranjan Sahay/Mrs Bhavana Sahay for 2,000 shares with Rs. -5.05 over 2 days and 2 trades; Mrs Shahnaj Khatoon/Mrs Rita Kumar for 4,000 shares with Rs. 13.70 over 4 days and 4 trades; and Mrs Rita Kumar/Mrs Bhavana Sahay for 4,000 shares with Rs. -12.45 over 4 days and 4 trades.

The corrigendum does not change any other part of the adjudication order; it expressly states that all other contents remain unchanged, and the original order numbered Order/SM/RG/2026-27/32369-32379 must be read together with this corrigendum. A copy is to be served on the noticee and on SEBI. The corrigendum is dated April 27, 2026, at Mumbai, and is signed by Sudeep Mishra, Adjudicating Officer.
