rows.title: Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/251 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 20 September 02, 2026 To All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks Madam / Sir Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks Please refer to Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of the A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No.92, dated April 4, 2003, in terms of which AD banks were required to: a. Furnish an up-to-date list of all its offices/branches maintaining Rupee accounts of non-resident banks, as at the end of December each year before 15th January of the following year to the Central Office of Reserve Bank, and b. Report temporary overdrawals by overseas branches/ correspondents over permissible limit, if not adjusted within five days, to the Central Office of Reserve Bank. 2. On a review, it has been decided to dispense with the above reporting requirements with immediate effect. 3. The directions contained in this circular have been issued under sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999) and are without prejudice to permissions/approvals, if any, required under any other law. Yours faithfully (N. Senthil Kumar) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has removed two reporting obligations for Authorised Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I) banks with immediate effect, as of **September 2, 2026**. Previously, under Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 92 dated **April 4, 2003**, AD banks had to (1) send the RBI Central Office an up-to-date list of all offices/branches maintaining **rupee accounts of non-resident banks** as of **December 31** each year, by **January 15** of the following year, and (2) report **temporary overdrawals** by overseas branches/correspondents that exceeded the permissible limit if those overdrawals were not adjusted within **five days**.  

The circular states that, following a review, both of those requirements are now **dispensed with immediately**, so affected banks no longer need to make those specific annual and exception reports to the RBI under those provisions. The change applies to **all Authorised Dealer Category-I banks** and relates specifically to their handling of **non-resident bank rupee accounts** and monitoring/reporting of **overdrawals by overseas branches/correspondents**. The RBI notes that the directions are issued under **sections 10(4) and 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and that they do not affect any permissions or approvals that may still be required under other applicable laws.

rows.title: Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half-Yearly Return
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/250 CO.FIDD.FSD.No.S544/05-10-001/2026-27 September 02, 2026 The Chief Executive Officer / Managing Director All Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) All Local Area Banks/ Urban Cooperative Banks/ Rural Cooperative Banks/ Non- Banking Financial Companies / AIFIs Madam / Dear Sir, Relief Measures in Areas Affected by Natural Calamities - Reporting through Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) Portal - Introduction of Half- Yearly Return The regulatory framework governing the relief measures to be extended by the Regulated Entities (REs) in areas affected by natural calamities has been revised vide the amendment directions on Resolution of Stressed Assets dated April 29, 2026 (list enclosed), which came into effect from July 1, 2026. 2. These directions require REs to submit data relating to relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities through the CIMS portal on a half-yearly basis. Accordingly, in order to align the existing reporting mechanism with the revised regulatory framework, REs shall furnish the required information in the revised reporting format through the CIMS portal. 3. The return shall be submitted within 30 days from the end of each half-year, i.e., by October 30 for the half-year ending September 30, and by April 30 for the half-year ending March 31. 4. REs shall ensure that the information submitted through the CIMS portal is accurate, complete, and duly validated. Appropriate internal systems and processes may be 2 established to facilitate timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the required information. 5. Further, the existing monthly return which was applicable to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (including Small Finance Banks and excluding Regional Rural Banks) on relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities stands discontinued with effect from July 1, 2026. Yours sincerely, (R Giridharan) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has revised the reporting framework for relief measures extended in areas affected by natural calamities under the amended Resolution of Stressed Assets directions dated April 29, 2026, which became effective on July 1, 2026. Under the new requirement, regulated entities must now report data on such relief measures through the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS) portal in a revised format on a half-yearly basis, rather than under the prior reporting approach.

The half-yearly return must be filed within 30 days after the end of each half-year: by October 30 for the period ending September 30, and by April 30 for the period ending March 31. This applies broadly to all regulated entities covered by the circular, specifically Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks, as well as Local Area Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, and All India Financial Institutions. Entities are required to ensure the submitted information is accurate, complete, and properly validated, and they should establish internal systems and processes to support timely collection, verification, consolidation, and submission of the data.

The circular also states that the existing monthly return for relief measures in natural calamity-affected areas, which applied to Scheduled Commercial Banks including Small Finance Banks but excluding Regional Rural Banks, has been discontinued effective July 1, 2026. In practical terms, compliance teams should treat the half-yearly CIMS filing as the operative reporting obligation going forward and stop the prior monthly submission for the affected bank categories from that date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/249 DOR.MRG.REC.No.217/00-00-011/2026-27 September 2, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to Chapter VIII of Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, on Investment in non-SLR securities. In view of the establishment of Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) as the nation's central digital payment fraud intelligence platform and to enable UCBs to acquire its membership, there is a need to amend the extant instructions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (hereinafter called the Act), read with Section 56 thereof, and all other laws enabling the Reserve Bank in this regard, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. (i) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Second Amendment Directions, 2026. (ii) These Amendment Directions shall come into effect from the date of issue. 4. The Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025, are amended as provided below. (i) Paragraph 101.(5) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “101.(5) Equity shares of Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB sector and Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC) for acquiring membership;”. (ii) Paragraph 107.(1) shall be substituted by the following, namely:- “107.(1) Equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), Umbrella Organization (UO) of UCB Sector, IDPIC, and CCBs / StCBs, if it becomes necessary to do so for
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio** directions were amended on **September 2, 2026** through the **Second Amendment Directions, 2026**, and these amendments take effect **immediately from the date of issue**. The stated purpose is to reflect the establishment of the **Indian Digital Payment Intelligence Corporation (IDPIC)** as the country’s central digital payment fraud intelligence platform and to allow UCBs to become members of IDPIC.

The key substantive change is in the treatment of eligible equity investments. **Paragraph 101(5)** of the 2025 Directions is replaced so that UCBs may invest in **equity shares of the Umbrella Organization (UO) of the UCB sector and of IDPIC, specifically for acquiring membership**. In other words, IDPIC is now expressly added as a permitted investment target in the membership context.

A related change is made to **Paragraph 107(1)**, which is also substituted to expand the list of permitted equity-share investments. The revised text includes **equity shares of Market Infrastructure Companies (MICs), the UCB sector’s Umbrella Organization (UO), IDPIC, and CCBs/StCBs where necessary for acquiring membership**. For compliance purposes, the amendment means UCBs should now treat IDPIC-related membership equity as expressly authorized under the investment portfolio framework, alongside the previously recognized entities, and apply the amended provisions as of **September 2, 2026**.

rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/248 DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.214/13.03.00/2026-27 August 25, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Directions’), dated November 28, 2025 (Updated as on June 17, 2026), wherein temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits of 3-5 year tenors and restriction on interest rates on NRE deposits of 3 year and above tenors, including the deposits that are renewed upon maturity, have been provided with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026. These Amendment Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co- operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. These Amendment Directions shall come into force with immediate effect. 5. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Directions, as under: i. In paragraph 24(4) subscript ( 1 ), the phrase “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until September 30, 2026” shall be substituted with “with effect from June 17, 2026, for the period until August 31, 2026”. ii. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026** amends the earlier **Directions dated November 28, 2025** (updated June 17, 2026) that had granted a **temporary relaxation** on deposit pricing for rural co-operative banks. The underlying relaxation, which began **June 17, 2026**, had allowed the **temporary withdrawal of the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits with 3–5 year tenors** and had also **restricted interest rates on NRE deposits with tenors of 3 years and above, including renewals upon maturity**, originally running through **September 30, 2026**. This amendment shortens that end date by replacing **“September 30, 2026” with “August 31, 2026”** in the relevant provisions, so the temporary relaxation now applies only until **August 31, 2026**.

The amendment is issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and states that it is made in the public interest. It is titled the **Second Amendment Directions, 2026** and **takes effect immediately** upon issuance dated **August 25, 2026**. Operationally, compliance teams at affected rural co-operative banks should ensure that deposit-rate practices for the specified FCNR(B) and NRE categories are aligned to the revised sunset date and that any systems, product documentation, customer communications, or rate-setting controls referencing the earlier **September 30, 2026** deadline are updated to **August 31, 2026**.

For **fresh FCNR(B) deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years**, the exemption from **CRR and SLR maintenance** continues to apply only to deposits mobilized by banks **between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026). Likewise, for **fresh NRE term deposits** with a **tenor of 3 years or more**—including deposits renewed upon maturity—the CRR/SLR exemption now applies only to deposits mobilized **between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026** (instead of through September 30, 2026). The amendment specifically replaces the date **“September 30, 2026” with “August 31, 2026”** in the relevant paragraphs of the 2025 Directions, so compliance teams should ensure deposit classification, reserve computations, and any related reporting reflect the earlier deadline for eligibility.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/237 DOR.CRE.REC.210/07-03-008/2026-27 August 25, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026 The Reserve Bank has issued the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Directions’ ). On a review, it has been decided to revise the large exposure framework for Infrastructure Debt Fund-Non-Banking Financial Company (IDF-NBFC) in the Upper Layer. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Chapter III B of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and all other provisions / laws enabling the Reserve Bank of India (‘RBI’) in this regard, RBI being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. These Amendment Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Non- Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026. 4. These Amendment Directions shall come into force with immediate effect. 5. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Directions as under: (1) After paragraph 39 in ‘Chapter IV - Guidelines Applicable to NBFC – Upper Layer’, a new paragraph 39A shall be inserted as under: 39A. The large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFC shall also be applicable to IDF-NBFC that are subject to Upper Layer regulations in terms of paragraph 60A of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 read together with 2 paragraph 18 (4) (i) of the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025. (Dr. Sudarsana Sahoo) Chief General Manager
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026** on **August 25, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. The amendment updates the existing **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025** by revising the **large exposure framework** for a specific class of entities: **Infrastructure Debt Fund–NBFCs (IDF-NBFCs)** that fall within the **Upper Layer** regulatory category.

Substantively, RBI has inserted a new **paragraph 39A** into **Chapter IV – Guidelines Applicable to NBFC – Upper Layer**. This new paragraph states that the **large exposure limits applicable to NBFC-IFCs** will also apply to **IDF-NBFCs** that are subject to Upper Layer regulation under **paragraph 60A of the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**, read together with **paragraph 18(4)(i) of the RBI (Commercial Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**. In practical terms, any IDF-NBFC in the Upper Layer must now comply with the same concentration/large exposure limits that apply to NBFC-IFCs, rather than relying on a separate framework.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that affected **Upper Layer IDF-NBFCs** must immediately align their exposure monitoring, internal limits, and concentration-risk controls with the **NBFC-IFC large exposure regime**. The amendment does not specify new numerical thresholds in this text itself; instead, it imports the existing NBFC-IFC limits by reference. The change is regulatory in nature, is mandatory, and applies as soon as the amendment is in force.

rows.title: Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/236 DOR.AML.REC.204/14.06.001/2026-27 August 19, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 21 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16435, dated August 18, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries mentioned in Annexure 1 on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 3. Press release dated August 18, 2026 regarding the above can be found at https://pres
rows.summary:
This RBI circular updates regulated entities on changes to the UNSC 1267/1989 ISIL (Da’esh) and Al‑Qaida Sanctions List and must be read together with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (dated November 28, 2025, amended December 29, 2025). It reiterates that, under section 51A of the UAPA, 1967, regulated entities must not maintain any account in the name of any individual or entity appearing on the UNSC-approved list of persons/entities suspected of terrorist links. The circular is addressed to commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions.

The trigger for this update is Ministry of External Affairs intimation of UNSC press release SC/16435 dated August 18, 2026. That UNSC action, taken under resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015) and adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, amended the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al‑Qaida Sanctions List by changing 21 entries. The amendments are shown in Annexure 1 using strike-through and underline, and the list remains tied to the UN sanctions measures of asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo under Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).

For compliance purposes, the practical requirement is that firms must review the updated list and ensure their customer and sanctions-screening controls reflect the 21 amended entries immediately upon issuance of this circular. Any match to the updated UNSC list must be handled in accordance with the UAPA section 51A process and the RBI KYC Directions, including ensuring no account is maintained in the name of a listed person or entity. The circular also points readers to the UNSC press release dated August 18, 2026 as the source document for the amendments.

Compliance teams should use the updated list circulated through the MEA/RBI framework and ensure sanctions screening logic, watchlists, and customer due diligence records reflect the amended UNSC entries without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/232 FIDD.CO.PSD.BC.No.08/04.09.001/2026-27 August 07, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 Please refer to the Governor’s Statement dated June 5, 2026, and RBI circular FMOD.MAOG.No.S-56/01.06.016/2026-27 dated June 08, 2026 on ‘Swap Facility for FCNR (B) Deposits’, wherein it has been decided to introduce a US Dollar-Rupee swap facility for fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) [FCNR (B)] dollar funds, mobilised for a minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years. 2. Further, reference is also invited to the Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Second and Third Amendment Directions dated June 08, 2026 and June 19, 2026, as applicable to various banks, wherein exemption has been provided from maintenance of Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio on fresh FCNR (B) deposits of minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) between June 08, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and on fresh Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) term deposits of tenor of three years or more mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026. 3. In this connection, please refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on January 19, 2026). It has been decided that the following advances extended in India will be excluded from calculation of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC): a) advances against the fresh FCNR (B) deposits of minimum tenor of three years and maximum tenor of five years mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) by the banks between June 08, 2026 and September 30, 2026, and b) advances against NRE term deposits of three years or more mobilised (including deposits that are renewed upon maturity) by the banks betwe
rows.summary:
This amendment to the RBI’s Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Directions for 2026-27 grants a PSL-calculation exclusion for certain advances made against specified foreign currency and NRE deposits, aligning PSL treatment with the RBI’s concurrent FCNR(B) swap and CRR/SLR relief measures. Specifically, banks’ **advances in India** will be **excluded from Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)** if they are made against **fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits** with a **minimum tenor of 3 years and maximum tenor of 5 years** mobilised, including renewals on maturity, **between June 8, 2026 and September 30, 2026**, and against **NRE term deposits of 3 years or more** mobilised, including renewals on maturity, **between June 19, 2026 and September 30, 2026**. The document ties the FCNR(B) treatment to the RBI’s **US Dollar-Rupee swap facility** announced in the Governor’s Statement of **June 5, 2026** and the circular dated **June 8, 2026**, and notes that the same FCNR(B) and NRE deposits had already been given **CRR and SLR exemptions** under the RBI’s **Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio Second and Third Amendment Directions** dated **June 8, 2026 and June 19, 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that banks must **identify and segregate advances against these qualifying deposits** so they are **not counted in ANBC** for PSL target/classification calculations. The FCNR(B) exclusion applies only to deposits mobilised within the specified date window and only where the deposit tenor falls within the stated range; the NRE exclusion applies to term deposits of at least 3 years, also only if mobilised within the specified window. The document is an amendment to the **Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025 (updated as of January 19, 2026)** and is issued as **RBI/2026-27/232, FIDD.CO.PSD.BC.No.08/04.09.001/2026-27, dated August 7, 2026**. No separate filing deadline is stated, but banks should apply the exclusion immediately for eligible transactions within the stated mobilization periods when calculating ANBC and PSL compliance.

The extant instructions have since been reviewed and it has been decided to issue comprehensive instructions on conduct related matters in recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies to all NBFCs, excluding Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Core Investment Companies, NBFC-Account Aggregators, Standalone Primary Dealers, Non-Operating Financial Holding Companies, and NBFCs not having any customer interface, under the Reserve Bank of India (Non- Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025. 2. Short Title and Commencement (1) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Third Amendment Directions, 2026. (2) These Directions shall come into effect from January 1, 2027. 4. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025 as under: In Chapter-X on ‘Fair Practices Code’, the sub-section A.15 Guidelines for engaging Recovery Agents and paragraph 170 thereunder shall be deleted and substituted with a new sub-section and paragraph as under: “A.15A Conduct of HFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agents 170A. An HFC shall ensure compliance with the provisions of paragraphs 100A 2 to 100AB under Chapter III of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Respo
rows.summary:
This amendment replaces the existing HFC-specific recovery-agent guidance in Chapter X, “Fair Practices Code,” of the Reserve Bank of India (Housing Finance Companies) Directions, 2025. Specifically, the prior sub-section A.15, “Guidelines for engaging Recovery Agents,” and paragraph 170 are deleted and substituted with a new sub-section A.15A, “Conduct of HFCs in Recovery of Loan Dues and Engagement of Recovery Agents,” beginning with paragraph 170A.

The new paragraph 170A requires every Housing Finance Company (HFC) to comply with the conduct and recovery-agent provisions set out in paragraphs 100A.2 to 100AB of Chapter III of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025. In substance, this means HFCs are no longer governed by a standalone recovery-agent framework in Chapter X; instead, they must align their loan-recovery practices and recovery-agency engagement with the broader conduct rules applicable under the RBI’s responsible business conduct regime.

The amendment is issued under Section 30A of the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and was published as RBI/2026-2027/231, DOR.MCS.REC.No.201/01-01-039/2026-27, dated August 6, 2026. It takes effect on January 1, 2027, so HFC compliance teams should ensure their recovery policies, agent appointment/oversight procedures, staff training, and borrower-contact practices are updated and operational by that date.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is a substitution, not a minor clarification: the old HFC-specific paragraph is removed entirely and replaced with a cross-reference to the more comprehensive NBFC conduct standards. HFCs should therefore review the relevant paragraphs 100A.2 through 100AB in the NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 to identify the exact operational requirements that will now govern their recovery activities and third-party recovery arrangements.

(2) These Directions shall come into effect from January 1, 2027. 4. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) – Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026** were issued on **August 6, 2026** and will **take effect from January 1, 2027**. The RBI states that it has reviewed prior instructions on recovery-agent engagement and is now issuing **comprehensive rules on recovery conduct and recovery agencies** for **all NBFCs**, except **Mortgage Guarantee Companies, Core Investment Companies, NBFC-Account Aggregators, Standalone Primary Dealers, Non-Operating Financial Holding Companies, and NBFCs with no customer interface**.

A new definition is inserted in the principal directions for **“recovery agency”**, meaning any **entity or individual other than the NBFC’s own employees** engaged by the NBFC, regardless of the contractual label used, under an **outsourcing arrangement** to assist in the **recovery of loan dues from a borrower**. This means compliance teams should look through the form of the arrangement and treat outsourced recovery support as a regulated recovery agency relationship whenever it is used for loan collection activity.

The amendment expressly revises the 2025 Responsible Business Conduct Directions by adding these recovery-related provisions into the existing framework. In practical compliance terms, affected NBFCs will need to align their recovery practices, outsourcing arrangements, and agent oversight with the new RBI conduct requirements once they become operative on **January 1, 2027**. Since the document is an amendment direction, the key action point is to identify whether the NBFC falls within the covered population and, if so, ensure its recovery operations and third-party collection arrangements are brought into compliance before the effective date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/229 DOR.MCS.REC.No.200/01-01-040/2026-27 August 6, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026 Certain instructions on responsibilities of an All India Financial Institution (AIFI) employing recovery agents have been issued to AIFIs under the Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025. The extant instructions have since been reviewed and it has been decided to issue comprehensive instructions on conduct related matters in recovery of loan dues and engagement of recovery agencies to all AIFIs (hereinafter referred to collectively as “AIFIs” and individually as an “AIFI”) under the aforesaid Directions. 2. In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in public interest so to do, hereby issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. Short Title and Commencement (1) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026. (2) These Directions shall come into effect from January 1, 2027. 4. These Amendment Directions shall modify the Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 as under: (1) In paragraph 3A, the following definitions shall be inserted after sub-paragraph 3A(6), namely: “3A(6A) Recovery agency means an entity or individual (other than AIFI’s own employees) who has been engaged by an AIFI, irrespective of the contractual designation / nomenclature used for such engagement, under an outsourcing arrangement to assist in recovery of loan dues from a borrower in default, including taking possession of a security. 2 3A(6B) Recovery agent means a representative of a recovery agency who is involved in recovery related activitie
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (AIFI) Responsible Business Conduct Third Amendment Directions, 2026** are issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and will **take effect on January 1, 2027**. RBI states that it has reviewed the earlier, limited instructions applicable to AIFIs that used recovery agents and has now decided to issue **comprehensive rules on conduct in the recovery of loan dues and the engagement of recovery agencies** for all AIFIs covered by the 2025 Responsible Business Conduct Directions.

The amendment first expands the definition framework in **paragraph 3A** by inserting new definitions for **“recovery agency”** and **“recovery agent.”** A **recovery agency** is defined as any entity or individual **other than the AIFI’s own employees** that is engaged by an AIFI, regardless of the contractual label used, under an **outsourcing arrangement** to assist in recovering **loan dues from a defaulting borrower**, including **taking possession of security**. A **recovery agent** is defined as a **representative of a recovery agency** who is involved in recovery-related activities; this is meant to capture the actual persons carrying out recovery work, not just the formal outsourcing counterparty.

For compliance teams, the material significance is that the RBI is broadening the regulatory scope beyond narrow “recovery agent” references to cover the full outsourcing structure used for loan recovery. Any AIFI that engages outside parties for collection, recovery, or repossession activities will need to ensure its policies, contracts, oversight, conduct controls, and borrower-facing practices align with the amended directions once they become operative on **1 January 2027**. The document excerpt provided stops after the new definitions begin and does not include the full substantive conduct rules, so only the definitional change and commencement date can be stated with certainty from the supplied text.

From that date, the 2025 Directions will be modified by inserting a new definition of **“recovery agency”** into paragraph 4: it means **any entity or individual other than the LAB’s own employees** that is engaged by the LAB under an outsourcing arrangement to help recover defaulted loan dues, **including taking possession of security**. This means LABs cannot avoid recovery-agency obligations by treating such persons or entities as something else contractually; if the activity is recovery-related, the conduct and outsourcing rules applicable to recovery agencies will apply.

The document does not itself set new numerical thresholds, fee caps, or separate deadlines beyond the effective date, but it does establish that the RBI expects **uniform, comprehensive oversight of recovery practices and agency engagements** across all LABs under the 2025 Directions.

rows.summary:
This Master Direction consolidates and updates all operative RBI instructions on Relief/Savings Bonds as of June 30, 2018, and supersedes earlier scattered guidance by placing the current rules in one location; it was issued on July 2, 2018 and is stated to be updated whenever rules, regulations, or policy change. It applies to the designated Receiving Offices named in the circular: State Bank of India, all nationalized banks except Punjab and Sind Bank and Andhra Bank, Axis Bank Ltd., ICICI Bank Ltd., HDFC Bank Ltd., and Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd. (SHCIL). The first operational change concerns broker enrollment/registration: Receiving Offices may use a simple registration process, under which a broker submits a request on business letterhead along with business data, and the Receiving Office must allot a code number that the broker must quote on all bond applications tendered for brokerage claims. The document also addresses appointment of sub-agents by Receiving Offices and notes a concern that some offices have engaged other banks as brokers/agents for receiving applications while those intermediaries use RBI’s name in publicity material and billboards, indicating that such arrangements and branding use are being scrutinized or should not misrepresent RBI involvement.

The directions also cover brokerage payment/rates for Savings Bonds and nomination facilities for Relief/Savings Bonds, with the detailed instructions contained in the later sections and appendix of the Master Direction. From a compliance perspective, the key obligation is to follow the updated RBI-prescribed procedures exactly, ensure only properly enrolled brokers are used for brokerage claims, and ensure the broker code system is implemented so applications can be tracked and brokerage paid only where properly claimed. Because the directions are a living compilation updated by RBI, compliance teams should treat this as a standing requirement to monitor subsequent amendments on the RBI website rather than a one-time circular.

rows.title: Master Direction – Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers (Updated as on November 22, 2018)

Successful PDs shall provide sufficient funds in their current account with the RBI on the auction settlement days before 3:00 pm to meet their obligations against the subscriptions in the primary auctions failing which the shortage will be treated as an instance of ‘SGL bouncing’ and will be subjected to the applicable penal provisions. 3. The turnover ratio in respect of outright transactions should not be less than 3 times in Government dated securities and 6 times in T-Bills/CMBs (Turnover ratio is the ratio of total purchase and sales during the year in the secondary market to average month-end stocks). 3.3 Secondary Market Transactions - Short-selling PDs shall adhere to the guidelines issued by the R
rows.summary:
This update to the RBI Master Direction on Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers reiterates and clarifies several existing operational requirements for primary dealers (PDs) in government securities markets. First, PDs must follow the RBI’s rules for submitting non-competitive bids in G-Sec auctions, as set out in RBI/2008-09/479 dated May 22, 2009, as amended from time to time. It also confirms that PDs may sell securities allotted in primary issues on the same day they are received, but only in accordance with the specific circulars cited in the direction: IDMC.PDRS.No.PDS.1/03.64.00/2000-01 dated October 6, 2000; RBI/2005/461–IDMD.PDRS.4777/10.02.01/2004-05 dated May 11, 2005; and RBI/2012-13/133-IDMD.PDRD.188/03.64.00/2012-13 dated July 16, 2012. For such same-day sales, PDs are permitted to use brokers to execute the sale contracts.

A key settlement requirement is that primary auction settlement is independent of secondary market settlement and must therefore be funded separately. Successful PDs must ensure sufficient funds are available in their RBI current account on the auction settlement day before 3:00 p.m. to cover their auction subscriptions. If funds are short, the deficiency will be treated as an instance of “SGL bouncing,” which triggers the applicable penal provisions. Compliance teams should therefore treat auction-day liquidity management as a standalone obligation, not something that can be covered by secondary market settlement balances.

In the secondary market, PDs are required to act as market makers in Government securities by quoting two-way prices in G-Sec on the NDS-OM platform, in the OTC market, and on recognized stock exchanges in India, while also taking principal positions in the secondary market. The direction also imposes annual turnover targets: PDs must achieve a minimum turnover ratio of 5 times for Government dated securities and 10 times for Treasury Bills/Cash Management Bills, measured against average month-end stock holdings. For outright transactions specifically, the minimum turnover ratio is lower but still mandatory: at least 3 times for Government dated securities and 6 times for T-Bills/CMBs. The turnover ratio is defined as total secondary-market purchases and sales during the year divided by average month-end stocks.

The document also begins a separate requirement on short-selling in the secondary market, stating that PDs must comply with RBI-issued guidelines on that activity, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full rule text. For compliance purposes, the material obligations visible in this excerpt are the funding deadline of 3:00 p.m. on auction settlement days, the prohibition on failing to fund primary auction obligations without incurring SGL bouncing treatment, the mandatory market-making function, the specified annual turnover ratios, and adherence to the cited RBI circulars governing same-day sale of auction allotments and non-competitive bidding.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2026 Directions on “Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs” set out the framework for appointing agency banks, paying commission for government business, and monitoring compliance. The directions are issued on April 30, 2026, and apply to agency banks conducting Government business under RBI appointment; the document’s operative details govern which government transactions are eligible for agency commission, how they must be reported, and what documentation is required to claim payment. It also specifically distinguishes transactions that do **not** qualify for commission, so banks need to check each transaction type against the eligibility rules rather than assuming all government collections or payments are compensable.

A major substantive part of the directions is the commission framework for government business: the RBI specifies the rates of agency commission, clarifies when a **single challan is to be treated as a single transaction**, and lays out the exact procedure ABs must follow to submit commission claims. The directions also require ABs to report government transactions to RBI in the prescribed manner, which is tied to the commission claim process, and to submit specified supporting documents when seeking payment. The document additionally includes clarifications on commission claims and introduces a penalty mechanism in the form of **penal interest for wrong claims of agency commission**, meaning banks may face financial consequences if they claim commission incorrectly or inconsistently with the directions.

For compliance purposes, the key operational issue is that the directions are not just fee-setting rules; they create an end-to-end control regime over government business conducted by agency banks. ABs must ensure their transaction tagging, challan treatment, reporting, and claim support are aligned with RBI’s prescribed rules, especially for transactions linked to Government schemes, which receive separate treatment in the directions. The final chapter on oversight indicates RBI will supervise government business conducted by ABs, so banks should expect ongoing monitoring of appointment compliance, transaction reporting, claim integrity, and adherence to the eligibility rules for agency commission.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs)] Directions, 2026 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs) Directions, 2026”** (issued **April 30, 2026** and updated **June 24, 2026**) sets out the operating rules that **agency banks** must follow when paying government pension, including central, state, and related government pension disbursements routed through banks. The directions apply to **all agency banks authorized to disburse government pension**, and they replace/organize the compliance framework around pension payment timing, implementation of government orders (including **dearness relief (DR)** changes), error recovery, special handling for vulnerable pensioners, reimbursement, and life-certificate processing.

A core obligation is that agency banks must **promptly implement government orders** relating to pension changes, especially **DR and similar revisions**, and must keep themselves updated through the Government’s published orders available on the relevant government website. Banks are required to ensure pension is disbursed in line with the government’s instructions and at the prescribed time each month; the directions emphasize that pension should be credited **on the due date prescribed by the government/RBI framework**, not delayed by internal bank processing. Compliance teams should treat this as a strict operational requirement, because the directions place responsibility on the paying bank to avoid delayed credit and to ensure government-issued revisions are reflected without avoidable lag.

The document also addresses **recovery and refund of excess pension payments**. Where an excess payment occurs due to an error attributable to the **agency bank**, the bank is responsible for arranging recovery/refund in accordance with the directions and the applicable government instructions. Where the excess arises from a **government-attributed error**, the bank must still follow the prescribed process for correction, but the obligation and recovery mechanics differ from bank-attributed mistakes; this distinction matters for liability allocation, reporting, and reconciliation. Compliance staff should ensure the bank has controls to identify whether an overpayment originated from bank processing or from government input, because that affects how the excess is recovered and who bears the operational burden.

A separate chapter provides special instructions for **old, sick, disabled, and incapacitated pensioners**. These pensioners must be allowed to withdraw pension through the permitted modes set out in the directions, and banks are expected to use customer-friendly procedures to facilitate payment when the pensioner cannot personally visit the branch in the normal manner. The directions also require banks to **display the relevant withdrawal instructions prominently in branches**, so staff and customers can see how such pensioners may access their pensions. This is a branch-level compliance obligation, not just a back-office one, and should be reflected in staff training and inspection checklists.

The directions further cover **reimbursement of pension payments** made by agency banks and the associated documentation/processing expected for claiming reimbursement from the government system. In addition, the document contains a dedicated chapter on **life certificates**, indicating that banks must follow the prescribed life-certificate verification and submission process as a condition for continuing pension payments. For compliance purposes, the most important takeaway is that agency banks must maintain end-to-end controls over pension implementation: timely application of government orders, accurate monthly disbursement, proper handling of overpayments and recoveries, accessible procedures for vulnerable pensioners, visible branch instructions, and correct reimbursement and life-certificate processes.

The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, except for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** are intended to strengthen customer grievance redressal in NBFCs by requiring an **apex-level internal review before a complaint is finally rejected**. The RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to extend any suspension period.

For in-scope entities, the core obligation is to maintain an Internal Ombudsman framework that allows customer complaints to be **reviewed before rejection**, rather than simply denied at the first-line grievance stage.

From a compliance perspective, the key operational dates are: **effective immediately upon issuance on January 14, 2026**, with a **hard compliance deadline of June 30, 2026** for the specified clauses. NBFCs that fall within scope should assess whether their current grievance-redress process already includes the required **independent internal review mechanism**, and if not, they will need to implement or revise procedures, governance, and escalation workflows to ensure complaints are routed for review before rejection. The document’s stated policy objective is not merely procedural formality; it is to ensure **speedy and meaningful resolution of customer complaints** through a higher-level internal authority within the NBFC.
