The document indicates that it will set out: the circumstances under which commercial banks may use or offer digital banking channels; the prudential conditions they must satisfy; the technology and security expectations applicable to those channels; and general compliance obligations for banks operating them. Because the document is an RBI direction rather than guidance, affected banks should treat its requirements as mandatory from the effective date.

For a compliance team, the key immediate takeaway is that **all covered commercial banks must align their digital banking channel authorisation, controls, and governance arrangements to the new RBI framework by January 1, 2026**. No numerical thresholds, rates, or deadlines other than the **January 1, 2026** commencement date are visible in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/147, DOR.LIC.REC.No.66/22-01-001/2025-26) were issued on **November 28, 2025** and set out the authorization framework for opening and operating **banking outlets, ATMs/CDMs/BNAMs, and Digital Banking Units (DBUs)**, along with the governance obligations placed on bank boards. The directions apply to **commercial banks** and specifically address **domestic commercial banks** and **foreign banks operating in branch mode**; the document also contemplates off-site/mobile **ATMs**, **cash deposit machines (CDMs)**, and **bunch note acceptor machines (BNAMs)**, as well as DBUs.  

A core requirement is that each bank’s **Board of Directors** must approve a formal **branch authorization policy** and retain oversight of the bank’s expansion and outlet-opening strategy. The board is assigned key responsibilities under the directions, meaning compliance is not just operational but also governance-driven: banks must have documented policy approval, board-level review of expansion decisions, and internal controls to ensure new outlets or digital units are established only in line with the RBI framework.  

For **banking outlet authorisation**, the directions distinguish between the rules for **domestic commercial banks** and **foreign banks in branch mode**, so the applicable permission process depends on the bank’s legal form and operating model. The document also separately regulates **off-site/mobile ATMs, CDMs, and BNAMs**, indicating that these are treated as distinct authorization/use cases rather than ordinary branches and therefore require adherence to the RBI’s outlet-specific conditions. While the excerpt provided does not reproduce the detailed thresholds or approval triggers, the chapter structure shows that banks must follow specific authorization requirements for each type of outlet rather than applying a single generic branch-opening rule.  

For **Digital Banking Units (DBUs)**, the directions provide **general permission to open DBUs**, but that permission is not unconditional: banks must comply with the stated requirements on **infrastructure and resources** and **cyber security**. This indicates that DBUs are permitted as a recognized delivery channel only if the bank can demonstrate readiness in physical/operational setup and security controls appropriate to a digital-only or digital-led service point. Any compliance review should therefore focus on whether the bank’s proposed DBUs meet the RBI’s prescribed operational, technical, and security standards before launch and on an ongoing basis.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Commercial Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation – Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** (RBI/DoR/2025-26/146; DoR.HOL.REC.65/16-13-100/2025-26). These directions set out the process and conditions for the **voluntary amalgamation of commercial banks**, replacing the earlier framework on this topic and establishing the required approvals, shareholder protections, promoter-shareholding norms, and RBI oversight for such transactions.

For a corporate compliance team, the key point is that **any voluntary merger/amalgamation involving a commercial bank must now follow this RBI-prescribed procedure**. The document is organized to require: prior **approval of the board of directors**, then **approval of shareholders**, followed by **RBI approval or sanction** before the amalgamation can proceed. It also expressly addresses the **entitlements of dissenting shareholders**, meaning the process must include protections or exit treatment for shareholders who do not support the transaction.

The directions further impose **norms for buying and selling shares by promoters** in the context of the amalgamation, so compliance teams should expect restrictions or procedural conditions affecting promoter transactions around the deal period. The document also includes a **repeal and savings** section, indicating the earlier corresponding instructions are superseded, while preserving certain actions already taken or rights accrued under the prior framework. It states that other applicable laws are **not barred**, so companies must still comply with all other relevant banking, corporate, securities, and merger laws in addition to these RBI directions. The final sections also provide interpretive guidance and an annex, suggesting implementation details or forms may be included there and should be checked before executing any transaction.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025”** (dated **November 28, 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/145 DOR.HOL. REC.64/16.13.100/2025-26**) sets out the RBI framework governing when commercial banks may **acquire or hold shares or voting rights**, with the document organized around (i) preliminary matters, (ii) **prior approval for acquisition**, (iii) **continuous monitoring arrangements**, and (iv) repeal/saving and interpretive provisions. The document clearly signals that banks are not free to acquire such interests at will: it creates a regulated approval and monitoring process, including a **fit-and-proper assessment** and a **formal procedure for prior approval** before acquisition where required. It also requires banks to maintain **ongoing due diligence and monitoring systems** so they can identify and track holdings and detect any **violations of Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that this is not just a one-time pre-transaction review; it imposes **continuous monitoring obligations** after any acquisition, with specific expectations for due diligence, detection of statutory breaches, and reporting. The document also includes a **reporting requirements** chapter, meaning banks must be prepared to notify the RBI in the manner the directions prescribe when breaches, threshold issues, or other reportable events arise. Because the title and structure indicate a dedicated RBI direction on ownership/voting-rights acquisitions by commercial banks, compliance teams should treat it as the controlling instrument for determining whether a proposed shareholding or voting-rights acquisition is permissible, whether prior approval is mandatory, and what monitoring/reporting controls must be embedded in governance and post-transaction surveillance. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or procedural timelines, so the full text would need to be reviewed to identify the exact acquisition limits, filing formats, and deadlines applicable to particular transactions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks) Guidelines, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.desc: DOR/2025-26/144 November 28, 2025 Reserve Bank of India (Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks) Guidelines, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026) A. Background The global financial crisis of 2008 demonstrated that the growing complexity and interconnectedness of financial institutions, coupled with the lack of effective cross- border resolution regimes, severely constrained the ability of home and host authorities to cope with the failure of too big to fail (TBTF) and too connected to fail (TCTF) institutions. Globally, several policy options have been proposed to address these challenges, including measures to contain the negative externalities arising out of size and interconnectedness, strengthening the capital and liquidity buffers, and enhancing the resolvability of such institutions. The lessons from the global financial crisis support the case for domestic incorporation of foreign banks. The main advantages of local incorporation include: (1) Creation of separate legal entities with their own capital base and local board of directors; (2) Clear delineation between the assets and liabilities of the domestic bank and those of its foreign parent, with ring fenced capital and assets within the host country; (3) Clarity and certainty regarding the applicability of the laws of country of incorporation on the locally incorporated subsidiary; (4) A locally incorporated bank has its own board of directors which are required to act in the best interests of the bank and safeguard the interests of depositors and creditors; (5) Local incorporation provides effective control to the local regulators. Accordingly, several jurisdictions require foreign banks to adopt local incorporation mainly for (i) protecting local retail depositors, (ii) easing the resolution process, and (iii) affording greater regulatory comfort. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) allowed foreign banks, if eligible, to establish presence through a single mode i.e. either the branc
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Guidelines on Setting Up of Wholly Owned Subsidiaries by Foreign Banks confirm RBI’s policy preference for local incorporation of foreign banks in India, mainly to improve resolvability, ring-fence local assets and liabilities, protect depositors/creditors, and give Indian regulators clearer control over India operations. The document is framed as a continuation of RBI’s post-crisis approach, under which an eligible foreign bank may establish an Indian presence through a single mode—either a branch network or a wholly owned subsidiary (WOS)—rather than both, and the WOS structure is emphasized as the locally incorporated model with its own capital base and board.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the guidelines apply to foreign banks seeking to enter or restructure their presence in India through a wholly owned subsidiary, and the Indian subsidiary is expected to be a separate legal entity subject to Indian law, with the parent’s assets and liabilities clearly segregated from the Indian entity. The document states that the board of the locally incorporated bank must act in the best interests of the bank and protect depositors and creditors, and that local incorporation gives effective supervisory control to RBI. The document also notes the policy rationale used by other jurisdictions—protecting retail depositors, making resolution easier, and giving regulators more comfort—indicating that the RBI is treating these governance and resolution features as core compliance objectives for WOS structures.  

This excerpt is largely background and policy framing rather than a full operational rulebook, so it does not in the provided text specify numerical thresholds, application deadlines, capital requirements, governance filing procedures, or step-by-step approval conditions. The only explicit date information shown is the issuance date of the circular/guidelines as November 28, 2025, with the document marked “Updated as on April 1, 2026.” For a compliance team, the material takeaway from the portion provided is that foreign banks considering Indian market entry or conversion of an Indian presence should assess whether RBI’s locally incorporated WOS model is required or preferable, and should plan for separate legal entity governance, local board oversight, and ring-fenced balance-sheet treatment under Indian supervision.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Universal Banks – Licensing) Guidelines, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Universal Banks – Licensing” Guidelines, 2025** set out the **on-tap licensing framework for private-sector universal banks** and replace the earlier licensing regime with a detailed application and approval process. The document applies to **new private-sector bank applicants**, including certain **NBFCs that seek to promote or convert into a bank**, and it is centered on RBI’s assessment of promoters, ownership structure, capital adequacy at entry, governance, and the feasibility of the proposed business plan. The guidelines are issued as **DOR/2025-26/143 dated November 28, 2025**.

A key requirement is that applicants must satisfy **eligibility and “fit and proper” standards** for promoters and controlling shareholders, and must maintain a corporate structure that is acceptable to RBI. The guidelines prescribe **minimum voting equity capital requirements** and rules on the **pattern of shareholding** in the proposed bank, indicating that RBI will scrutinize who controls the bank and how ownership is distributed from the outset. They also address the **regulatory framework** applicable after licensing, including **prudential norms, exposure limits, and corporate governance requirements**, meaning that a proposed bank must be able to operate within the full bank-supervision regime immediately on licensing.

The document also regulates **foreign shareholding** in the proposed bank, so applicants must structure any overseas investment to remain within RBI’s permitted limits and conditions. Applicants must submit a **business plan** for the bank, and RBI will evaluate whether the plan is credible, sustainable, and consistent with the proposed institution’s scale, governance, and risk profile. In addition, there are **“other conditions”** that the bank must satisfy after licensing, which indicates ongoing compliance obligations beyond the initial application stage.

For **NBFCs that are promoting or converting into a bank**, the guidelines impose **additional conditions**, reflecting RBI’s concern with conversion from a non-bank financial model to a deposit-taking universal bank. The document includes a dedicated **procedure for application** and a separate **procedure for RBI decisions**, which means applicants must follow the prescribed submission process and wait for RBI’s formal determination before proceeding. Overall, the guidelines create a controlled, case-by-case licensing process in which RBI assesses not only capital and ownership, but also governance, fit-and-proper status, foreign ownership, and the applicant’s ability to operate a universal bank safely and in compliance with banking regulation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend” Directions, 2026** are a new prudential framework issued on **March 10, 2026** for **small finance banks (SFBs)** governing when and how they may declare and pay dividends. The directions replace prior RBI dividend-related norms for SFBs through a repeal-and-savings mechanism, but the document also preserves the effect of anything already done or suffered under the earlier rules to the extent covered by the saving clause. The directions are organized into rules on applicability, dividend declaration governance, eligibility, payout limits, treatment of ineligible profits, reporting, restrictions on payment, and penalties for non-compliance.

For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that **an SFB cannot treat dividend declaration as a routine board decision**; the bank’s **Board must exercise oversight and confirm that the bank meets RBI’s prudential eligibility criteria before declaring any dividend**. The directions establish a framework requiring the bank to assess whether it satisfies the specified conditions on capital, asset quality, and other prudential indicators before any dividend can be proposed or paid. The document also sets out that **some categories of profits are ineligible for dividend distribution**, meaning dividends cannot be paid out of amounts that RBI excludes from distributable profits under the directions.

The directions further specify a **limit on the quantum of dividend payable**, so even where a bank is eligible to pay a dividend, the amount is capped rather than left entirely to board discretion. This means compliance teams must verify that the proposed dividend amount falls within RBI’s prescribed ceiling and is sourced only from profits that are eligible under the directions. The bank must also follow a **reporting system** to RBI before payment, which implies a pre-payment compliance workflow rather than ex post disclosure only. In practical terms, the bank should expect to prepare internal board papers, compliance certifications, and RBI submissions demonstrating satisfaction of the eligibility conditions and the basis for the proposed dividend.

The directions impose a **restriction on payment of dividend** if the prescribed prudential conditions are not met, so a bank that fails the tests is prohibited from declaring or remitting dividends until compliance is restored. The document also includes a **penal consequences** chapter for non-compliance, signaling that violations may attract supervisory or enforcement action from RBI in addition to any dividend restriction. Finally, the directions clarify that they do **not bar the application of other laws**, so SFBs must comply not only with these RBI directions but also with any other applicable corporate, banking, accounting, and company-law requirements governing dividend declaration and payment.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Small Finance Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** under reference **RBI/DoR/2025-26/204** and **DoR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.123/13-04-001/2025-26**. Based on the portion provided, the document appears to consolidate and operationalize compliance requirements for **small finance banks (SFBs)**, with a particular focus on the **Board’s governance obligations** and the handling of the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The table of contents shows that the directions begin with general provisions on **short title, commencement, applicability, and definitions**, then move to **board-approved policies, board responsibilities, and board review requirements**, followed by a detailed chapter on the **DEAF**, including **credits to the fund, refunds and interest, registration guidelines, transfer/claim procedures, and reporting returns**.

For compliance purposes, the material point is that the RBI is imposing a structured set of obligations on SFBs rather than a single isolated rule. The board is expected to maintain **RBI-compliant, board-approved policies**, oversee the bank’s compliance with the directions, and conduct formal reviews of the applicable processes and controls. The DEAF chapter indicates that SFBs will have explicit duties around identifying amounts that must be transferred to the fund, processing customer refunds, accounting for interest where applicable, registering claims, and following prescribed procedures for transfer and claim handling. The inclusion of a dedicated “Returns” section suggests periodic regulatory reporting will be required, so banks should expect operational controls, reconciliations, and reporting calendars to be aligned to RBI-prescribed formats and timelines.

The extract provided does **not** include the operative clauses, so it does not disclose the exact thresholds, transfer triggers, interest rate treatment, deadlines, or filing frequency. However, the structure makes clear that the directions likely replace or supplement prior RBI instructions for SFBs on these topics, and compliance teams should treat them as a governance-and-operations update affecting **all small finance banks** covered by RBI’s applicability clause. Once the full text is reviewed, a compliance officer should verify: the exact date the directions take effect; whether any transitional arrangements apply; the specific types of balances that must be transferred to DEAF; the timing and manner of customer refunds/claims; any interest computation rules; and the exact reporting return requirements and submission deadlines.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025** were issued on **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/203 DOR.SFG.REC.No.122/30.01.021/2025-26**. They apply specifically to **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and establish a mandatory governance, risk-management, and green-deposit framework covering climate finance and climate-change risk management. The directions consolidate the RBI’s expectations for how SFB boards must oversee climate risk, how green deposits may be accepted and deployed, and what reporting, verification, and disclosure controls must be in place.

At the board level, the directions require the **Board of Directors** to take responsibility for approving and overseeing the institution’s climate-related policy framework and ensuring that climate-related financial risks are integrated into the bank’s overall governance and risk-management processes. The board must ensure appropriate internal systems, controls, monitoring, and reporting arrangements are in place, and that management is assigned clear accountability for implementing the climate-finance and climate-risk requirements.

A major new compliance area is the **framework for acceptance of green deposits**. SFBs may accept green deposits only under a formal policy and financing framework that defines what qualifies as green, how proceeds will be used, how those uses will be monitored, and how the bank will disclose compliance. The directions address the **denomination, interest rates, and tenor** of such deposits, meaning SFBs cannot structure green deposits arbitrarily and must adhere to RBI-prescribed conditions on those commercial terms. They must also have a documented **use-of-proceeds** process so funds raised as green deposits are deployed only for eligible green activities, with controls to track allocation and prevent misuse.

The framework further requires **third-party verification/assurance** of the green-deposit process and an **impact assessment** to evaluate the environmental outcomes of the financed activities. SFBs must also follow prescribed **reporting and disclosure** requirements, which implies ongoing documentation to evidence compliance, transparency to stakeholders, and submission or publication of the required information in the format and frequency set by the RBI. Finally, the directions include **repeal and saving** provisions, meaning earlier inconsistent instructions are superseded except for actions already taken or rights/obligations already accrued under the prior framework. The table of contents also shows an **application** provision in Chapter IV, but the excerpt provided does not include the text of that section, so any exact transition date or grandfathering detail would need the full chapter text to confirm.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Small Finance Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/202 DOR.ORG.REC.No.121/21-04-158/2025-26**. The document is directed at **small finance banks (SFBs)** and sets out a revised/standalone regulatory framework for how they may outsource activities while remaining accountable for the underlying risks, governance, and compliance obligations.

At a high level, the directions require every SFB to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and a governance framework that keeps **ultimate responsibility with the bank’s board and senior management**, even where third parties perform functions. The Board is responsible for approving the policy, defining oversight expectations, and ensuring the bank has effective controls to identify, monitor, and mitigate outsourcing risk; senior management is expected to implement the policy, maintain supervision of vendors, and ensure compliance with RBI requirements. The framework covers outsourcing of financial services and related support functions, but it is not a blanket permission structure: the bank must determine whether the activity is suitable for outsourcing, how it will be monitored, and whether the arrangement creates operational, legal, reputational, or customer-protection risk.

The directions also identify certain **activities that cannot be outsourced**, meaning SFBs must retain them in-house and cannot shift responsibility to a third party. While the excerpt provided does not list the specific prohibited activities, the document expressly includes a dedicated prohibition section and a rule that outsourcing does **not** transfer accountability away from the bank. This means compliance teams should treat any vendor arrangement as subject to a “bank remains responsible” principle, with clear ownership for oversight, auditability, internal controls, and regulatory access.

In addition, the document establishes a **risk management and governance structure** for outsourcing arrangements. SFBs must have documented procedures for due diligence before entering into outsourcing contracts, ongoing monitoring of service providers, escalation of breaches or service failures, and periodic review of the arrangement’s risk profile. The framework also places obligations on the bank to ensure that outsourcing contracts, policies, and supervisory arrangements preserve RBI’s ability to examine the bank’s conduct and enforce compliance, rather than allowing a vendor relationship to dilute the bank’s obligations.

Because the provided content is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not** show the detailed operative provisions, specific thresholds, implementation deadline(s), or any numeric limits beyond the document’s issuance date and reference number. A compliance officer should therefore assume the full directions may contain additional requirements in later chapters and should review the complete text for any item-specific outsourcing restrictions, mandatory contract clauses, reporting expectations, transition periods, or board/management approval requirements that are not visible in the excerpt.

The document’s structure shows specific operational standards for **customer service in branches**, **customer guidance and protection**, **financial inclusion and accessibility**, **payment and remittance services**, **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, and **responsible lending conduct**, indicating that the compliance burden is not limited to disclosures but extends to how products are designed, sold, serviced, and resolved across the customer lifecycle.

The inclusion of a **“Comprehensive Notice Board”** format in Annex I suggests mandatory branch-display requirements, and Annex II’s **“Rates at a Quick Glance”** indicates that the RBI is requiring standardized public communication of key rates/charges/terms in a readily accessible format. Because the table of contents shows a dedicated chapter on **deposit accounts and other liabilities** and another on **responsible lending conduct**, the document likely sets binding rules for account opening/operation, servicing of liabilities, and lending practices, rather than only aspirational conduct guidance. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/200, DOR.AML.REC.No.119/14.01.007/2025-26, dated **November 28, 2025**, updated through **December 29, 2025**) sets out the KYC, customer due diligence, recordkeeping, and reporting framework specifically for **small finance banks** to prevent use of the banking system for **money laundering (ML)** and **terrorist financing (TF)** and to support financial system integrity and stability. The document is organized into chapters covering preliminary provisions, general principles, customer acceptance policy, risk management, CIP, CDD, record management, FIU-India reporting, obligations arising from international agreements/communications from international agencies, other instructions, and repeal/transition provisions. A compliance team should treat this as the governing KYC regime for SFBs and review all onboarding, monitoring, and reporting controls against the updated requirements.

At a high level, the directions require banks to maintain a formal **customer acceptance policy**, apply a **risk-based approach** to KYC/CDD, and implement procedures for **customer identification** before establishing a business relationship or carrying out specified transactions. The bank must ensure that CDD is not a one-time event: it must be performed at onboarding and updated based on risk, with enhanced scrutiny for higher-risk customers and activities. The directions also require appropriate internal controls for record retention and suspicious transaction reporting to the **Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND)**, and they incorporate handling requirements when the bank receives communications connected to **international agencies or international agreements**. Where the document refers to specific thresholds or trigger events, compliance teams should map those directly into system rules, because the directions are intended to be operationalized through customer-facing and back-office procedures rather than treated as narrative guidance.

The document’s compliance burden is centered on **ongoing identification and due diligence**, not merely document collection. Small finance banks must ensure that the identity of customers is established using the prescribed KYC documentation and that the bank can evidence who the beneficial owner is where applicable, with controls to detect and respond to red flags, inconsistencies, or missing information. The directions also require banks to maintain adequate **risk categorization** of customers and to tailor the depth and frequency of CDD accordingly, which means that higher-risk relationships should face more intensive onboarding checks, closer monitoring, and more frequent review/update cycles than lower-risk relationships. In addition, the bank must preserve records for the required statutory periods and ensure they are retrievable for regulatory inspection and for FIU-IND or other lawful requests.

The updated directions further emphasize the bank’s obligations to **report prescribed transactions and suspicious activity** to FIU-IND within the applicable timelines and formats, and to maintain procedures for responding to directions or communications tied to international enforcement and intelligence cooperation. They also include **repeal and savings** provisions in Chapter XI, meaning compliance teams should verify which earlier RBI KYC instructions have been superseded and ensure legacy policies, forms, and workflow rules are migrated to the 2025 framework. Because the document is structured as a full replacement/updated master direction set, the main operational task is to align all onboarding, periodic KYC refresh, record retention, watchlist/sanctions-related handling, and FIU reporting processes to the new text and any annexed forms or procedural details in Annex I and Annex II.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Small Finance Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** (issued November 28, 2025 and updated as on July 1, 2026) sets the accounting presentation, disclosure, and certain prudential reporting rules that **all Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** must follow when preparing standalone and consolidated financial statements. It is not a general accounting overview; it is a binding regulatory direction that governs the **format of the balance sheet and profit and loss account, the required notes to accounts, consolidated financial statements, and several bank-specific treatment rules** such as inter-branch accounts, Nostro reconciliations, reserve fund transfers, and fraud provisioning.

At the core, the Directions require SFBs to present their financial statements in the RBI-prescribed format and to comply with the accompanying notes/instructions for compilation, along with additional guidance on how particular accounting standards are to be applied in the banking context. The document’s structure indicates that the bank must prepare both the **balance sheet and profit and loss account** in the specified manner, then provide a detailed set of **notes and disclosures** and, where applicable, a full **consolidated financial statement package**. Because the title is updated as of **July 1, 2026**, compliance teams should treat the document as the operative version reflecting changes up to that date and ensure their reporting templates, accounting policies, and disclosure checklists match the latest RBI-issued text.

The disclosures chapter is material because it requires banks to make specific notes to accounts and present them in a prescribed way, rather than relying solely on generic financial statement disclosure practice. This means compliance should verify that disclosures are complete, internally consistent, and mapped to the RBI-required presentation order and terminology, especially where the Directions override or supplement standard accounting presentation. The document also includes a separate chapter on **consolidated financial statements**, so if the SFB has subsidiaries or other entities requiring consolidation, the group reporting package must comply with the RBI’s specified consolidated format and disclosure rules as well.

The final chapter contains several operational and compliance-sensitive instructions that banks must implement in practice. These include the treatment of **inter-branch account net debit balances**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and outstanding entries**, **transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds**, and **provisioning for fraud**. For a compliance function, these are not merely accounting preferences: they imply ongoing controls, reconciliation processes, classification rules, and provisioning discipline that must be embedded in finance and operational workflows so that the bank’s reported financial statements and internal balances are compliant with RBI requirements.

The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. The stated purpose is to require a **fair, transparent, non-discriminatory process consistent with natural justice** for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter, and to ensure that credit information on such borrowers is shared so other lenders are cautioned and further institutional finance is not extended to them. These Directions are specifically aimed at **small finance banks** and replace the prior framework for this subject.

The document establishes a governance structure and board responsibility for how a small finance bank identifies, reviews, and acts on wilful default cases. It also sets out the treatment of borrowers once they are identified as wilful defaulters, including the reporting obligations to credit information systems and RBI, and it separately addresses **large defaulters** through reporting requirements. The Directions further require banks to implement **preventive controls** and place responsibility on auditors to help identify gaps or irregularities relevant to wilful default classification and monitoring.

A key compliance change is that the bank must follow formal procedures before classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter, rather than making an ad hoc or purely internal decision. The framework is designed to ensure the borrower is given due process and that the classification is based on an objective review of conduct involving intentional non-payment or diversion/siphoning of funds, as contemplated by the RBI’s wilful default regime. Once classified, the borrower’s details must be disseminated through the prescribed reporting channels so that the information is available to other lenders.

The Directions also create a separate reporting framework for **large defaulters**, meaning compliance teams must not only track wilful default cases but also maintain processes to identify and report specified large default exposures in the format and timeline prescribed by the RBI. The document includes two required annexure formats: one for submitting the **list of large defaulters** and another for submitting **data on wilful default cases**, which means banks must capture the required fields in a consistent, report-ready form. Overall, the practical compliance effect is that small finance banks need robust internal policies, board oversight, documentation standards, borrower-notice/review procedures, and periodic reporting controls for both wilful default and large default monitoring.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Small Finance Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025 (dated November 28, 2025 and shown as updated through July 1, 2026) establish a dedicated stressed-asset resolution framework for small finance banks, replacing or supplementing earlier ad hoc approaches with formal requirements on identification, review, restructuring, and disclosures. The directions apply to small finance banks and govern the treatment of stressed exposures, including the need for board-approved policies covering how stress will be identified, monitored, escalated, and resolved, as well as how the bank will structure its internal governance and reporting around such accounts.

A central requirement is early identification and reporting of stress: banks must detect signs of borrower distress early, report and escalate those cases internally, and maintain related disclosures for supervisory scrutiny. The document also requires supervisory review, meaning the RBI can assess whether the bank’s processes, policies, and account-level decisions are consistent with the framework and with prudential expectations. The directions therefore create an ongoing compliance obligation, not merely an event-driven one: small finance banks must continuously maintain a stress-resolution apparatus, not only respond once an account is already non-performing.

For accounts that enter a formal resolution workflow, the directions prescribe a “review period” during which the bank and relevant lenders must assess the borrower’s situation and finalize a resolution plan. Where multiple lenders are involved, the framework requires an inter-creditor agreement so that the lenders coordinate decision-making and implementation rather than acting in isolation. The resolution plan must then be implemented within the timelines and conditions specified in the directions, and the framework contemplates different prudential outcomes depending on whether implementation is timely or delayed.

A key compliance consequence is additional provisioning if implementation of the resolution plan is delayed. The document establishes a specific prudential penalty for lagging execution, meaning the bank may have to recognize extra provisions against the exposure until the plan is properly implemented. This creates a direct capital and earnings impact and makes timely execution of the agreed resolution plan a material compliance and financial-control issue.

The directions also address prudential norms applicable to restructuring, indicating that restructurings of stressed exposures must be handled under specified regulatory conditions rather than as informal extensions or renegotiations. In practice, compliance teams should treat the document as imposing formal governance, documentation, monitoring, inter-lender coordination, and provisioning controls around stressed asset resolution for small finance banks, with RBI supervisory review and financial consequences if implementation slips.

A key implementation requirement is the RBI’s instruction on **automation of income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning (IRACP) processes**: SFBs must have system-driven processes for these prudential functions rather than relying on manual treatment, so compliance, risk, and IT functions need to ensure the bank’s core systems correctly apply classification and provisioning logic and produce reliable reports. The directions also emphasize the **Board’s role** in setting the overall prudential and credit-risk framework, along with requirements on **prudence in lending and consumer education**, meaning SFBs must ensure credit policies, borrower communication, and customer education practices support sound lending and transparent borrower understanding. The document also includes **disclosure requirements**, so banks must make the specified prudential disclosures in their financial/reporting framework.

The asset-classification chapter establishes the rules for **when an account becomes a non-performing asset (NPA)** and how it should be treated, including specific instructions for **accounts regularized near the balance-sheet date** and **special cases of asset classification**. It also sets out the **categories of NPAs**, which determines the applicable provisioning and supervisory treatment, so compliance officers should expect detailed definitions that affect loan monitoring, overdue tracking, and reporting cutoffs. Because the document is titled as a full directions circular rather than a narrow amendment note, the practical compliance obligation is to ensure all SFB lending portfolios, including legacy accounts and any system-based NPA identification logic, are aligned with the RBI’s classification and provisioning standards as of the updated effective version.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**) set out the governance framework for **all Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and replace/standardize requirements on board composition, director appointments, senior management roles, committees, remuneration, and regulatory approvals/reporting. The directions apply to SFBs generally and are organized into binding rules on: constitution of the board; appointment, tenure, and responsibilities of directors; the roles of the **MD&CEO, part-time chairman, and whole-time directors**; board practices; mandatory board committees; and appointments of key control positions such as the **Chief Risk Officer (CRO), Chief Financial Officer (CFO), and Chief Technical Officer (CTO)**. Because the document is a governance directions instrument, the primary compliance obligation is to ensure the bank’s constitutional documents, board processes, committee charters, senior appointments, and remuneration policies are aligned with the RBI’s prescribed governance model and that any required approvals or notifications are obtained before implementation.

Materially, the directions tighten and formalize how SFB boards must be constituted and operated, including the rules for appointing directors and identifying the responsibilities of individual directors and senior executives. The board must oversee governance through specifically designated committees, including an **Audit Committee of the Board**, a **Risk Management Committee**, and a **Nomination and Remuneration Committee**, each with RBI-prescribed roles and composition expectations. The document also creates specific requirements around the appointment of the **CRO, CFO, and CTO**, indicating that these control/technical leadership positions are not discretionary but must be filled and governed in the manner set by the RBI directions. The directions further address remuneration controls for **non-executive directors (NEDs), whole-time directors (WTDs), the MD&CEO, material risk takers, and control function staff**, signaling that pay structures for both board and key risk/control personnel are subject to regulatory governance constraints rather than purely internal policy.

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that an SFB must review whether its current board composition, committee structure, senior appointments, and compensation practices satisfy the RBI’s framework as of the directions’ effective commencement date (not stated in the excerpt provided). The bank should verify whether any existing directors, committee mandates, or executive appointments require re-appointment, re-designation, or RBI approval under the new directions, and should ensure board documentation and internal governance policies are updated accordingly. The document also contains a chapter on **regulatory approvals and reporting**, which means certain governance actions will likely require prior RBI approval, intimation, or periodic reporting, depending on the specific provision involved. In short, the directions are a comprehensive governance rulebook for SFBs, and compliance officers should treat them as a mandatory framework governing board constitution, leadership appointments, committee oversight, and remuneration controls.

These limits restricted banks’ exposures to individual borrower and group borrowers to a certain percentage of capital funds, laying the foundation for mitigating concentration risk on assets side of their balance sheets. No fresh proposals for organization of new UCBs or for conversion of co- operative credit societies into UCBs are being considered by Reserve Bank of India. In this context, Urban Co-operative Banks shall mean Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of Banking Regulation Act, 1949. B. Categorization of UCBs for Regulatory Purposes 2. Given the heterogeneity in the urban cooperative sector, a four-tiered regulatory framework has been adopted to balance the spirit of mutuality and cooperation more prevalent in banks of smaller sizes and those with limited area of operation vis-à-vis the growth ambitions of the large-sized UCBs to spread their area of operation and undertake more complex business activities. Accordingly, the UCBs are categorized into the following four tiers for regulatory purposes: (1) Tier 1 - All unit UCBs and salary earners' UCBs (irrespective of deposit size), and all other UCBs having deposits up to ₹100 crore; (2) Tier 2 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹100 crore and up to ₹1000 crore; (3) Tier 3 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹1000 crore and up to ₹10,000 crore; (4) Tier 4 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹10,000 crore. 3. The deposits referred to above shall be reckoned as per the audited balance sheet as of 31 st March of the immediately preceding financial year. 2 4. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This 2026 RBI Supervisory Directions consolidate and restate the Reserve Bank of India’s expectations for commercial banks on a wide set of operational, conduct, governance, and control matters. They are issued by the Department of Supervision on 31 July 2026 under RBI/DoS/2026-27/416 and apply to commercial banks as covered by the document’s applicability section. The directions span IT system access, monitoring of end-use of funds, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), interest-charging practices, inoperative and unclaimed accounts, nomination, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, and vigilance governance.

A major theme is tighter control over access, accountability, and monitoring. Banks must ensure controlled access to IT systems and maintain procedures that support traceability and supervision of user activities. They also must implement monitoring of end use of funds, which means they are expected to track whether borrowed or sanctioned funds are actually used for the stated purpose, with heightened controls where misuse risk is present. The PCA chapter establishes RBI’s framework for supervisory escalation when banks’ financial condition deteriorates; affected banks may be placed under corrective actions once specified trigger points are breached, and they must then comply with the RBI-directed restrictions and remediation steps that accompany the framework.

The directions also reinforce customer-protection requirements. Banks must follow the Fair Practices Code on charging of interest, meaning interest must be levied in a transparent, non-exploitative manner and in line with RBI’s fair-lending expectations. For inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, banks are required to maintain systems and procedures to identify dormant accounts, handle unclaimed balances appropriately, and support claim resolution. The nomination chapter requires banks to provide and administer nomination facilities so depositors and other eligible customers can designate nominees for account balances and related claims.

Fraud prevention is a substantial component of the document and covers multiple scenarios that compliance teams should treat as control requirements. The directions address frauds involving collusion by bank officials, large-value frauds, bulk retail-loan sanctions, frauds using fake title deeds of property, frauds in non-resident accounts, and safekeeping of critical documents. Banks must also manage accounts opened by employees with enhanced scrutiny, maintain a legal compliance certificate and a legal compliance audit process, and carry out forensic scrutiny where needed. The document further addresses the exercise of discretionary powers and sets out a “best practices” code for banks, indicating that internal decision-making authority must be documented, disciplined, and subject to control review rather than left to informal discretion.

The Protected Disclosure Scheme chapter requires banks to provide a protected complaint mechanism for reporting wrongdoing. It covers the scheme’s scope, the procedure for lodging complaints, and the protected disclosure policy, meaning banks must be able to receive complaints confidentially and protect whistleblowers from retaliation while ensuring appropriate inquiry and handling. The vigilance chapter then adds governance expectations for anti-corruption and integrity controls: it introduces vigilance-angle assessment, the role and appointment of a Chief of Internal Vigilance, tenure expectations, restrictions on association with sensitive matters, and reporting/return submission and review requirements. It also requires preventive vigilance measures, staff rotation, and mandatory leave in sensitive roles, plus established complaint-handling and investigation arrangements, including the use of investigation agencies and review of cases entrusted to them.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026**, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The directions apply to **commercial banks only**—specifically **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India**. They define **“Supervisory Returns”** broadly to cover **all periodic and ad hoc data submitted to RBI in prescribed formats**, regardless of the technology platform, frequency, or submission mode, and define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance standpoint, the directions require the **Board and Senior Management** to treat **data quality risk** as part of the bank’s overall risk management framework. The framework must include **ownership/accountability, governance, controls, approvals, and escalation mechanisms** for the preparation and submission of supervisory returns, so compliance is not just a filing exercise but a board-level control responsibility. The document also places responsibility on banks to maintain a **robust data architecture and IT infrastructure** that supports accurate, complete, and timely supervisory reporting, which means banks need systems capable of producing regulatory data reliably and in a controlled manner.

The directions further require banks to ensure the **accuracy and integrity of reporting**, including processes to verify returns before submission and to correct errors when identified. In practice, this means banks must have procedures for **validation, reconciliation, review, and authorization** of supervisory data, with clear internal controls to prevent misreporting. The document also contemplates **operational guidelines, a list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, penalties, and other instructions** in Chapter III, indicating that banks will need to monitor the specific return-wise filing calendar and comply with any format- or event-driven reporting obligations prescribed by RBI from time to time.

Finally, the directions include standard legal provisions on **repeal and saving**, application of other laws not barred, and interpretation, meaning these directions sit alongside other applicable statutory and regulatory requirements rather than replacing them wholesale. Based on the text provided, **no specific numeric filing deadlines, thresholds, or penalty amounts are stated in the excerpt**, so a compliance team should review the full Chapter III tables and instructions for the exact return list, due dates, exception handling, and any consequences for late or inaccurate submissions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026” take effect immediately on issuance and apply to commercial banks in relation to the appointment and reappointment of their Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) and Statutory Auditors (SAs). The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, and the State Bank of India Act, and they supersede the prior RBI framework for statutory audit of commercial banks. The document is directed at banking companies, except where the text later distinguishes specific bank categories or overseas branches for special treatment.

For compliance purposes, the core change is that the RBI is formalizing detailed governance, eligibility, tenure, appointment, and reporting requirements for bank statutory auditors, with explicit board and senior management responsibility for the process. The board must ensure a robust auditor selection process, monitor auditor independence and performance, and make sure audit-related governance is documented and escalated appropriately. The directions also require banks to follow prescribed procedures for appointment/reappointment, including any limits on the number of auditors, branch coverage rules, and coordination for overseas branches where applicable.

The directions set out detailed eligibility and independence criteria for SCAs/SAs, including professional standards, fit-and-proper expectations, and restrictions intended to avoid conflicts of interest. They also establish tenure and rotation requirements so that auditors cannot remain indefinitely, and they prescribe how audit fees and expenses are to be determined and handled. In addition, there are specific procedural requirements for appointing auditors, including the submission and approval steps banks must follow and the special process for appointing auditors for overseas branch(es).

A major operational requirement is the Long Form Audit Report (LFAR), for which the directions establish both procedure and timelines and separately address the reports prepared by SCAs and by branch auditors. The LFAR framework includes defined objectives, strategy, scope, and coverage expectations, along with indicative coverage areas that auditors must examine. Banks must ensure that the required LFAR information is gathered, reviewed, and submitted within the stipulated deadlines, and that any findings are integrated into governance and remediation processes.

Finally, the directions include repeal-and-saving provisions and clarify that they do not bar the application of other laws. The document also contains annexes that appear to provide the operational detail, forms, and implementation guidance needed to execute the audit framework. For a compliance team, the key action is to review whether current auditor appointment practices, audit committee/board oversight, independence checks, rotation tracking, and LFAR workflows align with the new RBI requirements as of the issuance date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Internal Audit Function Directions, 2026** require all **commercial banks**—defined to include **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks, corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India**—to operate under a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework rather than a purely transaction-centric audit model. The directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**; the document is dated **July 31, 2026**. The RBI states that the purpose is to strengthen banks’ internal control and risk management systems by aligning internal audit with current governance standards and international best practices.

At the governance level, the **Board of the bank** (or the **Local Advisory Board** in the case of a foreign bank) must approve a **formal RBIA policy** and the **risk assessment methodology** used by the Internal Audit Department. The directions make clear that internal audit is expected to evaluate not just transactions but also the **adequacy of risk management systems and internal controls**, so the board’s oversight must extend to how audit coverage is planned and prioritized based on risk. Senior management is expected to support implementation of the RBIA framework and ensure the audit function has the information, access, and organizational support needed to operate independently and effectively.

The directions also require each bank to put in place an **internal audit policy and framework** that is **risk-based, documented, and periodically reviewed**, with the scope of audit determined through a structured risk assessment. The Internal Audit Department must use a methodology that identifies, measures, and ranks risks across the bank’s activities, so that audit frequency, depth, and coverage reflect risk significance rather than simply transaction volume. The framework must include procedures for **functional independence**, so internal audit is not placed in a position where its judgment is compromised by the business lines it reviews.

The document further addresses **scope, communication, performance evaluation, and outsourcing** of internal audit, indicating that banks must define what activities and functions are covered by RBIA, how audit findings are escalated and reported, how the effectiveness of internal audit is assessed, and under what conditions audit work may be outsourced. It also creates specific requirements for the **Head of Internal Audit**, including provisions on **authority, stature, independence, tenure, and reporting line**, to ensure the function has sufficient standing and direct access to appropriate senior governance bodies. Finally, the directions include **repeal and saving provisions**, preserve application of other laws where not inconsistent, and provide interpretive guidance for implementation.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory framework for commercial banks to **prevent fraud, detect it early, escalate red flags, and report incidents promptly to law enforcement and the RBI**. The directions are issued under **Sections 21 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply to the entities covered under the document’s applicability provisions (commercial banks). They are intended not just to govern reporting after a fraud is found, but also to require governance, internal controls, early warning systems, staff accountability, and procedures for cases under resolution or involving third parties.

A major requirement is that banks must maintain a **fraud risk management governance structure** with clear oversight responsibilities, and must implement an **Early Warning Signal (EWS) / Red-Flagged Account (RFA) framework** for both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking or non-credit transactions**. This means banks are expected to identify suspicious indicators early, classify affected loan accounts appropriately as red-flagged, and follow specified internal escalation and reporting processes before losses deepen. The document also requires banks to obtain **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where relevant, so reliance on outsourced or external inputs does not weaken fraud controls.

The directions impose explicit obligations on **reporting frauds to LEAs and to RBI**, including reporting incidents of fraud, using the **Central Fraud Registry**, following RBI’s specified reporting modalities, and completing closure reporting for fraud cases once resolved/closed. In addition, there is a separate reporting obligation for **cheque-related frauds**, which must be reported both to law enforcement and RBI under the dedicated chapter. The framework further addresses the treatment of accounts classified as fraudulent and then **sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies**, indicating that fraud classification and related consequences do not simply disappear on transfer.

The document also covers **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning banks must investigate internal responsibility and apply consequences where employee conduct, negligence, or collusion is implicated. For larger exposures, banks must conduct a **legal audit of title documents for large value loan accounts**, and the directions state that auditors have a role in the fraud risk environment as well. Finally, the directions include a separate reporting requirement for **cases of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, and a repeal/saving section clarifying how these directions interact with earlier RBI instructions and other laws. The title indicates a 2026 instrument, and the document itself is dated **July 31, 2026** (RBI reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/412** and **DoS.CO.FMG.6/23.04.001/2026-27**).
