The document, issued on April 1, 2025 (RBI/2025-26/11; DoR.STR.REC 07/09.27.000/2025-26), states that it is only a consolidation of all instructions issued up to March 31, 2025 on guarantees, co-acceptances, and letters of credit, and explicitly says it does **not** introduce any new instructions or guidelines. For compliance purposes, the operative obligation is to ensure internal policies, procedures, and controls reflect the consolidated RBI directions as updated through March 31, 2025, rather than expecting any new substantive rule change in this circular itself.

The circular covers the full RBI framework for: issuing guarantees, including broad guidelines, permissible purposes, maturity, volume, secured versus unsecured guarantees, and deferred payment guarantees; guarantees relating to commodities under selective credit controls; safeguards for issuing guarantees; immediate settlement of claims under bank guarantees; handling delays in obtaining certified copies of judgments; and correspondence with government departments. It also consolidates rules on co-acceptance of bills, including irregularities in co-acceptance and the required safeguards, as well as letter of credit (LC) facilities, including guidelines for granting LC facilities, LC treatment for commodities under selective credit controls, safeguards for opening LCs, and immediate settlement of claims under LCs. In addition, it includes the common framework for credit exposure norms and statutory/other restrictions applicable to non-fund-based limits.

From a compliance perspective, this means UCBs must review the annexed consolidated instructions and verify that all current business practices for guarantees, co-acceptances, and LCs comply with the RBI’s applicable limits, approval controls, documentary safeguards, and settlement expectations as in force through March 31, 2025. No new effective date, threshold, rate, or deadline is introduced in the circular text provided beyond the publication date and the cut-off date for consolidation, but the institution must treat the revised master circular as the current consolidated reference for these products.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/09 (DOR.CAP.REC.03/09.18.201/2025-26), applies to all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) and supersedes/consolidates the earlier master circular dated 1 April 2024. It states that it updates all instructions and guidelines on prudential norms for capital adequacy issued up to 31 March 2025, with the detailed rules collected in the annexures referenced in the circular.

Substantively, the circular reiterates that capital is a buffer against losses and a licensing/continuation requirement for a bank, and then restates the statutory minimum capital position for co-operative banks under the Banking Regulation Act (AACS): a bank may not commence or carry on banking business unless its aggregate paid-up capital and reserves are at least ₹1 lakh. It also indicates that the circular covers the computation of net worth, capital adequacy norms/CRAR, risk weights, market risk capital, share-linking to borrowings, refund of share capital, and investor-protection measures for regulatory capital instruments, with specific operational guidance contained in Annexes 1 through 5.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that UCBs must use this Master Circular as the current consolidated source for capital adequacy compliance as of 31 March 2025, and must follow the detailed requirements in the annexures on: how to compute net worth; the applicable risk weights for capital adequacy calculations; the rules for issuing preference shares and debt capital instruments; the format for returns; and any procedural safeguards for investors in such instruments. The document also includes a section on returns, implying ongoing reporting obligations under the prescribed pro forma.

No new numerical capital adequacy ratio, deadline, or rate is stated in the excerpt beyond the ₹1 lakh statutory minimum paid-up capital and reserves threshold; the circular’s primary compliance change is the consolidation and update of the earlier instructions into one current master circular effective from 1 April 2025.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular updates and consolidates all RBI instructions on the **Board of Directors of Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, superseding the prior circular dated **April 1, 2024**. It is addressed to the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all UCBs and reiterates that boards must consist of persons of **high integrity and knowledge**, with the bank required to maintain **at least two professional directors at all times**—meaning directors with suitable banking experience (at middle/senior management level) or relevant professional qualifications. The circular applies to the governance of UCBs under the RBI’s supervisory powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **RBI Act, 1934**.

The document covers the **constitution of the Board**, the **role and responsibilities of directors**, the **committees of the Board**, the **calendar of reviews and matters to be placed before the Board**, and controls relating to **donations to trusts/institutions where directors or their relatives have an interest or position**. It also includes rules on **payment of fees and allowances to directors**, and it consolidates earlier RBI circulars and the related guidance annexed in the master circular, including the **Madhava Das Committee recommendations** and the prescribed **reviews to be submitted to the Board**. For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that UCBs must ensure their governance structure, board composition, committee oversight, and periodic review mechanisms continue to satisfy RBI expectations as set out in the updated consolidated instructions.

The circular is effective from **April 1, 2025** and is intended to be read as the current master reference on board governance for UCBs. Compliance teams should treat the circular as the governing compilation of all existing instructions on this subject, and should verify that board composition, director suitability, board committee structure, agenda/calendar items, donation approvals, and director compensation arrangements are aligned with the consolidated RBI framework.

This RBI Master Circular applies to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and sets out the Reserve Bank of India’s policy framework for **bank finance to non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)**. It is issued as a **statutory guideline under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The circular **revises and consolidates** the RBI’s earlier Master Circular on the same subject dated **April 24, 2024**, and the RBI states expressly that this version **contains no new instructions or guidelines**; it only compiles all instructions issued on the topic **up to March 31, 2025**.

For compliance purposes, the document confirms that banks must follow the RBI’s existing rules on lending to NBFCs across the full set of subject areas covered in the circular, including: finance to **NBFCs registered with RBI**, finance to **NBFCs not requiring registration**, **activities not eligible for bank credit**, finance to **factoring companies**, other prohibitions on bank finance, **bridge loans/interim finance**, **advances against collateral security of shares to NBFCs**, restrictions on **guarantees for placement of funds with NBFCs**, **prudential exposure ceilings** for banks’ aggregate exposure to NBFCs, restrictions on **bank investments in securities/instruments issued by NBFCs**, and the **risk weight** applicable to bank credit to NBFCs. The document’s operative effect is therefore to serve as the current consolidated reference for all existing RBI requirements governing bank funding and related exposures to NBFCs, rather than introducing a substantive policy change.

The key practical point is that compliance teams should treat this as the **current, consolidated master reference** for bank-to-NBFC finance as of **April 1, 2025**, and ensure internal credit policies, exposure monitoring, permissibility checks, and investment/guarantee controls are aligned to the annexed RBI instructions referenced in the circular. Since the circular itself does not create new thresholds or deadlines in the text provided, the material compliance obligation is to **continue applying the existing RBI restrictions and prudential limits exactly as consolidated in the updated master circular**.

This Master Circular, effective **April 1, 2025**, consolidates and updates RBI’s existing **Basel III capital adequacy / prudential capital guidelines** for **all Scheduled Commercial Banks other than Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks**. It supersedes the prior consolidated Master Circular dated **April 1, 2024** and states that the earlier instructions have been **suitably updated/amended** to reflect all relevant circulars issued up to the date of this circular; the list of source circulars is in **Annex 26**. The RBI also expressly notes that **Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks are not covered by this circular** and should instead follow their own licensing and operating guidelines for capital adequacy.

From the content shown, the circular is a comprehensive restatement of the Basel III capital framework for covered banks, including the **minimum capital requirement (Pillar 1)**, the **scope of application**, **composition of regulatory capital**, **recognition of minority interest**, **regulatory deductions/adjustments**, and **transitional arrangements**. It then sets out the detailed **credit risk capital charge** framework, covering exposures to **domestic and foreign sovereigns and central banks, public sector entities, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, primary dealers, corporates and NBFCs, retail portfolios, residential mortgages, commercial real estate, NPAs, specified categories, other assets, and off-balance-sheet items**. The table of contents also shows specific treatment for items such as **counterparty credit risk on off-balance-sheet exposures**, indicating that the circular is not merely high-level policy but a detailed operational rulebook that affects how banks calculate risk weights and capital charges across major asset classes.

For compliance purposes, the key action is that affected banks must ensure their **capital adequacy calculations, exposure classifications, deductions, and transitional treatment** are aligned with the updated consolidated instructions as of **April 1, 2025**. Because the circular consolidates prior instructions rather than creating a single isolated rule change in the excerpt provided, a compliance team would need to check the annexed consolidated circular list and the body of the Master Circular for any **new or revised risk weights, deduction thresholds, reporting expectations, or capital composition requirements** applicable to their portfolios and regulatory filings.

rows.summary:
This RBI Master Circular, dated **June 16, 2025** and addressed to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, consolidates all Reserve Bank instructions issued up to that date on **credit facilities to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs)**. It does not introduce a single new standalone rule in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and consolidates the RBI’s existing requirements and expectations for banks to **step up advances to SC/ST borrowers**.

A key compliance point is the **planning and coordination framework** banks must use. The **District Level Consultative Committees (DLCCs)** under the Lead Bank Scheme remain the principal coordination mechanism between banks and development agencies, and the **district credit plans** prepared by Lead Banks must clearly show how credit is linked with **employment generation and development schemes**. Banks are also expected to maintain **closer liaison with District Industries Centres (DICs)** in the districts for promotion of **self-employment** opportunities. At the **block level**, planning must give **weightage to SC/ST communities**, meaning credit planning is not to be neutral in a purely population-agnostic way but should deliberately reflect SC/ST participation and needs.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure the bank’s **district credit planning, branch/block-level business planning, and developmental coordination processes** explicitly incorporate SC/ST lending objectives and can demonstrate that linkage in records and planning documents. Because the circular is a **master consolidation**, the operative compliance requirement is not just monitoring one policy note, but ensuring internal credit policy, rural and priority sector planning, and reporting systems align with the consolidated RBI instructions listed in the appendix. The document excerpt does not specify numerical lending targets, caps, dates for phased implementation, or special pricing terms; the material requirement shown is the **institutional obligation to plan, coordinate, and weight credit delivery in favor of SC/ST borrowers through formal district and block-level mechanisms**.

rows.title: Master Circular – Lead Bank Scheme
rows.desc: RBI/2025-26/04 FIDD.CO.LBS.BC.No.03/02.01.001/2025-26 April 01, 2025 The Chairman/Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer SLBC/UTLBC Convenor Banks/Lead Banks Madam/Dear Sir, Master Circular – Lead Bank Scheme The Reserve Bank of India has issued a number of guidelines/ instructions on Lead Bank Scheme from time to time. This Master Circular consolidates the relevant guidelines/ instructions issued by Reserve Bank of India on Lead Bank Scheme up to March 31, 2025 as listed in the Appendix I. 2. This Master Circular has been placed on the RBI website https://www.rbi.org.in Yours faithfully, (Nisha Nambiar) Chief General Manager-in-Charge Encl.: As above 2 Structure 1 Introduction 2 Fora under Lead Bank Scheme 2.1 Block Level Bankers’ Committee 2.2 District Consultative Committee (DCC) 2.2.1 Constitution of DCC 2.2.2 Conduct of DCC Meetings 2.2.3 Agenda for DCC Meetings 2.2.4 Role of LDMs 2.2.5 Quarterly Public Meeting and Grievance Redressal 2.2.6 District Level Review Committee (DLRC) Meetings 2.2.7 DCC/DLRC meetings – Annual Calendar of Meetings 2.3 State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) 2.3.1 Constitution of SLBC 2.3.2 Conduct of SLBC Meetings 2.3.3 Revised Agenda for SLBC Meetings 2.3.4 SLBC – Yearly Calendar of Meetings 2.3.5 SLBC Website – Standardization of information/data 2.3.6 Liaison with State Government 2.3.7 Capacity Building/Training/Sensitization Programmes 3 Implementation of Lead Bank Scheme 3.1 Preparation of credit plans 3.2 Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs) 3.3 Monitoring the performance of credit plans 3.4 Revised mechanism of Data Flow for LBS fora meetings 4 Assignment of Lead Bank Responsibility 5 Banking Penetration 5.1 Roadmap for provision of banking services in unbanked villages 5.2 Roadmap for opening brick and mortar branches in villages with population more than 5000 without a bank branch of a scheduled commercial bank 5.3 Aligning roadmap for unbanked villages having population more than 5000 with revised guidelines on Branch Auth
rows.summary:
This Master Circular consolidates RBI’s Lead Bank Scheme instructions issued up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to SLBC/UTLBC convenor banks and lead banks, superseding/compiling prior guidance rather than introducing a single isolated rule. For compliance teams, the key point is that the circular is a consolidated operational framework covering the governance structure for Lead Bank Scheme forums, credit-planning and monitoring responsibilities, data-flow requirements, and banking-penetration obligations, with the detailed operative instructions contained in the circular’s sections and the appendix of source instructions. It applies to institutions participating in the Lead Bank Scheme framework, especially lead banks, convenor banks, and the bodies they service at district, state, block, and local levels.

The document establishes the fora under the Lead Bank Scheme, including Block Level Bankers’ Committees, District Consultative Committees (DCCs), District Level Review Committees (DLRCs), and State Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs), and lays out requirements for their constitution, meeting conduct, agendas, annual meeting calendars, and related reporting/review processes. It specifically identifies the role of Lead District Managers (LDMs), requires quarterly public meetings and grievance-redressal mechanisms at the district level, and standardizes the SLBC website information/data architecture and liaison with state governments. It also calls for capacity-building, training, and sensitization programmes, indicating that compliance is not just documentary but includes active operational coordination and stakeholder engagement.

On implementation, the circular covers preparation of credit plans and Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs), monitoring performance against those plans, and a revised mechanism for data flow for Lead Bank Scheme forum meetings. That means banks and convenor institutions must ensure timely, accurate submission and consolidation of data used for LBS meetings and reviews, and must maintain planning and monitoring processes that can evidence progress against district/state credit objectives. The circular also includes rules on assignment of Lead Bank responsibility, which is relevant for any institution taking on or continuing that role.

A material compliance area is banking penetration and branch/service expansion. The circular continues the roadmap for providing banking services in unbanked villages and the roadmap for opening brick-and-mortar branches in villages with population above 5,000 where there is no branch of a scheduled commercial bank, while also aligning the roadmap for such unbanked villages with revised branch authorization guidelines. Even though the text provided here does not state the detailed thresholds or timelines beyond the “population more than 5,000” criterion, the compliance implication is that affected banks must track coverage gaps, service delivery obligations, and branch-opening priorities for eligible villages under the revised framework. The circular itself is dated April 1, 2025, and consolidates guidance effective through March 31, 2025.

rows.summary:
RBI has issued a new **Master Circular on Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)** dated **April 1, 2025** under **RBI/2025-26/02 FIDD.GSSD.CO.BC.No.01/09.01.003/2025-26**. This circular is addressed to **Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Small Finance Banks** and **replaces the earlier Master Circular dated April 16, 2024** on the same subject. The RBI states that the new master circular **consolidates and updates all instructions/guidelines issued up to date**, so compliance teams should treat it as the operative version for DAY-NRLM-related banking obligations.  

The document reiterates the background of the government program: the **National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM)** was launched by the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India, by restructuring **Swarnajayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY)** effective **April 1, 2013**, and was renamed **DAY-NRLM** effective **March 29, 2016**. The program is described as the Government of India’s flagship rural livelihood initiative aimed at **poverty reduction through building strong institutions of the poor, particularly women, and enabling access to financial services and livelihoods**.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway from the provided text is that banks in scope should refer to this master circular as the updated regulatory reference point for any lending, financing, or other banking support connected with DAY-NRLM entities or activities. Because the RBI explicitly says the circular **supersedes the prior master circular**, any internal policy, control, training, or product documentation that cites the April 16, 2024 version should be checked against the 2025 master circular and updated where needed.  

The excerpt provided does not include the later substantive instructions, thresholds, or operational norms that may appear in the rest of the master circular, so from this excerpt alone the only definite new requirement is the **replacement of the prior circular by the April 1, 2025 consolidated version**. Compliance teams should therefore obtain and review the full enclosed master circular to capture the detailed requirements applicable to DAY-NRLM financing and related banking processes.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by the RBI on 1 April 2025 (RBI/2025-26/01, FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26), is addressed to the Chairman/Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all scheduled commercial banks and consolidates all RBI instructions on the Self Help Group (SHG)-Bank Linkage Programme up to 31 March 2025. It does not itself announce a new standalone policy change in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and compiles the existing regulatory framework governing SHG lending and related bank obligations.

The document explains the policy rationale for SHG-bank linkage: SHGs are intended to connect the formal banking system with the rural poor, with NABARD studies cited as showing higher SHG loan volumes, a shift from consumption/non-income-generating borrowing toward productive activities, near-100% recovery in some cases, lower transaction costs for banks and borrowers, and rising member incomes. It also notes that around 85% of bank-linked SHGs were formed exclusively by women, highlighting the program’s gender dimension. On this basis, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, following the Union Budget 2008-09 direction on “Total Financial Inclusion.”

The excerpted text says scheduled commercial banks should meet the full credit needs of SHG members for: income-generation activities, social needs, and other approved purposes referenced in the underlying Budget language. For a compliance team, the key point is that this Master Circular is the authoritative consolidation of RBI guidance on SHG-bank linkage as of 31 March 2025, so internal policies, credit processes, product structures, and monitoring arrangements for SHG lending should be checked against the consolidated RBI instructions contained in the full circular and its appendix.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued for public comment the draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”**, following the announcement in the RBI’s **Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 05, 2026**. The draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of interest-rate instructions with a **harmonized, principles-based framework for all regulated entities (REs)** covering both **fixed-rate and floating-rate loans and advances**, with the framework to be calibrated to the **nature, complexity, and scale** of each RE’s operations.

The RBI says the existing regime is uneven: for **Commercial Banks** (including **Small Finance Banks** and **Local Area Banks**), there are detailed rules already in place for **internal and external benchmark-based lending**, including the setting of **spreads over benchmarks**; by contrast, the rules for **NBFCs, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks** are mostly limited to conduct-related requirements. The RBI also notes that among commercial banks it has observed **divergent practices in determining the MCLR (internal benchmark) and its components**, and that current guidance on **fixed-rate loans** is very limited. The proposed directions are meant to address these gaps and align interest-rate setting practices more consistently across REs.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is still a **draft consultation document**, so the immediate obligation is to **review and submit comments/feedback** rather than to implement final rule changes yet. However, the substance of the proposal signals that, once finalized, it may impose a more uniform supervisory standard on all REs for how loan and advance interest rates are determined, including both benchmark-linked floating-rate structures and fixed-rate lending. The document excerpt provided does not yet give a final effective date, transition period, or operative thresholds/rates; those would need to be checked in the final directions once issued.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’
rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. The comments on the draft Directions are invited from Regulated Entities, market participants, and other interested parties till August 28, 2026. The comments / feedb
rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft revised Directions on the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework and invited public comments by August 28, 2026. The draft replaces the RBI’s existing CVA framework issued in 2011, which had been based on the 2010 Basel Committee standards, and is intended to align Indian rules with the Basel III revisions to CVA treatment.

Substantively, the RBI is proposing to allow Indian banks to use the Basel “basic approach” for CVA capital calculation (BA-CVA), with banks permitted to adopt either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. In addition, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may, consistent with BCBS guidance, calculate their CVA capital charge at 100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge instead of using the BA-CVA methodology. The draft also clarifies when CVA hedges are eligible for recognition, increases the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties based on sector and credit quality, and separates systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation to better reflect indirect CVA hedges.

The RBI states that these changes are meant to make the framework more risk-sensitive and more consistent with current international standards. The new draft Directions, titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**, apply to commercial banks in India that are subject to RBI regulation and to their CVA capital computation for derivative exposures. The consultation is open to regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties, who may submit comments up to the August 28, 2026 deadline.

rows.title: Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co-operative Banks
rows.desc: August 06, 2026 Review of Guidelines on Concentration Risk Management - Rural Co- operative Banks In pursuance of the announcement made with regard to the captioned subject in the Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 5, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India has today issued the following draft Directions for public comments: (i) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2026 to replace Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) – Directions, 2025 (ii) Draft Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) – Amendment Directions, 2026 to amend certain provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 2. The above draft Directions prescribe, inter alia, prudential exposure limits for single/group counterparty, enhanced housing loan limits, and prudential exposure limits on unsecured advances. Additionally, it is proposed to allow flexibility to larger Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) with deposits above ₹1,000 crore in deciding the tenor and moratorium requirements for housing loans, while increasing the ceilings for these parameters in cases of other RCBs. Further, the prescribed prudential sectoral exposure limits, except for real estate sector, are proposed to be withdrawn. 3. The comments / feedback on the draft Directions may be submitted by the regulated entities and other stakeholders / members of public on or before August 28, 2026 through the following channels: (i) The ‘Connect 2 Regulate’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted; or (ii) by email with the subject line ‘Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)’. rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft directions for public comment to update the concentration risk framework applicable to rural co-operative banks (RCBs). The package consists of two instruments: a new **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026**, which would replace the existing **2025** concentration risk directions, and a **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which would amend certain provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

The draft changes are intended to set out prudential exposure limits for **single and group counterparties**, raise **housing loan limits**, and specify prudential limits for **unsecured advances**. RBI also proposes to give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** more flexibility to determine the **tenor and moratorium** for housing loans, while for **other RCBs** it proposes to **increase the ceilings** for those housing-loan parameters. In addition, RBI proposes to **withdraw the general prudential sectoral exposure limits**, with the stated exception that the **real estate sector** exposure limit would remain in place.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that these are **draft directions** open for consultation, not yet final rules. RBI has set **August 28, 2026** as the deadline for comments/feedback from regulated entities and other stakeholders, which may be submitted either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the RBI website or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. Compliance teams at RCBs should review the draft closely for any changes to counterparty exposure, unsecured lending, and housing finance policies, especially where deposits exceed the **₹1,000 crore** threshold.

On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft amendments titled the **“Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026”** for public consultation. rows.desc: July 21, 2026 Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments Foreign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules'). The Union Budget 2026- 27 announced a comprehensive review of the NDI Rules to create a more contemporary, user-friendly framework for foreign investments, consistent with India's evolving economic priorities. Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. The salient features of the proposed draft Rules, inter alia, are as under: a) Simplified and principle-based framework: Rationalization of provisions, harmonization of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity. b) Alignment with the FDI Policy: Clear demarcation of procedural FEMA provisions from policy and sector-specific requirements, improving regulatory coherence and facilitating timely policy changes. c) Enhanced ease of doing business: Streamlined procedures, reduced compliance burden and greater operational flexibility through a transparent and investor-friendly regulatory framework. d) Future-ready regulatory framework: Adoption of principle-based, investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions aligned with evolving business practices, while preserving necessary regulatory safeguards. � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 The Rules will be finalized after wider public consultations
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **draft rationalised Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (NDI Rules)** for public comments on **July 21, 2026**, following the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the foreign investment framework. The draft is intended to update and simplify the existing foreign investment rules in India by creating a more contemporary, user-friendly structure that better aligns with India’s current economic priorities and the evolving foreign investment environment.

For compliance teams, the key substantive change is that the RBI, based on a committee review and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, is proposing a **simplified, principle-based framework** with **harmonized definitions** and a more coherent regulatory architecture. The draft also aims to **separate FEMA procedural requirements from FDI policy and sector-specific requirements**, which should make it clearer which obligations arise under FEMA rules versus sectoral policy conditions and may allow policy changes to be implemented more efficiently. The document also emphasizes **reduced compliance burden, streamlined procedures, and greater operational flexibility**, with the stated goal of improving ease of doing business and making the regime more investor-friendly while retaining necessary safeguards.

No specific numeric thresholds, ownership caps, rates, deadlines, or sector-specific eligibility changes are stated in the press release itself. The only procedural deadline mentioned is that the draft will be **finalized after wider public consultations**, meaning the current publication is a consultation stage rather than an immediately effective rule change. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as a signal that the NDI Rules are likely to be materially reworked, but should wait for the final notified text to identify any actual legal obligations, transition requirements, or date-specific implementation steps.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as potentially applicable to their data governance frameworks and control environment.

The RBI’s stated objective is to respond to the increasing digitalisation of financial services and the growing dependence on technology-driven business models, where data has become a critical asset. The draft explains that as data volume, variety, and velocity increase, regulated entities need stronger governance so that data remains **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose** across business functions and systems. The RBI also highlights that weak data governance can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks**, indicating that the guidance is intended to support broader risk management and supervisory expectations, not just IT controls.

The RBI is seeking comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders **by August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted via the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”** No final compliance obligations are imposed yet in this press release, but the issuance of the draft signals that regulated entities should review their data governance practices and be prepared for future final guidance once the consultation closes.

rows.summary:
On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released for public comment a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”**. The draft is intended to broaden and update RBI’s earlier August 5, 2024 draft **“Regulatory Principles for Management of Model Risks in Credit,”** reflecting the fact that model use has expanded significantly across regulated entities and that entities are increasingly using models, including those based on **Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning**. The stated policy objective is to strengthen governance and risk-management practices for the use of models, and the draft appears to shift the focus from only credit-related model risk to a wider model-risk framework.

The draft Guidance would apply to a wide set of RBI-regulated entities: **Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, All India Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, and Credit Information Companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as relevant to their model governance, validation, oversight, and risk-control frameworks, particularly where models are used in credit, decisioning, or AI/ML-enabled processes. The press release does not state final requirements yet, but it clearly signals that RBI is moving toward formal principles for identifying, governing, and managing model risk across these institutions.

RBI is seeking comments from **regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders** by **July 24, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management.”** There are no monetary thresholds, rates, or implementation dates stated in the press release itself beyond the comment deadline; the immediate compliance action is to review the draft, assess whether the institution falls within the listed regulated entities, and determine whether to submit feedback before the deadline.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), on June 10, 2026, issued a public consultation on draft Amendment Directions for the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR). The document explains that the current framework still requires banks to compute counterparty credit risk (CCR) exposure using the Current Exposure Method (CEM), even though RBI had already issued final SA-CCR-based guidelines in 2016 for “Guidelines for Computing Exposure for Counterparty Credit Risk arising from Derivative Transactions” and “Guidelines on Capital Requirements for Bank Exposures to Central Counterparties,” originally intended to apply from April 1, 2018 but later deferred.

RBI says the earlier SA-CCR framework has now been comprehensively reviewed because of major legal and regulatory changes since 2016, including the enactment of the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020 and the implementation of the margining framework under the RBI’s “Margining for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives” Directions, 2024. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) has also issued multiple FAQs over time to clarify SA-CCR application, and the draft amendments are intended to align the directions with those developments.

The draft directions are described as making several substantive changes to the 2016 version currently reflected in the “Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions, Directions, 2025.” These include clarifying the scope of CCR across both banking book and trading book exposures; setting out how multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets should be treated in light of the new netting and margining framework; and giving specific treatment for transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments. The draft also adds guidance on deferment of option premium, how to compute the effective notional amount for options, and begins incorporating disclosure-related requirements, though the excerpt cuts off before the full disclosure provisions are listed.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that RBI is preparing to replace or materially update the deferred SA-CCR framework and is seeking comments before finalizing the rules. Banks and other affected institutions should review their derivative exposure measurement, netting set documentation, margining processes, clearing-member activity on SEBI-recognised exchanges, and option valuation/exposure calculations to assess whether systems and policies need to change once the amended directions are finalized and brought into force.

The drafts cover six separate sets of directions, each tailored to a regulated entity type: commercial banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, payment banks, local area banks, and urban co-operative banks.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued **revised draft Amendment Directions** for public consultation on the **conduct of regulated entities in recovery of loans and engagement of recovery agents**, following an earlier draft released on **February 12, 2026**. These revised drafts are being issued because RBI received **substantial stakeholder feedback** that led to changes in many key provisions, including feedback on whether lenders should be allowed to use **technology-based mechanisms** to restrict or disable certain functions of a financed device—such as a **mobile phone or tablet**—as a means of recovering dues when a borrower defaults. RBI says the accepted feedback has been incorporated into the revised drafts, and that this is being circulated for **another round of public comments** rather than being finalized immediately.

The revised draft package covers multiple categories of regulated entities, including **commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, and all India financial institutions** (the list is introduced as individual amendment directions for each entity type). The document is therefore relevant to compliance teams at any regulated lender within those classes, especially where the institution uses, or is considering using, recovery practices involving **recovery agents** or **device-level technology controls** on financed consumer electronics.

From a compliance perspective, the key point is that this is **not yet an operative final rule**; it is a revised draft for consultation. No implementation deadline, transition period, numerical threshold, or effective date for binding compliance is provided in the text excerpt. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an early-warning regulatory consultation, review the proposed changes carefully, and assess whether their current recovery policies, agent management controls, borrower communication practices, and any contemplated device-restriction technologies would need to be modified once the directions are finalized.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft amendment directions on April 10, 2026, proposing changes to the methodology for identifying Non-Banking Financial Companies in the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) and to include Government-owned NBFCs within the NBFC-UL framework. The RBI is seeking public comments from NBFCs, members of the public, and other stakeholders by May 04, 2026, and comments may be submitted via the “Connect 2 Regulate” section on the RBI website, by email, or by sending them to the Chief General Manager-in-Charge, Department of Regulation (SIG-NBFCs), Reserve Bank of India, 12th Floor, Central Office Building, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001, with the specified subject line referencing the draft Amendment Directions.

Substantively, the draft would replace the current two-pronged NBFC-UL identification method under the Scale Based Regulatory (SBR) framework—which now uses the top ten eligible NBFCs by asset size plus a parametric scoring methodology—with a simpler, more objective asset-size threshold. The document states that the proposed threshold is ₹1,00,000 crore in asset size, indicating that NBFCs meeting or crossing that level would be identified as NBFC-UL under the revised approach. This change is intended to create a transparent, simple, and absolute criterion for classification rather than relying on the existing ranking and scoring system.

The RBI also proposes to bring Government-owned NBFCs into the NBFC-UL category, which means such entities may become subject to the same upper-layer regulatory expectations applicable to NBFC-ULs once the amendments are finalized. The notice references two draft legal instruments: the draft “Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Second Amendment Directions, 2026” and the draft “Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Third Amendment Directions, 2026,” indicating that the proposed changes affect both the general SBR classification framework and related concentration risk requirements. The document is a consultation notice rather than a final rule, so the key compliance action at this stage is to assess whether the proposed ₹1,00,000 crore threshold or the inclusion of Government-owned NBFCs would affect the organization and, if so, submit comments before the May 04, 2026 deadline.

rows.desc: Non-Confidential Circular Department: LISTING Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/19 Date: August 07, 2026 To, All Listed Entities Subject: Adherence to Compliance Requirements for Handling Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 Suggested Best Practices SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 “(PIT Regulations)”, as amended from time to time, and the relevant circulars issued by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges detail, inter-alia, the manner in which the listed companies are required to deal with Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI). The provisions of the PIT Regulations are further supplemented and clarified through the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) issued by SEBI. In light of the observations made in certain cases, it is considered imperative that listed companies diligently adhere to best practices to ensure full compliance with the PIT Regulations as amended from time to time including the following: 1. Listed companies shall maintain a structured digital database containing the nature of UPSI, the names and PANs (or any other identifier authorized by law) of persons who have shared the information, and the names and PANs of persons with whom such information has been shared. In case where UPSI is shared with a listed company, intermediaries, or fiduciaries, the names and identifier of the individuals handling such information shall be recorded. 2. Listed companies shall diligently implement and periodically review internal policies designed to prevent the leakage of UPSI. Such measures must be in alignment with the statutory and regulatory provisions prescribed under the PIT Regulations. 3. To ensure a culture of compliance, companies shall conduct periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries regarding the prescribed manner of handling UPSI. 4. Listed companies shall ensure compliance with the Code of Conduct formulated by the company wi
rows.summary:
This circular is addressed to **all listed entities** and is issued by the NSE Listing Department as **Circular Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/19 dated August 07, 2026**. It does not create a wholly new regulatory regime; rather, it reinforces and reiterates the obligation to strictly comply with the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (PIT Regulations)**, as amended from time to time, together with SEBI and stock exchange circulars and the SEBI FAQs that supplement those regulations. The circular says recent observations in certain cases make it necessary for listed companies to follow stated best practices to ensure full compliance in how **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)** is handled.

The first key requirement is that listed companies must maintain a **structured digital database** of UPSI disclosures. That database must record the **nature of the UPSI**, the **names and PANs** (or any other legally authorized identifier) of the people who shared the information, and the **names and PANs** of the people with whom it was shared. Where UPSI is shared with a **listed company, intermediary, or fiduciary**, the company must also record the **names and identifiers of the individuals** who actually handled the information. This is a concrete recordkeeping obligation, not just a general control expectation.

The circular also requires listed companies to **diligently implement and periodically review internal policies** intended to prevent UPSI leakage, and those policies must be aligned with the PIT Regulations and related legal requirements. In addition, companies must run **periodic training and awareness programs for all employees and fiduciaries** on the proper handling of UPSI, reflecting an expectation of ongoing compliance education rather than one-time training. Further, listed entities must ensure compliance with their own **Code of Conduct** formulated under the PIT framework, meaning internal insider-trading policies and procedures must be actively followed and enforced.

No new monetary thresholds, reporting deadlines, or rate changes are introduced in this circular, but the compliance expectation is immediate in the sense that listed entities are expected to already be following these requirements under the PIT framework and to strengthen execution wherever gaps have been observed. For a compliance team, the practical implication is to verify that the structured digital database is complete and capture-ready, that internal UPSI controls are documented and periodically reviewed, that training is conducted on a recurring basis, and that the company’s Code of Conduct and related insider-trading procedures are actually being implemented in day-to-day operations.

In this connection, we are pleased to inform you that the single filing system has been extended for the XBRL filing pertaining to the below mentioned event with effect from June 20, 2026, along with the release of the few new XBRL utilities as mentioned in the below table. At the initial stage, the PDF filings will be considered by the Exchange as compliance under Regulation 30 of the SEBI LODR Regulations 2015. Further, all listed entities would be required to submit the filings in XBRL mode within 24 hours of submission of the said PDF filing. The XBRL utility for the new events mentioned in the table below will be made available at the path COMPLIANCE >> Common XBRL Upload>> Equity Announcement- XBRL. Further, it may be noted that the said XBRL filing, will also be made available in iXBRL format (readable format) to the listed entities/stakeholders on the website of the Exchange at path https://www.nseindia.com/companies-listing/corporate-filings-announcements-xbrl (selection of announcement type) Further, please note that the XBRL utility and filing of single event of Para B of Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR 2015 i.e. Awarding, bagging/ receiving, amendment or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the normal course of business, will be discontinued effective June 20, 2026 and will be merged with the single utility of Para B events. With this, the Single filing system through API-based integration shall now be available for below mentioned disclosures: - National Stock Exchange of India CONFIDENTIAL
rows.summary:
This circular updates NSE’s single filing system under the earlier circular dated September 30, 2024 and applies to **all listed entities** that make **Regulation 30 disclosures under the SEBI LODR Regulations, 2015**. Effective **June 20, 2026**, the single filing system is being **extended to XBRL filing** for the newly covered event(s), and the Exchange has also released additional XBRL utilities. For the initial phase, companies may continue to submit the **PDF filing first**, and NSE will treat that PDF submission as compliance under Regulation 30; however, the listed entity must then **submit the corresponding XBRL filing within 24 hours** of the PDF submission. The XBRL utility for the newly covered events will be available in the Exchange portal under **COMPLIANCE >> Common XBRL Upload >> Equity Announcement- XBRL**, and the same filing will also be made available in **iXBRL/readable format** on NSE’s website at the specified corporate filings/announcements XBRL page.

The circular also states that the **XBRL utility and separate filing process for the Para B event in Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR 2015**—specifically **“Awarding, bagging/receiving, amendment or termination of awarded/bagged orders/contracts not in the normal course of business”**—will be **discontinued effective June 20, 2026** and **merged into the single utility for Para B events**. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that, from that date, these disclosures are routed through the updated single filing/API-based integration workflow and that the 24-hour XBRL follow-up requirement is met after any PDF submission.

rows.summary:
This NSE circular (NSE/CML/2026/16 dated June 12, 2026) is addressed to all listed entities and provides FAQs for submitting the quarterly Integrated Filing – Governance, formerly called the Corporate Governance Report. NSE states that the FAQs are for guidance only and do not replace or amend the underlying requirements in law, SEBI regulations, or exchange circulars, but listed entities are specifically instructed to take note and comply accordingly.

The key compliance deadline confirmed in the FAQs is that the Integrated Filing – Governance report must be filed within 30 days from the end of each quarter, consistent with Regulation 27(2) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations. For newly listed entities, the filing obligation begins from the quarter ending immediately after the date of listing, so the first report is not due for the listing quarter itself but for the next quarter-end reporting period.

The document also makes clear that the filing must be submitted through the XBRL utility, and it covers the governance reporting format in detail across board composition, committee composition, board meetings, committee meetings, and “other” disclosures, as well as quarterly disclosures under Schedule III of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. Although the extract shown does not include the detailed answers for each topic, the circular signals that listed entities must use the FAQ framework to ensure their quarterly governance filing is completed correctly in the prescribed electronic format and within the statutory deadline.

The portion of the FAQs visible in the excerpt does not yet state any new substantive thresholds, ratios, or special exemptions, but it does emphasize that the filing obligation applies to listed entities generally and that the guidance should be read alongside the existing SEBI/LODR and exchange filing framework. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as an operational reminder and process guidance document, not as a replacement for the governing regulations, and should continue to ensure timely quarterly governance filings starting from the first quarter after listing.

rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/15 Date: June 01, 2026 To All Listed Companies, Sub: Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 54L of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Attention is invited to the provisions relating to Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (“PPIRP”) under Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”). In this regard, as advised by SEBI, it is clarified that, the exemptions available under various SEBI Regulations in respect of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 31 of the IBC are not available in case of a Resolution Plan approved under Section 54L of the IBC under the PPIRP framework. Accordingly, listed entities undergoing PPIRP shall be required to comply with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements prescribed under the relevant SEBI Regulations. The listed companies are advised to take note of the above and ensure compliance of the same. For and on behalf of National Stock Exchange of India Limited Yukti Sharma Head - Listing
rows.summary:
The NSE’s circular dated **June 1, 2026** clarifies how **Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP)** cases under **Section 54L / Chapter III-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)** are to be treated for listed companies. SEBI has advised that the **regulatory exemptions that are available when a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC do not apply** if the plan is approved under the **PPIRP framework under Section 54L**.

For compliance purposes, this means that a **listed entity undergoing PPIRP must continue to comply with all applicable procedural and regulatory requirements under the relevant SEBI Regulations**; it cannot assume that the usual listing-regulation exemptions linked to Section 31-approved resolution plans will be available. The circular does not create a new deadline or filing format, but it is an immediate compliance clarification for **all listed companies** that may enter PPIRP. Listed companies are specifically advised to take note and ensure they meet the full set of obligations under the applicable SEBI framework during PPIRP.

rows.summary:
The NSE has updated its **single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges** by expanding the **XBRL filing** functionality to additional disclosure events, effective **May 29, 2026** for most items listed in the circular. This update is issued under **Circular Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/14 dated May 29, 2026**, and it refers back to the earlier framework in **NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024**. The practical compliance change is that eligible listed entities can now use the single filing/API-based exchange integration for these disclosures rather than filing separately across exchanges, subject to the applicability shown by category of listed entity.

For **Schedule of analysts or institutional investors meet, investor presentation, transcripts, and audio/video recordings** required under **Regulation 30 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 read with sub-para 15 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**, the API-based single filing system is available from **May 29, 2026** and applies to **only equity** and **equity + debt** listed companies, but not to **exclusively debt** entities or **REITs/InvITs**. The same effective date and applicability applies to disclosures of **actions initiated or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority, or judicial body** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 19 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**, and **actions taken or orders passed by any regulatory, statutory, enforcement authority, or judicial body** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 20 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**; these are available for **only equity** and **equity + debt** companies, but not for **exclusively debt** entities or **REITs/InvITs**.

The circular also states that **Initiation of forensic audit** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 17 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III** has been enabled through the single filing system with effect from **May 5, 2026**, again applicable only to **equity** and **equity + debt** listed companies. In addition, **Prohibition of Insider Trading** disclosures under **Regulation 7(2) and 7(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015** are available through the same API-based filing system from **May 5, 2026**, and this row shows applicability to **only equity**, **equity + debt**, and **REITs/InvITs**, but not to **exclusively debt** listed entities.

The table in the circular also begins to list **Outcome of Board Meeting for Dividend, Buyback, Bonus and Voluntary Delisting events**, indicating this disclosure is part of the expanded API-based single filing framework as well, though the excerpt provided cuts off before the full applicability matrix and effective-date details are visible. For compliance teams, the key operational point is that listed entities must now route the above covered disclosures through the **single filing/API integration between exchanges** as soon as the relevant effective date applies, and confirm whether their entity type falls within the permitted categories for each disclosure type.

rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has discontinued the old NEAPS submission path for insider trading disclosures under Regulation 7(2) and Regulation 7(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. Going forward, all listed companies, REITs, and InvITs must file these disclosures only in XBRL format using the new process: the XBRL utility is to be downloaded through **NEAPS → Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities**, and the disclosures are to be submitted through **NEAPS → Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → Prohibition of Insider Trading**. rows.title: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: National Stock Exchange of India Circular Department: Listing Circular Ref. No.: NSE/CML/2026/13 Date: May 04, 2026 To, The Company Secretary, All Listed Entities/Intermediaries/Fiduciaries Subject: XBRL based filing for Violations related to Code of Conduct (CoC) under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 SEBI vide Circular No. SEBI/HO/ISD/ISD/CIR/P/2020/135 dated July 23, 2020, prescribed the format for reporting violations of the Code of Conduct under SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. To enhance accuracy and efficiency in disclosures, the Exchange has introduced an XBRL utility for reporting such violations through NEAPS with effect from May 05, 2026. All Listed Companies/Intermediaries/Fiduciaries shall submit the reporting through the following paths: To download XBRL utility: NEAPS  Compliance  Download XBRL Utilities For Submissions: NEAPS  Compliance  Common XBRL Upload  Violation of Code of Conduct under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 It may be noted that reporting by listed entities shall be made only in XBRL mode without submission of any PDF. Further, any unlisted entity reporting in the capacity of Intermediary or Fiduciary shall continue to submit the disclosures through email at pit_coc@nse.co.in, as per Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2020/44 dated August 26, 2020. The disclosure pertaining to violations of the Code of Conduct shall not be disseminated on the Exchange website. All listed entities are advised to mandatorily submit the reporting through NEAPS only. Submission through any other mode shall not be taken on record and shall be considered invalid. Listed entities, Intermediaries and Fiduciaries are advised to take note of the above and comply accordingly. Yours faithfully, For National Stock Exchange of India Limited Harshad Dharod Chief Manager-Listing Compliance
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India has introduced a new XBRL-based filing process for reporting violations of the Code of Conduct under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. This change is based on SEBI’s earlier circular dated July 23, 2020, which had prescribed the reporting format for Code of Conduct violations, but the NSE circular now requires use of an XBRL utility to improve accuracy and efficiency.

The new process is effective from May 05, 2026. From that date onward, all listed companies, intermediaries, and fiduciaries must use the NEAPS platform to submit these violation reports, with the utility downloadable through NEAPS under Compliance → Download XBRL Utilities and submissions made through Compliance → Common XBRL Upload → “Violation of Code of Conduct under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015.” For listed entities specifically, the filing must be made only in XBRL mode and must not be accompanied by any PDF submission. Any submission by a listed entity through a channel other than NEAPS/XBRL will not be taken on record and will be treated as invalid.

The circular preserves the existing treatment for unlisted entities that are reporting in the capacity of intermediaries or fiduciaries: they must continue to send the disclosures by email to pit_coc@nse.co.in, as required under NSE Circular No. NSE/CML/2020/44 dated August 26, 2020. The circular also states that disclosures relating to Code of Conduct violations will not be disseminated on the Exchange website. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that listed entities switch to mandatory NEAPS XBRL filing immediately from the effective date, while unlisted intermediaries/fiduciaries continue using the email route.

NSE has updated its **single filing system through API-based integration between stock exchanges**, expanding the scope of disclosures that can be filed once and then shared across exchanges. This update is issued under **Circular Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/08 dated April 20, 2026**, and it references the earlier framework from **NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024**.

The main change is that, **with effect from April 20, 2026**, the single filing system now also applies to **XBRL filings for Annual Report filings under Regulation 34 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. The circular indicates that this facility is available for **listed entities that are Equity and Equity+Debt listed companies**, and it is **not available** for **Exclusively Debt**, **REITs**, or **InvITs** for this disclosure. The circular specifically marks the Annual Report-XBRL item as applicable from **April 20, 2026**.

The circular also states that the API-based single filing system is available for certain **Regulation 30 LODR disclosures**, including disclosures relating to **acquisition, amalgamation, merger, de-merger, sale or disposal, or other restructuring** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 1 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**. It further covers disclosures for **changes in directors, key managerial personnel such as the Managing Director, Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Company Secretary, and other senior management, as well as changes in the auditor, compliance officer, and registrar to an issue and share transfer agent** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-paras 7 and 8 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**.

For resignation-related filings, the circular notes that the utility now provides an option to submit both the **resignation details and the resignation letter(s)** where required under **sub-paras 7A, 7B, and 7C of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**. It also expressly includes **resignation of the statutory auditor** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-para 7A**, and **resignation of an independent director, director, KMP, SMP, or compliance officer** under **Regulation 30 read with sub-paras 7B and 7C**. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to use the updated filing utility for the above covered events from the effective date, and ensure the correct supporting resignation documents are uploaded wherever the regulation requires them.

This circular is a forwarding notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. dated April 10, 2026, addressed to all listed entities, informing them of a SEBI circular dated April 08, 2026 titled “Ease of doing business - mechanism for lock-in of pledged shares under SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018.” The NSE letter itself does not set out the substantive rule changes; it says the SEBI circular is enclosed for reference and necessary action, and is also available on the NSE website.

From a compliance perspective, the key point is that SEBI has issued a new mechanism concerning the lock-in of pledged shares under the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018. Because the notice is addressed to all listed entities, companies with listed securities should review whether the SEBI circular affects their lock-in obligations, especially where shares subject to statutory lock-in are also pledged. The NSE communication does not specify any numerical thresholds, compliance deadlines, or transition dates beyond the circular date itself (April 08, 2026), so any actual operational requirements, process changes, or filing obligations would need to be taken from the enclosed SEBI circular. The practical action for a compliance team is to obtain and review the SEBI circular immediately, assess any impact on promoter/other locked-in share pledges and transfer restrictions, and update internal procedures and stakeholder instructions accordingly.

The NSE letter itself does not set out the detailed relief mechanics, thresholds, or timelines; it only references SEBI Circular No. HO/49/14/14(13)2026-CFD-POD2/I/8772/2026 dated April 7, 2026, and states that the circular is enclosed and also available on the NSE website. The affected population is all listed entities, specifically those that have not met the MPS requirement under the LODR Regulations. There are no standalone compliance deadlines, numeric thresholds, or filing dates stated in this NSE covering communication beyond the fact that the SEBI circular is dated April 7, 2026. For compliance purposes, the key action is to obtain and analyze the underlying SEBI circular immediately, since this letter serves as notice that the relaxation is in force and may affect current or planned MPS compliance actions.

The circular updates the NSE’s “single filing system” implemented through API-based integration between stock exchanges, expanding the types of XBRL/disclosure filings that can be filed once and then shared across exchanges. This update is issued by NSE Circular Ref. No. NSE/CML/2026/05 dated March 30, 2026, and it references the earlier circular NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024.

The main change is that, effective March 31, 2026, the single-filing API system is extended to cover the XBRL filing for the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) under Regulation 34(2)(f) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. The circular indicates this filing is available for listed entities that are equity-only and equity-plus-debt listed companies; it is not marked as available for exclusively debt listed entities, REITs, or INVITs.

The circular also lists other disclosures that are already covered or have specific effective dates within the single-filing framework, including prior intimation of board meetings under Regulation 29 of SEBI (LODR), effective March 7, 2026; closure of trading window under the SEBI PIT Regulations; fraud/default/arrest disclosures under Regulation 30 and Para A Part A Schedule III of SEBI (LODR), effective February 21, 2026; corporate debt restructuring disclosures; resolution plans/restructuring involving bank/financial institution borrowings, including Inter-Creditors Agreement and one-time settlement (OTS); and Issue Summary Document (ISD) filings for buybacks through open and tender routes under the relevant SEBI circular. The table shows these are applicable to equity and equity-plus-debt listed entities, while the debt-only, REIT, and INVIT columns remain unmarked for these items.

For integrated filing of financials under Regulations 23(9), 30 read with Section V-B of the Master Circular, and Regulations 32(1) and 33(3), the circular shows an effective date of January 3, 2026 for equity and equity-plus-debt listed entities, but states that applicability for exclusively debt listed entities and REITs/INVITs “shall be communicated later.” The table also includes “Annual Secretarial Compliance Report” as an item in the sequence of filings covered by the single filing system, but the excerpt provided cuts off before showing the full applicability/effective-date details for that line.

From a compliance perspective, listed entities should confirm whether they fall into the equity, equity-plus-debt, debt-only, or REIT/INVIT category before relying on the API-based single filing process. Entities that are in scope for the newly extended BRSR filing should begin using the single-filing mechanism for that disclosure from March 31, 2026, while continuing to track any separate exchange or regulatory instructions for categories that are not yet marked as covered.

This circular updates the existing “single filing system” created under Exchange Circular No. NSE/CML/2024/28 dated September 30, 2024 by extending the API-based, single-filing/XBRL integration to additional disclosure types for listed entities. The Exchange states that, with effect from **March 07, 2026**, the single filing system will now also be available for **XBRL filings** relating to **Prior Intimation for Board Meeting under Regulation 29 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. The table in the circular also shows that the following disclosure categories are now within the single-filing/API framework for the relevant classes of listed entities: **Closure of Trading Window** under the SEBI PIT Regulations; **Fraud/Default/Arrest** disclosures under **Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR** and **sub-para 6 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**; **Corporate Debt Restructuring** under **Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR** and **sub-paras 9 and 10 of Para A, Part A of Schedule III**; **Resolution plan / restructuring in relation to loans or borrowings from banks/financial institutions (including Inter-Creditors Agreement) and One Time Settlement (OTS)**; and **Issue Summary Document (ISD)** for **buyback through open and tender route** under the SEBI circular on ISD and issue advertisements.

The circular specifies that the applicability of these filings varies by issuer type. The table indicates that the single-filing system is available for **Equity-listed entities** and **Equity + Debt listed entities**, while the columns for **Exclusively Debt** and **REITs and INVITs** are marked as not applicable for the disclosed items shown. For some disclosure categories, the table already shows earlier effective dates: **Fraud/Default/Arrest** is marked effective **February 21, 2026**, **Integrated Filing – Financials** is marked effective **January 03, 2026**, and **Annual Secretarial Compliance Report** is marked effective **September 15, 2025**. The table also indicates that for certain categories shown, applicability for “Exclusively Debt” and “REITs and INVITs” will be **“communicated later,”** so those entities should not assume coverage unless and until a separate communication is issued.

From a compliance perspective, the practical change is that listed entities covered by the relevant rows should route the specified disclosures through the Exchange’s **API-based single filing system/XBRL mechanism** rather than treating stock exchange submissions separately, subject to the exact category and entity type. Companies secretaries and disclosure teams should align internal calendars and filing workflows to the stated effective date of **March 07, 2026** for the newly extended items and confirm whether any earlier-effective items already need to be in the single-filing process. The circular does not introduce monetary thresholds, rates, or penalties; its core requirement is procedural integration of filings across stock exchanges for the covered disclosure categories.
