The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Bima Vahak) Guidelines, 2023** on **9 October 2023** under **Section 14(2)(e) of the IRDAI Act, 1999**. The guidelines are intended to create a **women-centric distribution channel** to expand insurance awareness and inclusion at the **village/Gram Panchayat** level, with the stated policy goal of improving access to insurance across India’s rural and local markets. The document also says the channel is meant to identify and develop **local resources who understand local needs and are trusted by the community**.

These guidelines define **“Bima Vahak”** as either an **individual** (“Individual Bima Vahak”) or a **legal person** (“Corporate Bima Vahak”) registered under Indian law and engaged to provide services under the guidelines. Insurers are permitted to use this channel for **solicitation of insurance business** and to help with **policy servicing and claims servicing**. Specifically, an insurer may **engage a Corporate Bima Vahak** and/or **directly appoint Individual Bima Vahaks**; the excerpt indicates the insurer’s appointment/engagement framework is the central compliance mechanism for deploying this distribution model.

The guidelines are named as above and are stated to **come into force from the date of launch of “Bima Vistaar”**, which the document describes as a **comprehensive insurance product to be issued in due course**. That means the operative start date is not a fixed calendar date in the excerpt, but is tied to the launch of Bima Vistaar. For compliance purposes, the key trigger is that insurers should treat these rules as pending until that launch date, then ensure any Bima Vahak engagement is structured in line with the guidelines.

In practical terms, compliance teams at insurers should note that the regime is aimed at a **dedicated women-focused rural distribution structure**, and that any use of Bima Vahaks is tied to both **sales solicitation** and **service/claims support**, not just acquisition. The excerpt does not yet provide further operational thresholds, licensing criteria, compensation rules, training requirements, or reporting obligations, but it clearly establishes the permitted channel, the kinds of entities that can be engaged, the intended social objective, and the effective-date trigger tied to Bima Vistaar.

A key transition rule is that entities that have **already completed the security audit for FY 2022–23** do **not** have to retrofit that year; instead, they must begin complying with the new guidelines **from the next financial year**. The circular also makes clear that prior IRDAI cyber-security circulars are being superseded/updated by this framework, including the earlier **2017 insurer guideline**, the **29 December 2020** circular, the **2 September 2022** intermediary extension, and another **11 October 2022** reference noted in the text. For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to treat this as a sector-wide revised cyber-security mandate and verify that the organization falls within the covered entity types, then map existing controls and governance against the detailed requirements in the annexure.

This IRDAI guideline, issued on 31 March 2023 under sub-regulation (3) of Regulation 13 of the IRDAI (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, 2019, sets the operating process for running innovation proposals in insurance through the Regulatory Sandbox. It applies to any applicant seeking to promote or implement an insurance innovation in India and requires the applicant to submit its request in **Form RG-1**, under one or more of the categories permitted by **Regulation 4** of the 2019 Sandbox Regulations.  

A key substantive requirement is that the applicant must show IRDAI that the proposal will **increase insurance penetration** or **provide enhanced services to policyholders**; IRDAI will not entertain proposals that are merely seeking regulatory relaxation without being a genuine innovation. The guideline also states that the **Chairperson’s decision** on whether a proposal qualifies as innovative is **final**, so there is no internal appeal or reconsideration mechanism specified in the document.  

For application handling, the applicant must appoint an **experienced and responsible Single Point of Contact (SPOC)** to interface with IRDAI on the submission, and IRDAI will in turn nominate its own SPOC to coordinate with the applicant and facilitate guidance/communication during the sandbox process. The document is focused on process rather than substantive sandbox eligibility thresholds, and the excerpt provided does not include any numerical caps, fees, or timeline deadlines beyond the issuance date; however, compliance teams should note that the guideline formalizes the expectation of a documented application, a business justification tied to policyholder benefit or penetration, and a dedicated contact person on both sides.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on **28 September 2022** to address **conflicts of interest arising from common directorship** among registered **intermediaries and insurance intermediaries**, particularly where the Authority receives more than one application from entities in the same **group** for a Certificate of Registration (CoR). The guidance applies both where IRDAI has granted or is granting CoR to **more than one entity within the same group** to act as an intermediary/insurance intermediary, and where **common directors are existing or being appointed** either within the same group or across different groups.

The first substantive requirement is that the **maximum number of directorships must not exceed the limits in Section 165 of the Companies Act, 2013**. Where common directors are present, the intermediary/insurance intermediary must implement a **Board-approved policy** specifically to manage and review **related party transactions**, with “related party” understood as defined in **Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013**. All related party transactions involving the intermediary/insurance intermediary must comply with **Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013** and **Accounting Standard AS 18**.

The document also imposes a certification obligation on the statutory auditor: the auditor must **certify compliance with Section 188** of the Companies Act, 2013 **to IRDAI**, and this certification is stated to be required **as at the end of the financial year** (the text provided cuts off after “as at the,” but the evident requirement is annual year-end certification). In practical compliance terms, any intermediary or insurance intermediary with common directors—whether within the same corporate group or across groups—should review directorship limits, establish or update related-party governance procedures, ensure transaction-level compliance under Section 188/AS 18, and be prepared for statutory auditor certification to IRDAI.

The guidelines are addressed to the **Chairman-cum-Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of all general insurance companies**, **except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd**, and are intended to regulate and promote the sustainable development of surety insurance in India. The Authority states that the guidelines were issued under its powers under **section 14(2)(i) of the IRDA Act, 1999**, and they were also posted on the IRDAI website.

The core applicability rule is that **all insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to carry on general insurance business may transact surety insurance only if they satisfy the eligibility criteria in these guidelines**. In addition, **after the commencement date, no person may transact surety insurance in India unless that person is an “Indian Insurance Company” as defined in section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. This means the business is restricted to qualifying Indian insurers, and compliance teams at general insurers need to confirm both their legal status and their eligibility against the IRDAI criteria before offering these products.

rows.summary:

The document explains that trade credit insurance protects businesses against **non-payment for goods and services** by buyers, typically covering a **portfolio of buyers** and indemnifying an agreed percentage of unpaid invoices where non-payment results from **protracted default, insolvency, or bankruptcy**. IRDAI says the revised framework is intended to support the **sustainable and healthy development** of the trade credit insurance market, to allow insurers to provide cover not only to suppliers but also to **licensed banks and other financial institutions** for trade-financing-related non-payment and country risk, and to enable **customised covers for SMEs and MSMEs** in line with evolving market needs.

For compliance purposes, the immediate action point is that any general insurer writing, planning to write, or modifying trade credit insurance business must align its products and underwriting approach with the revised IRDAI framework effective **1 November 2021**. rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on 5 May 2021 to all general insurers and health insurers to create a **Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product (SDTIP)** with **uniform mandatory coverage** across the market, so customers can more easily compare and select a basic domestic travel policy. The product must include only the **basic mandatory covers specified in the guidelines**, and insurers may offer **only the optional covers expressly permitted** by the guidelines; insurers are allowed to set the premium, but only in compliance with the IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016 and the framework in these guidelines. The stated policy objective is to make domestic travel financially secure against unforeseen contingencies and to address the difficulty consumers face because existing travel insurance products differ widely in features.

For compliance teams, the key requirement is that any SDTIP marketed or filed must strictly follow the standard terms, conditions, and coverage structure laid out by IRDAI, with no deviation from the mandated base cover except where the guidelines expressly allow optional add-ons. The document also includes annexed materials that are part of the compliance package: the **Policy Terms and Conditions**, the **Customer Information Sheet format**, and the **form for filing the Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product**. In practice, this means insurers need to ensure product design, policy wording, disclosures, and filing documents match the prescribed standard format before offering the product. The circular is addressed to both **general insurers and health insurers**, so it applies to any insurer intending to distribute domestic travel insurance under this standard product framework.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) on 31 March 2021 as Ref. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees In the course of discharging of NFRA’s statutory functions, it has been noticed that there is a need to strengthen the communications between Statutory Auditors (Auditors), Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), including Audit Committees (ACs), in line with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013), the Standards on Auditing (SAs) prescribed under CA 2013, and other relevant Rules and Regulations. 2. Provisions of CA 2013 and other Relevant Rules: The CA 2013 has placed certain important obligations on the Board of Directors (BOD or the ‘Board’), Independent Directors (IDs), Audit Committees and Statutory Auditors of Companies in respect of Accounts and Audit of Companies. 2.1 Board of Directors: Section 134 of CA 2013 and related Rules require that the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statements, if any, be approved by the Board of Directors. A report by the Board shall be attached to the financial statements, which shall include, inter alia, an important statement called Directors’ Responsibility Statement. According to sub-section 5 of Section 134, this statement shall disclose the Board’s assertions regarding certain critical aspects, such as adherence to applicable accounting standards; selection and application of accounting policies and making of judgements/estimates on reasonable and prudent basis; maintenance of adequate records for safeguarding the assets of the company and preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; preparation of accounts on a going concern basis; implementation of adequate
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 07.01.2026, is addressed to all listed companies, companies and bodies corporate covered under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the statutory auditors of those entities. It does not create a new standalone legal regime, but signals NFRA’s expectation that communication between statutory auditors and those charged with governance (TCWG), including audit committees, be materially strengthened and brought into closer alignment with the Companies Act, 2013, the Standards on Auditing under that Act, and related rules and regulations.

The circular explains that the Companies Act, 2013 already imposes key responsibilities on the board of directors, independent directors, audit committees, and auditors in relation to financial statements and audit. It specifically highlights Section 134, under which the board must approve the financial statements, including consolidated financial statements where applicable, and attach a board’s report that includes the Directors’ Responsibility Statement. That statement must cover the board’s assertions that applicable accounting standards have been followed; accounting policies have been selected and applied with reasonable and prudent judgment/estimates; adequate records are maintained to safeguard assets and prevent and detect fraud and other irregularities; the accounts have been prepared on a going-concern basis; and adequate internal financial controls are in place and operating effectively.

The compliance message is that auditors and governance bodies must treat these statutory obligations as requiring more effective and timely two-way communication during the audit and financial reporting process, particularly with the audit committee. While the excerpt provided does not yet set out any new numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, or penalties, it clearly indicates NFRA has observed deficiencies in current practice and is issuing the circular to reinforce existing statutory and audit-standard-based communication requirements. Compliance teams should therefore expect a heightened supervisory expectation that management, the board, audit committees, and auditors actively exchange information on matters affecting financial statements, internal controls, and audit findings, rather than treating audit committee interaction as merely formal or periodic.

Complex group structures including special purpose vehicles, auto pilot structures, cross holdings of interests across group entities and shared servi
rows.summary:
The NFRA’s circular dated 3 October 2024 addresses the responsibilities of the principal auditor and other auditors in group audits for entities covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018. It reiterates that statutory audits of both standalone financial statements and consolidated financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013 must comply with the Standards on Auditing, the Standard on Quality Control, and the Code of Ethics, including independence requirements. The circular explains that audits of group financial statements—such as audits of companies with branches, subsidiaries, associates, and other components—require special attention because the principal auditor remains ultimately responsible for the group audit opinion, even where component work is performed by other auditors, and that SA 600 governs the use of another auditor’s work.

The document’s central point is that group audits often involve material or significant-risk areas because of modern group structures and business arrangements. It specifically notes complex structures such as special purpose vehicles, “auto pilot” structures, cross-holdings, and shared-services arrangements as examples of the kinds of group features that can make audit risk higher and component reliance more difficult. The circular is therefore aimed at ensuring that auditors treat group audits as a heightened compliance and audit-quality area, with the principal auditor actively managing and overseeing the work of other auditors rather than merely relying on their reports.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that audit teams involved in group audits must ensure full adherence to the applicable auditing framework, with documented compliance to the quality-control standards, the 35 standards on auditing, and ethical/independence requirements. The circular is directed to auditors of entities under NFRA’s jurisdiction and is intended to reinforce the existing legal and professional duties in group audit engagements, especially where the work of component auditors is used in forming the final group opinion. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or new reporting forms are set out in the excerpt provided, but the effective date of the circular itself is 3 October 2024.

rows.title: NFRA circular on Statutory Auditors’ responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company
rows.desc: / Government of India / National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25013/2/2023 Dated 26.06.2023 Circular To 1. Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies
rows.summary:
The NFRA has issued this circular because it has observed that statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated entities are not consistently carrying out their legal duties to report fraud, or suspected fraud, as required under the Companies Act, 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO), and the applicable Standards on Auditing. The circular is addressed to auditors of entities regulated by NFRA and reiterates that these reporting duties are mandatory, not discretionary.  

For fraud involving a company’s officers or employees, section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires an auditor who, in the course of audit work, has reason to believe that a fraud offence has been or is being committed to report the matter to the Central Government within the prescribed time and in the prescribed manner. Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 specifies the process where the suspected or actual fraud involves, or is expected to involve, an amount of **₹1 crore or more**: the auditor must report first to the **Board or Audit Committee** and also report to the **Central Government** in **Form ADT-4**.  

The circular also points auditors to the separate reporting obligation under **Clause (xi)** of the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, which requires disclosure of fraud and suspected fraud matters in the auditor’s reporting. In substance, NFRA is reminding auditors that fraud-related reporting must be completed through the correct statutory channels, using the prescribed form and process, whenever the threshold and legal test under the rules are met.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that auditors of NFRA-regulated entities must ensure they have procedures to identify, document, escalate, and report any fraud or suspected fraud meeting the statutory threshold, and they must not limit themselves to internal reporting alone. The circular signals NFRA scrutiny of auditor non-compliance in this area and reinforces that failure to report as required under section 143(12), Rule 13, CARO, and the SAs may constitute a breach of statutory audit responsibilities.

rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 29 March 2023, is addressed to all listed companies, unlisted companies covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the auditors of those companies. It states that, in exercising NFRA’s statutory mandate under section 132(2)(b) and 132(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(g) of the NFRA Rules, NFRA has identified apparent non-compliance in recent financial statement reviews in two linked areas: revenue recognition/measurement and the initial measurement of the related trade receivables.

The circular specifically flags compliance issues under Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, beginning with paragraph 46, which requires revenue to be recognized at the transaction price, excluding estimated variable consideration until the amount can be reliably determined in accordance with the standard. NFRA says these are critical areas because they affect both how revenue is measured and how the corresponding receivables are initially recorded, and it highlights the concern to the company’s management, audit committee, and statutory auditors for urgent attention. The document makes clear that the issue is not a general accounting reminder but a warning based on NFRA’s review findings that some companies are not following the prescribed Ind AS requirements.

For compliance purposes, the affected population is broad: every listed company and every unlisted company that falls within NFRA Rule 3 is expected to ensure its revenue policies, estimates, and trade receivables accounting are fully consistent with Ind AS 115. The circular does not introduce a new quantitative threshold, fee, or deadline, but it does require immediate review of existing accounting policies and practices, especially around transaction price determination, treatment of variable consideration, and the measurement of receivables arising from customer contracts. Management, audit committees, and statutory auditors should treat the circular as a prompt to verify that the company’s Ind AS 115 policy documentation, estimates, and financial statement presentation are compliant and supportable under the standard.

The order is issued under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11(6) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and it concerns NFRA’s suo motu examination of the auditor’s professional conduct in relation to a public interest entity.  

The order states that although the auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on both the financial statements and the internal financial controls over financial reporting for FY 2017–18, he nevertheless failed in key audit responsibilities. NFRA found that he did not exercise due diligence and acted with gross negligence in meeting his obligation to identify and report fraud under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and SA 240, despite there being several indicators of fraud. NFRA also concluded that he failed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in the course of the audit.  

For a compliance team, the practical significance is that the order reinforces that a disclaimer of opinion does not relieve an engagement partner of the duty to perform fraud-risk procedures, respond appropriately to fraud indicators, or gather sufficient appropriate evidence before concluding an audit. It also shows that NFRA is actively using its powers to scrutinize auditors’ conduct in prior-period audits of public interest entities, and that failures tied to fraud reporting and audit evidence can be treated as serious professional misconduct. The excerpt provided does not include the final penalty or sanctions section, so any monetary penalty, debarment period, or other disciplinary consequence is not visible in the supplied text.

rows.desc: SA 600 (REVISED) Request for Public Comments by 30.10.2024 (Refer accompanying note on NFRA website) SA 600 (Revised), SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS—AUDITS OF GROUP FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (INCLUDING THE WORK OF COMPONENT AUDITORS) (Applicable to PIEs under Rule 3 of NFRA Rules 2018 except PSUs, PSBs and PSIs and their branches) Introduction Scope of this SA 1. The Standards on Auditing (SAs) apply to an audit of group financial statements (a group audit). This SA deals with special considerations that apply to a group audit, including in those circumstances when component auditors are involved. The requirements and guidance in this SA refer to, or expand on, the application of other relevant SAs to a group audit, in particular SA 220 (Revised), 1 SA 230, 2 SA 300, 3 SA 315 (Revised), 4 and SA 330. 5 (Ref: Para. A1–A2) 2. Group financial statements include the financial information of more than one entity or business unit through a consolidation process, as described in paragraph 14(k). The term consolidation process as used in this SA refers not only to the preparation of consolidated financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, but also to the presentation of combined financial statements, and to the aggregation of the financial information of entities or business units such as branches or divisions. (Ref: Para. A3–A5, A27) 3. Groups and Components 4. A group may be organized in various ways. For example, a group may be organized by legal or other entities (e.g., a parent and one or mor
rows.summary:
NFRA has issued a draft revision of SA 600, “Special Considerations—Audits of Group Financial Statements (Including the Work of Component Auditors),” for public comment, with comments due by 30.10.2024. The draft applies to audits of group financial statements for PIEs under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, but specifically excludes PSUs, PSBs, PSIs, and their branches. The standard explains that group financial statements cover more than one entity or business unit brought together through a consolidation process, and that this includes not only consolidated financial statements under the relevant reporting framework but also combined financial statements and aggregation of information from branches, divisions, or similar units.

The revised SA 600 is intended to address the special risks and responsibilities that arise in group audits, especially where component auditors are involved. It cross-references and builds on other auditing standards, particularly SA 220 (Revised), SA 230, SA 300, SA 315 (Revised), and SA 330, meaning group audit teams must apply those standards with the additional requirements in SA 600. The document also notes that the guidance may be useful outside a formal group audit when the engagement team includes individuals from another firm—for example, for attending physical inventory counts, inspecting property, plant and equipment, or performing procedures at a remote shared service center.

For compliance teams, the immediate action item is the consultation deadline: public comments must be submitted by 30 October 2024. Substantively, the draft signals heightened focus on how group structures are organized and how auditors evaluate and coordinate work across components, so affected PIEs should expect tighter scrutiny over consolidation structures, the involvement of component auditors, and audit planning and supervision in group engagements.

rows.summary:
NFRA is seeking public comments on a proposed revision to Standard on Auditing 600 (SA 600), titled **“Special Considerations—Audits of Group Financial Statements (Including the Work of Component Auditors)”**. The proposed revised standard would apply to **audits of Public Interest Entities (PIEs) covered under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018**, but **does not apply** to **Public Sector Enterprises, Public Sector Banks, Public Sector Insurance Entities, or their respective branches**. NFRA is asking commenters to review all aspects of the proposal, and especially to respond to the specific questions in the consultation note; it requests that comments clearly identify the issue being addressed, include supporting data and rationale where possible, and, if disagreeing with any proposal, provide an alternative approach with reasoning and evidence.

The document sets a **comment deadline of 30 October 2024**. Comments may be submitted by email to **nfra-comments@nfra.gov.in** or by post to the **Secretary, National Financial Reporting Authority, 7th-8th Floor, Hindustan Times House, 18-20, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi 110001**. In both email and postal submissions, commenters should use the caption **“Comments on proposed SA 600 (Revised)”** for ease of reference.

A draft of the proposed revised SA 600 is available via the linked PDF provided in the notice. The notice also states that the consultation includes the **background and rationale** for the proposed changes, indicating that NFRA is not only soliciting line-by-line feedback but also broader input on the policy reasons for revising the standard. rows.title: Annual Transparency Report by Statutory Auditors of PIEs-Invitation for public comment
rows.desc: / Government of India � � � � � � � /National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi Dated: 16.01.2023 Invitation for Comment To Statutory Auditors of the NFRA Regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) Subject: Publication of Annual Transparency Reports (ATR) by Auditors/Audit Firms Auditors have a critical role in the financial reporting supply chain of PIEs. Audit of financial reports of PIEs by Independent Auditor enhances the credibility and integrity of the general purpose financial reports of PIEs. Therefore, the need for high-quality comprehensive financial information covering both financial and non-financial aspects of PIEs cannot be overemphasised. 2. Regulators have been prescribing obligations for PIEs to provide high-quality comprehensive financial and non-financial information commensurate with the nature, size and complexity of their operations to the various stakeholders. The role and responsibilities of the independent auditors of such entities have also evolved significantly with focus on the need to build commensurate professional and operating capabilities within the auditing profession. Audit professionals have been augmenting their capabilities and resources including building a network or alliances of firms, domestically and globally, developing in-house multi-disciplinary professionals or professional units, delivering variety of non-audit services, increasing use of digital audit tools and techniques, separating management and governance structures and so on. 3. In this backdrop, Regulators and Oversight Authorities in some overseas jurisdictions 1 require audit firms carrying out audit of PIEs to prepare and publish information in the form of Transparency Reports on annual basis. Accordingly, the audit firms in those jurisdictions have been publishing the Transparency Reports 2 4. Indian companies have become significant constituents of the global economy and India has evolved
rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued an invitation for public comment dated 16 January 2023 to statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) on the proposal to require publication of Annual Transparency Reports (ATR) by auditors/audit firms. The notice explains that because auditors of PIEs play a critical role in the financial reporting supply chain, and because audit quality increasingly depends on robust professional and operational capabilities, regulators in some overseas jurisdictions already require audit firms auditing PIEs to prepare and publish annual transparency reports. NFRA notes that Indian companies are now important participants in the global economy and implies that Indian audit firms and PIEs should align with higher transparency expectations seen internationally.  

The document is a consultation notice rather than a final rule, so it does not itself create an enforceable compliance obligation or set a specific effective date, deadline, filing format, or threshold in the text provided. However, the subject matter makes clear that the contemplated requirement would affect statutory auditors and audit firms serving NFRA-regulated PIEs, and would likely require them to disclose information annually about their firm’s capabilities, resources, governance, quality-related arrangements, and possibly other transparency information comparable to overseas ATR regimes. Compliance teams at affected audit firms should treat this as an early policy signal that public annual disclosure obligations for PIE auditors may be introduced, and should monitor NFRA’s next consultation or final issuance for the precise content, timing, and scope of any mandatory ATR requirement.

rows.summary:
This document is a **Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)** from the **National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)** dated **28.09.2021** to the **Secretary, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)** regarding **ICAI’s recommendations for revising the existing Accounting Standards under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013**. It records that ICAI had submitted an Approach Paper and draft revised texts for **18 revised Accounting Standards**, as part of a broader project expected to result in **32 revised Accounting Standards** in total, intended for companies **not required to follow Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**. NFRA notes the historical context: the revision project was developed after Ind AS implementation for certain classes of companies, and ICAI’s 2020 revision of its 2014–15 approach paper reflects the view that accounting recognition and measurement should, as far as possible, be broadly the same across companies.

The core compliance point is that the **revised ASs will apply to companies for which Ind AS is not mandatory**, meaning the regime will cover a **large number of Micro, Small and Medium-size Companies (MSMCs)** and will **replace the existing Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules**. NFRA emphasizes that this is not a minor technical update: because these standards are intended for a very large non-Ind AS population, the revision could have a **significant economic and administrative impact** on affected entities. The letter indicates NFRA is evaluating ICAI’s recommendations in light of that broad impact, especially because the changes would govern financial reporting for companies outside the Ind AS framework.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that organizations **not currently on Ind AS** should monitor the final outcome of this standards-revision exercise, because their accounting and reporting policies may need to change once the revised ASs are notified. The document itself does **not** set a new effective date, transition date, or threshold numbers for application in this excerpt, but it clearly signals that the revised standards are intended to become the **mandatory baseline** for non-Ind AS companies. The key obligation area is therefore readiness for updated accounting recognition/measurement requirements once NFRA/MCA complete the revision process and the revised standards are formally prescribed.

This consultation paper/report from the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA), Government of India, was issued as a March 2021 Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) report under the title “Enhancing Engagement with Stakeholders,” and it is framed as a consultation document released in June 2021. Its purpose is not to impose a specific new rule immediately, but to recommend how NFRA should interact more effectively with the financial reporting ecosystem—especially auditors, preparers, users of financial statements, regulators, academics, and others—and to strengthen transparency, guidance, enforcement, and communication.

The report explains that financial reporting is viewed as a “supply chain” involving auditors, preparers, users, regulators, academics, and other stakeholders, and it assesses NFRA’s role in each part of that chain. It records stakeholder views gathered through consultation, including expectations that NFRA should be more visible, clarify its scope relative to other regulators, provide timely guidance, use data more effectively, and improve engagement before and after enforcement actions. The report also discusses the Indian accounting and auditing landscape, the need for a clear road map, and the importance of building NFRA’s regulatory capacity and accountability.

The main recommendations are organized around stakeholder engagement, inspection/investigation/enforcement, settlement of disciplinary matters and remediation, communication and advocacy, data dissemination, a road map, regulatory capacity building, decision-making, timely guidance, and audit quality indicators/audit firm evaluation. In practical compliance terms, the document signals an expected shift toward more structured engagement by NFRA, stronger transparency around its decision-making and enforcement approach, and greater emphasis on audit quality measurement and firm-level evaluation. It also specifically points to settlement and remediation mechanisms for disciplinary matters, suggesting that entities subject to NFRA oversight may face not only enforcement but also processes aimed at corrective action and resolution.

No binding deadlines, numeric thresholds, fee rates, or immediate filing obligations are set out in the text provided. Instead, the document should be read as a policy and reform roadmap for NFRA’s future functioning, with implications for any audit firms, companies, auditors, or other market participants that fall within NFRA’s jurisdiction or are affected by its guidance, inspections, investigations, or disciplinary processes. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this report anticipates a more proactive, data-driven, and communication-heavy regulator, so affected entities should be prepared for closer scrutiny, more formalized interaction, and potential future changes in oversight practices.

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued Inspection Report No. 132.2-2024-06 for M/s Walker Chandiok & Co. LLP (WCCL), firm registration no. 001076N/N500013, dated March 27, 2026. The report is an audit quality inspection of the firm’s 2024 audit work and firm-wide quality controls, and it is framed under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013, which empowers NFRA to inspect auditors and assess compliance with applicable auditing and ethical requirements. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this is not a policy change document in the usual rulemaking sense; it is an enforcement/oversight report identifying areas where WCCL’s systems and selected engagement files were found non-compliant or deficient, with observations spanning independence, non-audit services, consultations, monitoring, and audit documentation.

A major focus of the report is independence at the firm level, including WCCL’s position as part of the GTIL network and the relationships between WCCL and Indian GTIL network entities. NFRA also specifically reviews WCCL’s self-regulated embargo in effect since April 1, 2025, and its non-audit services practices, indicating that compliance officers should pay close attention to whether prohibited or restricted services, network relationships, or internal embargo rules are being managed consistently with law and ethics requirements. The report addresses engagement-team independence separately, so compliance controls are expected not only at the firm-wide level but also at the individual audit team level.

The report also examines consultations and monitoring within the firm’s audit quality control system, which means NFRA is testing whether complex or contentious audit issues are escalated and whether internal reviews detect and correct failures. In the detailed engagement-file review, NFRA inspected audits covering revenue, loans and advances, borrowings, property, plant and equipment (PPE), related parties, impairment of investments, going concern, and documentation of material uncertainty related to going concern, across Companies A, B, C, and D. The contents show that NFRA identified “other matters of non-compliances” and an “audit trail issue found in all the selected engagements,” signaling a systemic documentation/control concern rather than an isolated file issue.

For compliance purposes, the report matters because it points to recurring weaknesses in audit evidence, documentation, and quality-control procedures that could affect the defensibility of audit opinions and the firm’s ability to demonstrate compliance with the Act, NFRA requirements, and independence obligations. The report includes WCCL’s response in Appendix A and a chronology of events in Part D, so any remediation program should be mapped against those responses and the timeline NFRA used in reaching its conclusions. A compliance officer should treat the report as a trigger to verify firm-wide independence controls, network-relationship disclosures, non-audit service restrictions, audit-trail retention and completeness, consultation protocols, and engagement-level documentation for high-risk areas such as revenue, going concern, related parties, impairment, and borrowings.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule, set to become effective on December 15, 2026.
rows.desc: At September 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Adopting Amendments to Quality Control Standard WASHINGTON, Sep. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule set to become effective on December 15, 2026. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s event page, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB

rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on August 10, 2026 that Kyle S. Hauptman was sworn in as a Board Member in a ceremony at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He had previously been appointed to the Board by the SEC on January 30, 2026, and his current term is set to expire on October 24, 2029. The announcement is informational rather than a rulemaking or enforcement action: it does not create any new compliance requirements, deadlines, filing obligations, or substantive changes to audit standards in the text provided.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is the personnel change at the PCAOB, which may be relevant because the Board oversees audits of public companies and sets the regulatory direction for the audit profession. Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis stated that Hauptman’s experience would support the PCAOB’s efforts to modernize and strengthen its role over the next 25 years and beyond. Hauptman said he expected to focus in particular on technological changes affecting both the audit industry and the PCAOB itself, which suggests technology-related audit oversight may remain an area of regulatory attention. Prior to joining the PCAOB, he served as Chairman of the National Credit Union Administration, was appointed by President Donald J. Trump and confirmed by the U.S. Senate to the NCUA Board in December 2020, was elevated to NCUA Chairman in January 2025, and previously held roles in Senate policy and the private sector.

rows.title: Advancing its strategic planning process, the PCAOB has requested public input on draft goals and objectives for its 2026-2030 strategic plan.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 2026-006 July 20, 2026 Summary: In early 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (the “Board” or “PCAOB”) initiated a process to develop a new strategic plan. The PCAOB’s 2026-2030 strategic plan (“Plan”) will articulate the organization’s goals and objectives in support of its statutory mission to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. In addition to serving as a five-year roadmap for the organization, the PCAOB’s strategic plan will be used to develop the PCAOB’s budget each year. As a new and initial step in the strategic planning process, on March 31, 2026, the Board requested public comment on the PCAOB’s strategic priorities. The stakeholder feedback received through that process helped to inform the development of the Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives. For the next phase of the strategic planning process, the Board is seeking input regarding PCAOB’s Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives. Additional input from our stakeholders will help the Board and staff further refine the strategic direction, goals and objectives before the final Plan is presented for Board consideration. The Board welcomes and will consider all comments received to inform the continued development of the Plan. All comments will be made public and posted on the PCAOB website. You are encouraged, but not required, to provide your name and professional affiliation. Public Comment: Interested persons may submit written comments to the Board. Comments should be sent by email to comments@pcaobus.org, or through the PCAOB website at www.pcaobus.org. Comments may also be sent to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. All comments should reference the Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and O
rows.summary:
The PCAOB is asking the public to comment on draft goals and objectives for its new 2026–2030 Strategic Plan, which is being developed in 2026 as the Board’s five-year roadmap and as the basis for the PCAOB’s annual budget process. This release is part of a two-step planning process: the Board first sought comments on strategic priorities on March 31, 2026, and says the feedback from that earlier round informed the current draft goals and objectives now open for comment. The stated purpose of the Plan is to support the PCAOB’s statutory mission of protecting investors and furthering the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports.

For compliance teams, this document does not impose new substantive auditing or reporting requirements on registrants or audit firms; rather, it is a public consultation item that may signal future PCAOB priorities and regulatory focus areas. The PCAOB expressly invites stakeholders to provide additional input before it finalizes the Plan, and says that all comments received will be made public and posted on the PCAOB website. Commenters may, but are not required to, include their name and professional affiliation.

Written comments may be submitted by email to comments@pcaobus.org, through the PCAOB website, or by mail to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. Comments should reference “Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives.” The document provided does not state a specific comment deadline in the excerpt shown.

rows.title: On July 20, the PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider requesting public comment on draft goals and objectives for the PCAOB’s 2026-2030 strategic plan.
rows.desc: At July 20 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Requesting Comment on Draft Goals and Objectives for 2026-2030 Strategic Plan WASHINGTON, Jul. 15, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Monday, July 20, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider requesting public comment on draft goals and objectives for the PCAOB’s 2026-2030 strategic plan. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s website, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open meeting on **Monday, July 20, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. ET** to consider whether to **request public comment on draft goals and objectives for its 2026–2030 strategic plan**. This is a planning/consultation action rather than a finalized rule change: the Board is only considering whether to solicit comments on the draft strategic priorities, so no direct compliance obligation, deadline, or substantive new reporting requirement is being imposed yet.

The meeting will be **open to the public** and held in the PCAOB’s **Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC**. Interested parties can also **watch via livestream on the PCAOB’s website**, and the PCAOB said a **recording will be posted after the meeting**.

For compliance teams, the only immediate relevance is that this may be an early signal of future PCAOB strategic priorities and potential downstream audit oversight focus areas affecting **public company audits** and **broker-dealer audits/compliance reports filed under federal securities laws**. The document does not specify any current enforcement action, deadline, threshold, or change to existing audit requirements; it simply announces the Board’s forthcoming discussion about whether to seek public input on its next strategic plan.

rows.title: The PCAOB has announced the members of the Inspections Modernization Council, a resource group composed of outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities.

A resource group composed of outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities, the IMC will provide perspectives to inform the PCAOB’s efforts to modernize its inspection program and thereby improve audit quality. rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on July 9, 2026 the membership of its new Inspections Modernization Council (IMC), a resource group made up of outside stakeholders with an interest in PCAOB inspection activities. The IMC is not described as a rulemaking body, but as an advisory/resource group intended to provide outside perspectives to help the PCAOB modernize its inspection program and, in turn, improve audit quality. The modernization topics the PCAOB says the IMC will help evaluate include producing more useful inspection-report outputs for users, using technology such as automation and artificial intelligence, and shifting inspections toward firms’ systems of quality control.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this announcement signals the PCAOB’s direction of travel rather than an immediate new compliance deadline or filing requirement. The PCAOB is considering inspection-process changes that could affect how audit firms are evaluated and how inspection findings are presented, which may in time change internal quality-control expectations, documentation practices, and technology-related audit oversight. The Board said it received more than 100 applications from across the financial reporting ecosystem and selected the following IMC members: David J. Cohen (Forvis Mazars, LLP), Kyle D. Crockett (Ford Motor Company), Ashley “Ash” Dalnoot (Grant Thornton Advisors LLC), Alicia R. Damley (Aarya Capital), Stacy Hammett (Canadian Public Accountability Board), Angelo Poulikakos (PROTIVITI), Manuel J. Ramirez (RJI International), Jen Sisson (International Corporate Governance Network), Dan G. Sunderland (Northeastern University), Huong Tran (Instacart), Brendan Whalen (S.R. Snodgrass, P.C.), and Lucia M. Wind (Committee of Sponsoring Organizations).

No effective date, compliance deadline, numeric threshold, or mandatory procedure is imposed by this announcement itself. The practical compliance relevance is prospective: firms subject to PCAOB inspections should monitor future PCAOB actions stemming from the IMC, especially any changes tied to inspection reporting, quality-control emphasis, or the use of automation and AI in the inspection process.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.
rows.desc: George Kostolampros Named PCAOB General Counsel WASHINGTON, Jul. 1, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George Kostolampros has been appointed the PCAOB’s General Counsel. As General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel on all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC). “OGC’s work underpins the PCAOB’s ability to execute its mission to protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We are grateful that George is joining us to fill this critical leadership role.” Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience advising organizations and senior leaders on complex legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. Matt Goldin, who was named Acting General Counsel in January 2026, will resume his role as Deputy General Counsel, advising the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assisting with OGC’s management. “Matt is a valued member of the OGC team, and we thank him for his distinguished service as Acting General Counsel,” said Chairman Logothetis.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corp
rows.summary:
The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) announced on July 1, 2026 that George Kostolampros has been appointed General Counsel, replacing the acting arrangement that had been in place since January 2026. In this role, he will provide legal advice and counsel across all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC), which the PCAOB described as central to carrying out its investor-protection mission. For a corporate compliance team, this is primarily a governance/personnel update rather than a new rule or filing requirement: the notice does not impose new obligations, deadlines, thresholds, or substantive compliance changes on registrants or other regulated entities.

The announcement also states that Matt Goldin, who had been Acting General Counsel since January 2026, will return to his prior role as Deputy General Counsel, where he will advise the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assist with OGC management. The PCAOB highlighted Kostolampros’s background as a Venable LLP partner advising public companies, boards, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, as well as his prior service as Senior Counsel in the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. The only date-specific operational point in the release is the transition itself: January 2026 for Goldin’s acting appointment and July 1, 2026 for Kostolampros’s permanent appointment.

There are no statutory, regulatory, or procedural changes described in this document, and no action is required by issuers, audit firms, or other outside parties based solely on this announcement.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on June 29, 2026 that Dr. Ying Li Compton has been appointed Chief Economist and Director of the Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OERA). OERA’s role is to provide independent, evidence-based economic and risk analysis that supports PCAOB oversight work, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews; the announcement is an internal leadership change and does not itself impose a new compliance rule, filing requirement, or deadline on registrants or audit firms. Dr. Compton joins from PwC International Limited, where she was a managing director advising the Global Assurance Leadership Team, and previously served as chief of staff to the PwC US Assurance Leader.

The announcement also notes her prior SEC experience, including service as Senior Accounting and Economic Advisor to the Chief Accountant in the SEC’s Office of the Chief Accountant and earlier as a financial economist in the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis, as well as earlier academic roles at George Washington University and Baruch College and a Ph.D. in accounting from MIT. The PCAOB stated that Dr. Erik Durbin, who had been Acting Chief Economist and Acting OERA Director since December 2025, will return to his prior role as OERA’s Deputy Chief Economist, Economic Analysis, where he is responsible for the processes and teams that develop economic analysis. For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that PCAOB economic/risk analysis leadership has changed, which may affect the analytical framing of future PCAOB inspections, rulemaking, and standard-setting initiatives, but the document itself does not announce any immediate substantive regulatory change.

rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will depart the Board on **July 15, 2026**, after **more than 17 years of service**. She joined the PCAOB in **February 2009** and held several roles before becoming **Chief Auditor in October 2022**, including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor.

For compliance teams, the practical significance is not a new rule in this announcement itself, but the document confirms that the PCAOB is **initiating a search for a replacement Chief Auditor**, so firms should expect continuity in the Office of the Chief Auditor but may see changes in leadership and oversight priorities over time. The notice also highlights several substantive PCAOB initiatives completed or advanced under Vanich’s tenure, especially **QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control**, which the PCAOB **adopted in May 2024** and which is scheduled to become **effective December 15, 2026**. That standard is described as using a **risk-based approach** intended to drive continuous improvement in audit quality, making its effective date a key compliance deadline for affected audit firms.

The announcement also notes that Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, implementation resources for audit firms, the **Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program**, the PCAOB’s **first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting**, and the creation of a **Firm Consultation Process** allowing **registered public accounting firms** to submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. For a corporate compliance team, the main takeaway is to continue monitoring PCAOB communications and implementation guidance, especially as the **December 15, 2026** effective date for **QC 1000** approaches and leadership transitions at the PCAOB may affect timing, interpretation, or outreach related to audit-quality and quality-control requirements.

rows.title: The PCAOB today announced the establishment of a Firm Consultation Process designed to provide timely and consistent guidance from PCAOB staff.
rows.desc: PCAOB Staff Launches Firm Consultation Process to Enhance Clarity and to Support Application and Implementation of PCAOB Standards WASHINGTON, Jun. 25, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced the establishment of a Firm Consultation Process, led by its Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA), designed to provide more timely and consistent guidance from PCAOB staff. The new process will allow registered public accounting firms to submit questions directly to OCA staff and receive informal staff views regarding the implementation of new standards and application of existing standards. “Delivering clear guidance is essential to the PCAOB’s efforts to drive further improvement in audit quality,” said Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “This staff-led consultation process is designed to help firms implement new standards and apply our standards more consistently, which will ultimately fulfill the PCAOB’s mission to protect investors.” As part of the Firm Consultation Process, registered firms may request a consultation with OCA on the interpretation and application of PCAOB auditing, attestation, and quality control standards and related rules and forms, as well as PCAOB standards and rules on ethics and independence. If the firm decides to proceed with a consultation under this new process, a request for consultation should be submitted by completing the Consultation Intake Form. OCA does not plan to make consultation requests public but may publish public guidance for questions that are frequently asked or may be of use more generally.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed p
rows.summary:
On June 25, 2026, the PCAOB announced a new **Firm Consultation Process**, administered by the **Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA)**, to give registered public accounting firms more timely and consistent staff guidance on PCAOB requirements. The process is not a rule change or new substantive audit standard; instead, it creates a formal channel for firms to **submit questions directly to OCA staff** and receive **informal staff views** on the **implementation of new standards** and the **application of existing standards**.  

The consultation process is available only to **registered public accounting firms**, and it covers the interpretation and application of **PCAOB auditing, attestation, and quality control standards**, along with the **related rules and forms**, and the PCAOB’s **ethics and independence standards and rules**. If a firm wants to use the process, it must submit a request by completing the **Consultation Intake Form**. The PCAOB stated that it **does not plan to make consultation requests public**, although it may later issue **public guidance** if questions are commonly asked or broadly useful.  

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that firms now have a more structured mechanism to seek PCAOB staff input before finalizing interpretations or implementation approaches, which may help reduce inconsistency across engagements and support compliance with evolving PCAOB requirements. The announcement does not specify a filing deadline, approval timeline, or mandatory use requirement, and it does not impose a new compliance obligation beyond the submission process if a firm chooses to consult.

rows.title: The PCAOB has launched an open comment period for stakeholders to provide input on its standard-setting and research agendas.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued **Release No. 2026-005 on June 23, 2026** to open a **public comment period** seeking stakeholder input on its **standard-setting and research agendas**. The document does **not** itself adopt a new auditing rule or impose an immediate compliance requirement on registrants or auditors; rather, it asks firms, investors, audit committees, preparers, and other interested parties to comment on **which topics the PCAOB should prioritize** in future standard-setting and research work.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the PCAOB is signaling where future requirements may emerge and is inviting feedback on the most pressing audit-related issues. The agenda discussion specifically highlights **data and technology**, with focused attention on **artificial intelligence** and **digital assets**, indicating these are likely areas of regulatory development or updated guidance. The release also discusses the PCAOB’s **approach to standard setting**, including its **conceptual framework**, its **standard-setting process**, and its consideration of **other standard setters** and **possible alignment with international auditing standards**.

Because this is a request for comment rather than a final standard, the practical obligation is external-facing: organizations that want to influence future PCAOB rulemaking should review the agenda and submit comments during the open comment period. The document’s material significance is that it may foreshadow future auditing standards affecting how audits are performed in technology-heavy areas, especially where AI tools or digital assets are involved, but it does not specify new thresholds, rates, deadlines for compliance, or effective dates for substantive obligations in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George G. Demos as Director of its Division of Enforcement and Investigations.
rows.desc: George G. Demos Named Director of the PCAOB’s Division of Enforcement and Investigations WASHINGTON, Jun. 15, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George G. Demos has been named Director of the PCAOB’s Division of Enforcement and Investigations (DEI). In this role, he will oversee and direct the PCAOB’s investigations and enforcement of violations of its rules, professional standards, and other applicable securities regulations. “Detecting and deterring misconduct is an essential part of how the PCAOB works to improve audit quality and protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “George’s enforcement experience will help the PCAOB advance its goals and fulfill its mission.” Mr. Demos was formerly a litigation partner at DLA Piper LLP, where he represented companies under federal and state investigation and conducted internal corporate reviews. Previously, he served as Senior Counsel at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Enforcement – leading investigations and prosecutions into accounting fraud, insider trading, and market manipulation – and has been an adjunct professor at UC Davis School of Law. Mr. Demos received a B.A. from Columbia University and a J.D. from Fordham University School of Law. “I am thankful for the opportunity to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the exceptional attorneys, accountants, and other experts on the PCAOB’s enforcement staff,” said Mr. Demos. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 11, 2026 Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers summarizes its 2025 oversight of audits of SEC-registered broker-dealers that are required to file audited financial statements with the SEC. The report confirms that the PCAOB has statutory authority over the auditors of these broker-dealers and that its inspection program is intended to promote investor protection and audit quality by evaluating whether PCAOB-registered firms are performing these audits in compliance with applicable standards and rules. This report is issued under PCAOB Rule 4020T, which governs interim inspection reporting for broker-dealer audits.

The document does not announce a new substantive rule change, but it does describe the compliance framework broker-dealers and their auditors operate under. It notes that under Exchange Act Rule 17a-5, SEC-registered broker-dealers generally must file annual financial reports with the SEC, including financial statements subject to audit by a PCAOB-registered firm. The annual report’s stated purpose is to provide information on the PCAOB’s 2025 inspection approach and a summary of inspection observations, which means compliance teams should use it as guidance on areas where auditors were found deficient or where risks were elevated.

The report organizes its findings around 2025 inspection results, selected firms and engagements, and observations from inspections, along with the PCAOB standards and rules associated with those observations. While the excerpt provided does not include the specific deficiencies or statistics, the report signals that broker-dealer audit oversight remains an active compliance focus and that firms auditing broker-dealers should expect PCAOB scrutiny of audit execution, documentation, and conformity with PCAOB standards. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that broker-dealers must continue using qualified PCAOB-registered auditors for their annual audited filings, and those auditors should ensure their broker-dealer audit work is aligned with PCAOB requirements because inspection findings may affect regulatory posture, audit quality assessments, and supervisory expectations.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open Board meeting on **Tuesday, June 9, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET** to consider whether to **issue proposed amendments for public comment** to **QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control**, which is the PCAOB’s quality control standard. rows.summary:

The PCAOB says it is looking for participants with **capital markets expertise** and knowledge of the PCAOB inspection program, and applicants must have a **demonstrated commitment to the interests of investors and the public**.

For compliance teams, the key point is that this announcement signals an upcoming PCAOB effort to gather market input on inspection modernization, which could lead to future changes in inspection methods, expectations, or related oversight practices, although no immediate substantive compliance obligations are imposed by this announcement itself.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued an order on January 13, 2026, imposing sanctions on Zwick CPA, PLLC and its owner Jack Zwick, CPA, based on violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audit of one issuer client’s financial statements. The Board censured both the firm and Zwick and revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, which means the firm cannot continue practicing before the PCAOB as a registered public accounting firm unless it later reapplies and is approved. The order also bars Zwick from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, although he may file a petition for Board consent to re-associate only after three years from the date of the order; similarly, the firm may reapply for registration only after three years from the date of the order.

Financially, the PCAOB imposed a civil money penalty of $50,000, assessed jointly and severally against the firm and Zwick. In addition to the monetary penalty, the firm must complete specified remedial quality-control measures before submitting any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those measures with any such application. Zwick must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education focused on PCAOB auditing standards, on top of any CPE required for his professional license, before he can file any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The sanctions indicate the PCAOB viewed the conduct as serious enough to require not just punishment but pre-clearance remediation and training before either respondent can seek to return to PCAOB-regulated practice.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s December 18, 2025 Order sanctions CPA Jennifer A. Crofoot for violations tied to her work on audits of four issuer clients, and it also addresses quality control failures at her former registered audit firm. The Board censured Crofoot, barred her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education on PCAOB auditing standards before she may seek Board consent to associate with a registered firm again. The document also signals that the disciplinary action is intended to protect investors and the public interest in accurate, independent audit reports, so any registered firm or associated person should view this as an enforcement reminder that audit evidence and quality control failures can trigger both individual sanctions and firm-related scrutiny.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB instituted disciplinary proceedings against TPS Thayer LLC and issued an order on December 4, 2025 censuring the firm, imposing a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requiring contingent remedial actions under Section IV of the order. The sanctions stem from TPS Thayer’s use, in five issuer audits, of audit work performed in a substantial-role capacity by a public accounting firm that was not registered with the PCAOB; the PCAOB found that TPS Thayer did not appropriately plan those audits and did not reasonably supervise the unregistered firm. The order notes that TPS Thayer had filed a Form 1-WD on April 7, 2025 seeking withdrawal from PCAOB registration, and that request would be handled under PCAOB Rule 2107; that withdrawal request is separate from the sanctions in this order.
